The final concern is not imagined embarrassment. Moses knows that a charge lies against him and fears that Pharaoh's people may kill him. The charge refers to the Egyptian who died when Moses intervened in a fight involving an Israelite, an event recounted in 28:15–21. The memory has a legal and political life beyond the original moment. A ruler who wants to silence a messenger can turn an old incident into a reason for execution.

Moses therefore understands the mission at two levels. He may be rejected as a messenger, and he may be attacked as a man with a vulnerable past. Tyranny often combines those tactics. It questions the speaker's character so that the message need not be answered, then uses the accusation to justify force. By mentioning the charge before he goes, Moses shows that he is not confusing faith with a denial of danger.

**A Wrong Act and a Prophetic Mission Must Be Distinguished**

Moses does not present the Egyptian's death as irrelevant. His fear acknowledges that the event has moral and legal weight. Yet a past act does not automatically make every later word false. The question is how the act is understood, repented of, and judged, not whether a servant must remain silent forever after having been in need of forgiveness.

This distinction matters whenever a ruler uses a person's history to avoid the truth of a present claim. Accountability should not be suspended, but neither should accusation become a substitute for examination. Moses will have to answer for what happened while also carrying God's command. The verse allows both facts to stand. A messenger can have a past that requires mercy and still be chosen for a task that confronts injustice.

**Fear of Death Is Not Lack of Faith**

Moses says he fears being killed. The Qur'an records the fear without treating it as cowardice. Human life has value, and a servant may recognize the danger of losing it. Faith does not demand that a person feel no attachment to life or no concern about violent power. It asks him to place that concern before God and to obey when the duty is clear.

The distinction between fear and surrender is important. Fear describes an emotion and an assessment of what may happen. Surrender would be abandoning the command because the danger is unpleasant. Moses has not yet refused to go. He is explaining why he needs support and protection. His prayer shows that courage can consist in moving forward while danger remains visible rather than pretending that danger has ceased to exist.

**An Accusation Can Be Used to Protect Injustice**

A charge against a messenger may be examined fairly, or it may be weaponized by people who benefit from the existing order. Pharaoh's court has an interest in keeping the focus on Moses' past instead of on the enslavement and arrogance that his message will expose. The verse prepares the reader for that shift in argument. A powerful audience may defend itself by putting the speaker on trial before it considers the charge against itself.

The just response is neither blind loyalty to Moses nor automatic trust in Pharaoh. It is moral clarity. The death must be understood in its circumstances, Moses' own acknowledgment must be heard, and Pharaoh's use of the accusation must be judged by what it seeks to conceal. Revelation does not ask the audience to ignore evidence. It asks the audience not to let a real accusation erase a larger truth.

**The Past Follows the Servant Into the Call**

Moses left Egypt because he feared the consequence of the killing. Years later, the mission sends him back toward the same power. The return is not a denial of history; it is the place where history is brought under a new purpose. The man who once fled now approaches with a command from God, still conscious of what happened and still dependent on protection.

This movement teaches that repentance does not always remove every worldly consequence. A forgiven person may still have to face people harmed by his actions or systems that remember them. What changes is the meaning of the encounter and the source of strength with which he meets it. Moses cannot rewrite his past, but he can refuse to let Pharaoh define the rest of his life by it.

**God's Protection Answers the Fear Without Denying It**

The next divine response will answer Moses' concern with reassurance. That answer will not imply that the charge never existed. It will mean that Pharaoh's threat cannot prevent the mission God has ordained. Divine protection often works by placing a servant inside a danger without allowing the danger to determine the final outcome.

Moses' prayer thus models a sound way to speak before God. Name the risk accurately. Do not hide a moral fault or inflate it into a reason for permanent silence. Ask for the protection and assistance that obedience requires. The servant who speaks this way is neither self-justifying nor paralyzed. He is ready to meet a powerful accuser under the judgment of the Lord who knows the whole event.

**A Servant May Need Protection While Telling the Truth**

The existence of a past charge does not make physical safety irrelevant. Moses asks for help because a righteous task can still expose a servant to an unjust response. Some people treat concern for safety as proof that conviction is weak; this verse rejects that measure. Care for life can coexist with readiness to obey, especially when the danger comes from a ruler who can turn law into an instrument of fear.

Protection, however, is not the same as arranging a life with no risk. Moses will have to return to the place from which he fled. The difference is that he will not return on his own terms or in his own strength. He goes under a divine commission, with a companion, and with signs. Courage receives its shape from these means rather than from a denial that death is possible.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:15

> Allah responded, “Certainly not! So go, both of you, with Our signs. We will be with you, listening.

**Expanded Commentary**

**God Answers Fear Before Giving Further Instruction**

The response begins with a firm denial: certainly not. Moses has feared rejection, speech failing, and death, but God does not allow those fears to become the conclusion of the mission. The answer is brief because the servant needs assurance before he needs more detail. Divine reassurance does not argue that the danger is imaginary. It declares that the danger will not defeat the purpose for which Moses is being sent.

The force of the answer also corrects Moses' estimate of what he can carry alone. He had described several weaknesses, and God answers them with a command that includes Aaron. The reassurance is therefore not empty encouragement. It is attached to a changed situation: both brothers will go, and they will go with signs. Fear is met by companionship, evidence, and divine oversight.

**The Plural of Signs Gives the Mission Breadth**

Moses and Aaron are sent with God's signs, not with personal eloquence alone. The plural points to the signs that will support their claim, including the miracles associated with Moses and the public demonstration before Pharaoh. These signs are not tricks designed to win a contest. They are marks that identify the source of the mission and expose the weakness of Pharaoh's claim to ultimate authority.

A sign does not remove the need for speech. It points to the message and gives the audience reason to take the messenger seriously. Moses will still have to state the command and face objections. The combination of sign and word is significant. Evidence without interpretation can be misread, while words without divine support can be dismissed as a private opinion. The mission receives both.

**Aaron's Presence Is Part of the Divine Answer**

God does not tell Moses to overcome every difficulty by an act of solitary will. The two brothers are ordered to go together. That command confirms that Moses' request for Aaron was not a failure of confidence. It was a means God chose to use. A servant may recognize a need for partnership without doubting the Lord who assigned the work.

The shared mission also gives the audience a visible witness to the truth being proclaimed. Pharaoh will not be dealing with a private complaint from one anxious man. Two messengers will stand before him with one source of authority. Their relationship models cooperation rather than rivalry. Prophetic service is strengthened when gifts are joined under a command larger than either individual.

**Being With Them Means Active Oversight**

God says that He will be with them, listening. The phrase does not suggest physical limitation or that God learns facts only by hearing them. It assures Moses that every word spoken and every response given lies within divine knowledge and care. The brothers will not enter the court of Pharaoh unnoticed or unsupported. Their encounter is heard by the Lord who sent them.

That assurance addresses both fear and loneliness. A person speaking before power may feel that the ruler controls the room and that his own words vanish without effect. Divine accompaniment changes that perception. The messengers' speech has an audience beyond Pharaoh's court, and the court's threats are heard by the One who judges it. Moses and Aaron can therefore speak with care without believing that the outcome depends on the ruler's mood.

**Listening Also Honors the Detail of the Encounter**

The mention of listening gives the mission a personal texture. God is not merely issuing a distant order and leaving the servants to improvise. He knows the exchange as it unfolds. This supports the broader Qur'anic teaching that God knows secret speech, public claims, and the inner motives behind them. Pharaoh may stage the encounter for his chiefs, but the true witness is already present.

For the messengers, that knowledge is comfort. For Pharaoh, it is warning. No performance can make oppression righteous, and no accusation can hide the motive behind it. The brothers need not shout to make God hear them, nor flatter Pharaoh to make their words count. They must speak faithfully because the Lord is attentive to every part of the mission.

**Reassurance Leads Immediately to Obedience**

The verse does not end with comfort alone. After denying Moses' fear, God says go. Reassurance is meant to move the servant, not to create a permanent retreat in prayer. The right response to divine support is action under the command that follows.

This pattern offers a general rule for moral work. Bring fear honestly to God, accept the help He provides, and then take the next required step. Do not wait for every uncertainty to disappear. Moses and Aaron are not promised an agreeable Pharaoh or a painless encounter. They are promised signs and divine attention. That is enough to make obedience possible, and the command to go turns that possibility into duty.

**Divine Company Reorders the Meaning of Risk**

The danger before Moses and Aaron does not become small because God is with them. It becomes properly placed. Pharaoh can threaten bodies, reputations, and public standing, but he cannot decide whether the mission is true or whether the Lord hears it. Divine company moves the center of the encounter away from the ruler's power and back to God's authority.

This is why the answer is stronger than a promise of personal success. Success could be measured by Pharaoh's surrender, while divine companionship remains true even when a ruler resists. The brothers are sent to testify, not to control the response. They can therefore speak with courage, accept the limits of their role, and leave the final judgment to the Lord whose signs accompany them.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:16

> Go to Pharaoh and say, ‘We are messengers from the Lord of all worlds,

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mission Requires a Direct Audience**

Moses and Aaron are told to go to Pharaoh and speak to him. The command does not allow them to keep the message at the level of private advice or indirect criticism. Pharaoh's power governs the order that has harmed the Children of Israel, so the ruler must hear the claim that stands above his rule. This directness is not a license for rudeness. It is clarity about where responsibility is concentrated.

The plural pronoun in we are messengers also matters. Moses is not presenting himself as a solitary reformer with a personal program. Aaron stands with him, and both are servants of a Sender. Their authority is derived, not self-created. They do not ask Pharaoh to admire their personalities or accept a new political faction. They carry a command from the Lord who owns authority over Pharaoh and over those Pharaoh has oppressed.

**Lord of All Worlds Leaves No Space for Rival Lordship**

The title Lord of all worlds, Rabb al-ʿālamīn, is a universal claim. It reaches beyond one nation, dynasty, or sacred geography. A lord gives existence, sustains it, and has the right to command it. If God is Lord of all worlds, Pharaoh cannot be ultimate lord of Egypt, and no ruler can turn a portion of creation into a private domain beyond divine judgment.

The claim therefore challenges Pharaoh before the details of the demand are stated. Moses does not begin by bargaining over labor, taxes, or royal custom. He names the source of the order that will judge those arrangements. Political injustice is not merely a failure of administration. It is rebellion against the Lord whose care extends to every people, including those whom the court treats as property.

**Messengers Speak Under One Authority**

Calling themselves messengers establishes a relationship among three parties: the Sender, the messengers, and the ruler who must hear. The messengers are not equal to God, and they are not petitioners begging Pharaoh to grant them credibility. Their role is to deliver what they have been given. That role requires accuracy and humility at once. They cannot change the command to make it easier, and they cannot claim independent power when challenged.

The shared title also protects the audience from treating the brothers as rivals. The two voices have one source and one purpose. Their agreement is not the product of political coordination alone; it is part of the sign that the mission is ordered by God. When the ruler addresses them, he is not free to divide them by flattering one or accusing the other. Their authority rests outside his court.

**A Universal Lord Can Address a Particular Tyrant**

The phrase Lord of all worlds may sound broad compared with the immediate audience, but its breadth explains why Pharaoh must be addressed. Universal sovereignty does not remain an idea above history. It enters a particular court, names a particular wrong, and commands a particular ruler to stop. God's care for every world includes attention to the people whose names Pharaoh's system tries to erase.

This movement from universal to particular is a mark of sound religious reasoning. It is easy to praise a universal God while leaving local injustice untouched. Moses' message prevents that escape. The One who sustains the heavens also sees forced labor, abuse of power, and the fear of a vulnerable people. Worship that never reaches the treatment of others has not yet understood the Lord of all worlds.

**The Wording Refuses a Bargain With Power**

Moses is not told to ask Pharaoh whether he will permit a harmless religious gathering. The message begins with the authority of the Sender, which means Pharaoh must reconsider his own position. A tyrant can negotiate with another human institution, but he cannot place God on the list of parties whose permission he may grant or withhold.

That does not remove the need for wisdom. The messengers will speak in a court where a careless word can be used against them. Wisdom, however, serves truth rather than disguising it. The direct address keeps the mission from becoming a compromise in which the oppressed receive a small concession while the structure of domination remains untouched.

**The Command Is Public Before It Is Victorious**

No promise of Pharaoh's immediate acceptance is attached to the instruction. The messengers are simply told what to say. This makes the moment a test of obedience before it becomes a story of outcome. The truth must be placed before power even when power appears able to reject it.

The verse thus prepares the confrontation in the right order. First comes the Sender's authority, then the messengers' delivery, and only afterward the ruler's response. Pharaoh may answer with ridicule or accusation, but his response cannot change the source of the claim. Moses and Aaron enter his court carrying a universal lordship into a local tyranny.

**The Opening Sentence Sets a Rule for Confrontation**

A messenger may address power firmly without pretending to possess power. Moses and Aaron identify the Lord, identify themselves as sent, and leave the ruler no excuse for mistaking the source of the claim. This is disciplined confrontation. It avoids both flattery, which would sell the message for access, and vanity, which would make the messenger's personality the center.

The rule is useful whenever truth must enter a hostile institution. State the authority that governs the matter, speak to the person who can act, and keep the demand tied to the wrong being done. The messengers do not threaten Pharaoh with a rival throne. They announce that every throne already stands beneath the Lord of all worlds.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:17

> ˹commanded to say:˺ ‘Let the Children of Israel go with us.’’”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Universal Claim Reaches the Enslaved**

The command now gives the first concrete consequence of God's lordship: Pharaoh must let the Children of Israel go with the messengers. The demand is not an abstract dispute about names. It concerns people held under a power that treats them as a resource. Divine sovereignty becomes visible in the release of those whom an earthly ruler has claimed as his own.

The phrase with us indicates movement out of Pharaoh's control. Moses and Aaron are not asking to become privileged intermediaries within the same system. They are calling for the community's departure from the arrangement that has confined it. The destination is not developed in this verse; the immediate point is that Pharaoh has no rightful ownership of the Israelites. A human ruler cannot convert a people created by God into permanent property.

**Letting Go Means Ending a Claim of Ownership**

The Arabic command has the sense of sending away or releasing. It is therefore stronger than a request for a holiday or a temporary suspension of labor. Pharaoh must relinquish his hold. The demand exposes the moral meaning of the political order: its power depends on refusing the Israelites the freedom to leave and to serve the Lord outside Pharaoh's control.

That is why the order is placed in the mouth of messengers. Liberation is not presented as a favor that a benevolent ruler may grant when convenient. It is a right grounded in God's authority. A ruler can exercise stewardship over a people only within justice; he cannot claim a people against their Creator. When power refuses release, it reveals that it has confused guardianship with possession.

**The Message Joins Worship and Social Freedom**

The demand to let Israel go is not separate from the proclamation of the Lord of all worlds. Worship and freedom belong together because the tyrant's control is also a claim over whom the people may obey. Pharaoh has made the Israelites serve his order; Moses calls them out so that their relation to God is no longer mediated by a ruler who oppresses them.

This does not mean that every political demand can be baptized as revelation. The verse is tied to a specific divine command and a specific wrong. It does show that devotion to God cannot be used to excuse the domination of human beings. When a religious claim leaves the enslaved in the hands of a ruler who treats them as disposable, it has failed to hear the practical meaning of God's lordship.

**Release Must Include the Whole Community**

The wording names the Children of Israel as a people rather than selecting a few acceptable individuals. Pharaoh cannot answer by releasing only the most useful, respectable, or least troublesome members. A community held under oppression is not liberated when the ruler chooses which families count as human enough to leave.

The collective name also protects memory. The Israelites have a history, kinship, and identity that precede Pharaoh's policy. Oppression often tries to rename its victims according to their labor or legal status. The command restores the name of the people and places their future under God's care. They are not merely workers being transferred between owners. They are a community whom the Lord addresses through His messengers.

**The Messengers Ask for Action, Not Sympathy**

Pharaoh might express concern, promise better treatment, or accuse the Israelites of disloyalty while leaving the structure intact. The command prevents such substitutions. Let them go is measurable. It requires a change in who controls their movement and labor. A ruler cannot answer a demand for justice with a speech about his good intentions.

This practical quality gives the mission its seriousness. Moses and Aaron must state a request that can be obeyed or refused in the public world. Their message will not be reduced to an inward comfort for the oppressed while oppression continues. The Lord of all worlds claims the right to alter the arrangement that keeps the people captive.

**Freedom Has a Direction Beyond Escape**

Release is not the final meaning of the command, but it is its necessary beginning. A people cannot freely obey God while a tyrant insists that their bodies, time, and worship belong to him. The verse therefore starts with removal from wrongful control. It does not yet describe every responsibility that follows freedom, and it should not be stretched to answer questions assigned to later verses.

What it establishes is enough: God's messenger must confront the ruler with the demand that the Israelites be released. The oppressed are not forgotten in the grandeur of theology. They stand at the center of the first practical command given to Pharaoh, and their freedom becomes evidence that divine lordship is not an empty title.

**Release Is a Test of Pharaoh's Claim to Rule**

A ruler who truly governs for justice should be able to release people whose captivity has no rightful basis. Pharaoh's resistance will show that his authority depends on treating a people as an instrument rather than as human beings under God. The request therefore tests more than his temper. It exposes what his kingdom is built to preserve.

The command also gives the oppressed a place in the public speech of revelation. They are not an afterthought added once theology has been settled. Their condition is one of the first matters through which God's lordship is declared. A claim about the Lord of all worlds must reach the bodies, families, labor, and future of those held under another man's power.

That is why the order remains concrete. Justice is not complete when a ruler admits a principle while keeping the captive under his hand. The hand must open, and the people must be allowed to move.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:18

> Pharaoh protested, “Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed several years of your life in our care?

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Answers a Divine Claim With a Personal Account**

Pharaoh does not begin by answering the title Lord of all worlds or the demand concerning the Israelites. He turns to Moses' childhood. His question presents the ruler's household as the place that raised and protected the man now standing before him. The tactic is personal and political at once. If Moses can be made to feel indebted, Pharaoh may avoid answering the charge brought against the state.

The account has a factual basis. Other passages describe Moses being taken into Pharaoh's household after infancy and growing under the protection of the palace. Yet a true fact can be used to draw a false conclusion. Care received during childhood does not give a ruler ownership of the adult conscience, and a household's role in preserving a child's life does not turn the child into an eternal subject of its benefactor.

**Upbringing Is Not a Permanent Title Over the Adult**

Pharaoh's wording treats years in his environment as though they settled Moses' allegiance forever. That assumption confuses nurture with lordship. A child depends on adults, but dependence in childhood does not erase the Creator's claim over the person who grows. Moses can acknowledge what occurred without accepting Pharaoh's conclusion about whom he must obey.

The issue appears in many forms of power. A patron may say that education, employment, shelter, or protection gives him the right to command every later choice. Gratitude then becomes a chain. Islam recognizes genuine obligations to parents and benefactors, but no created being may demand obedience in wrongdoing or worship. Pharaoh's argument fails because a past benefit cannot authorize present injustice.

**The Palace's Care Does Not Erase the Israelites' Suffering**

Pharaoh speaks of Moses' years in the household while the larger community suffers under Pharaoh's rule. That contrast exposes the narrowness of his moral accounting. He remembers what the palace gave one child and ignores what the regime took from a people. Personal favor becomes a screen behind which public oppression disappears.

A just judgment must hold both scales together. Moses' experience of protection may be real, and the Israelites' experience of domination may be real. One does not cancel the other. A ruler cannot point to a private act of kindness as proof that his system is righteous. Mercy toward one person can coexist with injustice toward many, and the injustice still demands an answer.

**The Question Is Designed to Shame the Messenger**

Pharaoh's words carry an accusation beneath their surface: after everything done for you, how can you oppose us? Shame is an efficient instrument of control because it turns the victim's attention toward his own gratitude and away from the wrong being named. Moses is invited to defend his personal history instead of demanding the release of the Israelites.

The tactic also seeks to isolate him from the people he represents. If he can be portrayed as a palace dependent who has betrayed his benefactors, his message will look like ingratitude rather than justice. The verse prepares the reader to see how power changes the subject of a conversation. A ruler who cannot answer the demand may accuse the messenger of having no right to make it.

**The Years Are Mentioned as a Claim of Possession**

The reference to several years emphasizes duration. Pharaoh does not say that Moses once passed through the palace; he stresses the length of his stay as though time itself creates ownership. But duration does not convert a created relationship into sovereignty. The Lord's claim is prior to Pharaoh's and extends over every stage of Moses' life, including the years when he was under royal care.

This is one reason the verse uses a question rather than a statement. Pharaoh is trying to make his interpretation sound self-evident: we raised you, therefore you owe us silence. The question invites the court to accept the conclusion before examining it. Moses will have to answer not only the facts but the moral meaning Pharaoh assigns to them.

**A Ruler Can Remember a Benefit Selectively**

Pharaoh remembers the palace's care because that memory serves his authority. He does not begin with the policy that made Moses' people vulnerable or with the violence that shaped Moses' early life. Selective memory is part of political rhetoric. A regime tells the story in which it is the generous parent and omits the story in which it is the oppressor.

The verse teaches a careful response to such rhetoric. Do not deny a benefit merely because the benefactor is unjust, but do not let the benefit silence the truth about injustice. Gratitude must be ordered by God. Moses can recognize the history of his upbringing and still stand for the people whose freedom Pharaoh denies. The next accusation will try to deepen the pressure by presenting his past action as proof that he has become ungrateful.

**Care Must Be Measured Against the Whole Record**

Pharaoh's question invites the court to remember only the palace's generosity. A just listener must ask what kind of care was offered, to whom, and at what cost to others. A household can shelter one child while a government harms a whole people. The good received by Moses should be acknowledged, but it cannot be used to make the wider record disappear.

This is a safeguard against emotional blackmail. Gratitude is a noble response when it leads a person to thank God and treat the benefactor fairly. It becomes corruption when it demands silence about victims. Moses' answer will have to hold gratitude, accountability, and present duty in their proper order. Pharaoh's memory is selective; divine judgment is not.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:19

> Then you did what you did, being ˹utterly˺ ungrateful!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Turns Moses' Past Into a Weapon**

The phrase what you did leaves the deed unnamed in the immediate speech. Everyone in the court is expected to know the incident: Moses struck an Egyptian during a quarrel, and the man died. By using a vague reference, Pharaoh can invoke the shame of the event without giving the circumstances a fair hearing. The omission is rhetorical. It lets the ruler control the frame and makes the accusation sound larger than the facts he is willing to state.

Pharaoh then calls Moses an ingrate. The Arabic word kāfir can mean one who covers or denies, and in this setting it can describe someone who refuses to acknowledge a benefit received. It need not mean that Pharaoh is carefully making a theological judgment about Moses' belief. He is claiming that palace care created a debt and that Moses repaid it with rebellion. The charge is designed to make the messenger look morally disqualified before he speaks.

**A Past Wrong Must Be Faced, Not Exploited**

Moses is not presented as having no history of error. The event in 28:15–21 was serious, and his later response shows awareness that he had wronged himself. A truthful account does not erase the deed to protect a respected servant. At the same time, acknowledging a wrong does not require accepting Pharaoh's use of it as a reason to preserve oppression.

This distinction is central to justice. An accuser may identify a real fault and still use it dishonestly. The validity of the charge must be separated from the purpose for which it is raised. Pharaoh wants the court to discuss Moses' past so that no one discusses the Israelites' present condition. A just listener examines both: what Moses did, and what Pharaoh is doing now.

**Ingratitude Is Defined by Pharaoh's Power**

Pharaoh's accusation assumes that anyone raised within the royal order owes loyalty to that order, even when the order harms others. Under that definition, leaving oppression is betrayal and exposing injustice is ingratitude. The charge reveals the ruler's idea of gratitude: benefits received from the palace must be repaid through obedience to the palace's interests.

The Qur'anic moral order is different. Gratitude is owed to God first, and gratitude to people cannot require complicity in wrongdoing. A person should recognize genuine help, but he may not turn that recognition into worship of a benefactor or permission for harm. Pharaoh's language becomes a test. Will Moses accept a human ruler's definition of gratitude, or will he measure gratitude by truth and justice?

**The Unnamed Deed Keeps the Court From Context**

A full account would include the fight, Moses' intention to help an Israelite, the accidental force that killed the Egyptian, and his flight when the danger became known. Pharaoh's compressed phrase suppresses those details. It does not necessarily make the event harmless, but it prevents the court from asking what actually happened and what Moses understood afterward.

This is a common feature of propaganda. A complex event is reduced to a label that can be repeated whenever the speaker needs to be discredited. Once the label becomes familiar, the audience may feel that investigation is unnecessary. The verse exposes that method by allowing us to hear the accusation in its stripped form. The reader is prepared to distrust a charge whose power depends on leaving its context hidden.

**A Benefactor Cannot Purchase the Conscience**

Even if Pharaoh's household did preserve Moses and provide years of care, the benefit would not give the ruler ownership of his conscience. A benefactor may be thanked, repaid, or honored within the limits of justice. He may not demand that the recipient call oppression good. The more powerful the benefactor, the more carefully this boundary must be guarded, because dependence can make gratitude feel like a command.

Moses' position is especially difficult because Pharaoh's court can combine the language of family with the threat of law. The ruler presents himself as a guardian while holding the power to punish. That mixture creates a debt that cannot be freely answered. The verse shows how tyranny speaks: it calls control care and calls resistance ingratitude.

**The Accusation Does Not Answer the Mission**

Pharaoh has not yet answered the claim that God is Lord of all worlds or the demand that the Israelites be released. He has changed the subject to Moses' childhood and deed. That shift is itself evidence of weakness in the argument. A ruler may have a legitimate question about Moses' past, but he still must answer the substance of the message.

The verse therefore teaches a rule for public reasoning. Do not let a speaker's flaw become a reason to ignore a true claim, and do not defend a true claim by denying the flaw. Hold both matters in their proper place. Moses' history can be judged by God, while Pharaoh's system must be judged for its treatment of the Israelites. Personal accusation cannot make injustice righteous.

**The Charge Invites a Better Kind of Repentance**

Pharaoh intends the accusation to end Moses' authority, but the remembered deed can also show why a messenger needs mercy. Moses is not a prophet because he has never needed forgiveness. He is a servant whom God has guided after a past mistake and entrusted with a task. That fact gives hope to people whose histories include real wrongs, while preserving the seriousness of repentance.

A repentant person should not use forgiveness as a reason to deny what happened. Nor should an accuser use the past to deny the possibility of moral change. Pharaoh does the latter. His charge freezes Moses in one deed so that the ruler need not face the new obedience God has placed before him.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:20

> Moses replied, “I did it then, lacking guidance.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Moses Answers Without Denying the Deed**

Moses does not pretend that Pharaoh has invented the incident. He says that he did it. The admission is brief, but it prevents the defense from becoming a contest of propaganda. A servant of God does not need to protect his reputation by calling a known wrong something else. Truth begins with refusing to falsify the past.

At the same time, the response does not accept Pharaoh's entire interpretation. Moses does not say that the deed proves he is an ingrate or that the palace owns his future. He separates the fact of the act from the accusation built around it. This is a model of moral speech: confess what happened, reject the unjust conclusion drawn from it, and leave the matter under God's judgment rather than hiding it behind clever language.

**Lacking Guidance Describes a Moment of Error**

The translation's lacking guidance renders a phrase that can also be understood as being among those who were astray or not yet guided to the right course. Moses is not claiming that he deliberately chose disbelief. The setting in 28:15–16 indicates a moment in which he acted under confusion and then recognized the need for forgiveness. The wording presents the deed as an error of judgment before prophetic guidance had been given to him.

This nuance matters. Human beings can be wrong without every wrong being the same kind of rejection of truth. A person may act impulsively, misunderstand a situation, or intervene with an effect he did not intend. Such distinctions do not remove responsibility. They make responsibility more accurate. Moses' answer neither glorifies the act nor accepts Pharaoh's attempt to define his whole character by it.

**A Confession Can Be Stronger Than a Denial**

Pharaoh expects the charge to make Moses defensive. Moses instead uses a plain admission. Confession takes away the ruler's power to reveal the deed as though it were a secret discovery. It also prevents the mission from resting on a false image of the messenger. Divine truth does not need a servant who appears never to have erred; it needs a servant who speaks honestly about error and obeys after it.

That strength should not be confused with carelessness about sin. Admission is not an excuse. Moses does not say that the Egyptian's death was irrelevant because his intention was good. He acknowledges a state of lacking guidance and allows the event to stand as a matter that required divine mercy. His honesty is therefore joined to humility, not to self-congratulation.

**The Reply Refuses Pharaoh's Moral Trap**

Pharaoh has tried to force Moses into one of two positions: deny the deed and look dishonest, or accept the label of ungrateful rebel and surrender the mission. Moses chooses neither. He admits the past while refusing to let the ruler's language control its meaning. The deed was an error; it was not a license for Pharaoh to enslave a people or to claim lordship over God's messenger.

This is how a person should answer a manipulative accusation. Do not deny a real wrong merely because an enemy mentions it. Do not accept a false conclusion merely because it is attached to a true fact. Examine the connection between the fact and the judgment. Pharaoh's care of Moses, Moses' past act, and the Israelites' oppression are related in the ruler's speech, but they do not form the moral chain he claims.

**The Past Does Not Exhaust a Person's Present Duty**

Moses' phrase then marks a time: I did it then. The word does not erase continuity, but it distinguishes the earlier act from the present commission. A person is responsible for what he has done, yet repentance and divine guidance can make the later self answerable for a new course. If no change were possible, confession would have no purpose and guidance would be only a label for the already perfect.

The Qur'an frequently places human beings between past error and present return. Moses' history is especially important because he will confront a ruler who wants to freeze him in that history. The verse protects the possibility of transformation without offering cheap absolution. The old act remains part of the record; it no longer has the right to dictate the servant's obedience to God.

**Guidance Is Needed Before Power Can Be Used Well**

Moses had strength and a sense of justice before this encounter, but strength without guidance led to a disastrous result. The phrase therefore carries a lesson about good intentions. Wanting to defend the oppressed does not guarantee that one's action will be wise or proportionate. Moral energy needs knowledge, restraint, and direction from God.

That lesson applies beyond the palace. A person may oppose wrong and still cause new harm if he acts through anger or confusion. The answer is not indifference to injustice. It is the discipline of seeking guidance before acting and returning in repentance when action goes wrong. Moses' admission gives the mission a foundation more reliable than confidence in his own instincts.

**A Prophet's Authority Comes After Humble Correction**

Moses' admission also answers the idea that prophets must have a past untouched by human weakness. The Qur'an presents his authority as a gift and a commission, not as a reward for self-made perfection. His history magnifies the role of God's guidance. The messenger speaks truly because God has sent him, while his earlier error remains a reminder that he is a servant and not a second lord.

This humility will keep the coming confrontation from becoming a personal quarrel between two proud men. Pharaoh wants to make it about gratitude to the palace. Moses' answer returns it to the deeper matter: a human being once acted without right guidance, and God now commands him to speak for justice. The admission is the first step in refusing Pharaoh's frame.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:21

> So I fled from you when I feared you. Then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Moses Answers the Threat With a Plain History**

Moses does not deny that he fled. He names fear of Pharaoh as the reason. The admission is important because Pharaoh has tried to turn the past into a weapon. Moses refuses both concealment and exaggeration. He left the reach of the court because he feared that the ruler would kill him, and that flight became the setting in which God prepared him for a different return.

The flight was not a celebration of fear or a permanent rejection of responsibility. It was a human response to an immediate threat. The fuller account in 28:21–22 describes Moses leaving Egypt in fear and then turning toward Midian while asking God for right direction. That detail keeps the event within a moral journey. Moses leaves danger, but he does not leave God. His movement away from Pharaoh becomes movement toward dependence.

**Flight Can Be Protection Before It Becomes Preparation**

A person may need to leave a place where a powerful wrongdoer can harm him. Such departure is not automatically cowardice or betrayal. Moses' flight preserves his life at a time when he is not yet equipped to confront the court. The same God who later commands him to return first allows a period outside Egypt. Protection and mission are not opposites; protection can be part of how a mission is made possible.

This point corrects a harsh idea of courage. Courage does not require a person to remain in every danger simply to prove sincerity. Wisdom may require withdrawal, patience, and a change of setting. The question is what the departure serves. Moses does not flee to build a private life free of obligation. He flees, receives formation, and is eventually sent back with a clearer commission.

**Ḥukm Names a Gift Beyond Mere Information**

Moses says that his Lord granted him ḥukm. The word can mean judgment, sound decision, authority to judge, wisdom, or understanding. Commentators differed because the term has a wide field of meaning. Some connected it with prophethood or authority, while others understood it as intelligence and the ability to judge rightly. Since the verse separately says that Moses was placed among the messengers, the narrower sense of practical wisdom and sound judgment is stronger here.

That gift answers the weakness exposed by the earlier deed. Moses had acted without proper guidance; now God gives him a capacity to distinguish, weigh, and decide. Wisdom is not merely an increase in facts. It is the ability to put facts, motives, timing, and consequences in their right relation. A messenger needs revelation, but he also needs judgment in delivering it to frightened people and confronting a ruler who turns every word into a weapon.

**The Years Away Are Not Empty Years**

The verse compresses the period between flight and return into one divine act: my Lord granted me wisdom. Exile can look like lost time when it is measured only by public achievement. Moses is not standing before Pharaoh during these years, but he is not outside God's care. The hidden period changes the man who will later stand in the court.

Waiting can expose habits that public success conceals. Away from the palace, Moses must live without the authority of his childhood environment and without the certainty that he will ever return. Such a life can teach humility, patience, and dependence. The verse does not romanticize exile or say that every hardship automatically produces wisdom. It asserts that God used this interval to give Moses what the mission required.

**Messengerhood Is a New Placement, Not Self-Appointment**

The final clause distinguishes wisdom from messengership. Moses was granted an inward gift and then placed among the messengers by God. He did not infer that personal intelligence entitled him to speak for the Lord. Authority came through divine selection. This protects the message from becoming a philosophy invented by a gifted man with a painful past.

The wording also gives Moses a new identity without erasing the old facts. He remains the man who fled, the man who acted without guidance, and the man who lived away from Egypt. Yet God now places him in a company whose task is to warn and deliver. Repentance and formation do not create a false past; they create a faithful present. Pharaoh wants to keep Moses in the category of fugitive and ingrate. God names him among the messengers.

**The Return Carries Both Memory and Guidance**

Moses' answer is strong because it neither boasts of transformation nor uses transformation to deny responsibility. He remembers the fear that drove him away, the wisdom God gave him, and the commission that now brings him back. Each part matters. Memory prevents pride, wisdom prevents reckless action, and messengership prevents the past from becoming a permanent sentence.

Anyone who has left a harmful situation can recognize the shape of this answer. Departure may protect life; a period of learning may repair judgment; a later return may serve a purpose larger than personal vindication. The return is not powered by confidence in Moses' own history. It is powered by the Lord who turned a flight into preparation and a prepared servant into a messenger.

**Wisdom Gives the Return Its Proper Measure**

Moses does not return to settle a personal score with Pharaoh. The gift of ḥukm teaches him to distinguish vindication from obedience. A person shaped only by anger might return to punish the ruler who frightened him. A person shaped by wisdom returns because God has commanded a message that concerns more than his own injury. The same past that could feed resentment becomes material for a carefully judged mission.

This is why the verse places wisdom between flight and messengership. Moses' courage is not the raw courage of a man who has forgotten danger. It is the settled courage of one who has learned what danger means and where authority lies. He remembers Pharaoh's threat without allowing Pharaoh to define the next act. God has changed the meaning of the return by giving the servant judgment before giving him the public confrontation.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:22

> How can that be a ‘favour,’ of which you remind me, when ˹it was only because˺ you ˹have˺ enslaved the Children of Israel?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Moses Rejects a Benefit Built Beside Oppression**

Pharaoh has presented Moses' upbringing as a favor that should purchase loyalty. Moses answers by exposing the moral cost hidden behind that claim. How can the palace's care for one child be called a favor when the same ruler has enslaved an entire people? The question does not deny that Moses received shelter or food. It denies that those private benefits can be weighed without the public wrong that made Pharaoh's rule what it was.

The contrast is deliberate. Pharaoh remembers the years he gave Moses; Moses remembers the Israelites whom Pharaoh held. One view narrows gratitude to a personal relationship with the ruler. The other asks how a ruler treats a whole community. Justice requires the wider view. A kindness toward an individual cannot cleanse a system that degrades many others.

**Mann Can Become a Debt Used for Control**

The verb translated remind has a broad Arabic range. Mann can mean to give a benefit, to count or recount it, and to press it upon the recipient as a reason for submission. The last sense is especially sharp here. Pharaoh is not simply recalling history. He is counting the favor in public so that Moses will feel indebted and the court will see his opposition as betrayal.

That is how benefaction becomes political control. The ruler gives something, records it, and later demands a return far beyond what was given. Gratitude is transformed into silence about wrongdoing. The Qur'an warns elsewhere against charity spoiled by reminders and injury, and the same moral danger appears in Pharaoh's speech. A gift ceases to be generous when it is used to own the conscience of the person who received it.

**A Private Benefit Cannot Cancel a Public Crime**

Pharaoh's argument would be persuasive only if personal care erased communal harm. It does not. Moses can acknowledge that he grew up in the palace and still say that the palace's rule was unjust. These truths do not contradict each other. The household may have preserved one child's life while the state oppressed the Children of Israel. Both facts must be judged, not forced into a single flattering story.

This principle applies to every institution that points to its good works while asking people to ignore its injuries. A government may build roads and still persecute a minority. An employer may offer benefits and still exploit workers. A family may provide care and still demand complicity in abuse. Good received should be recognized, but it cannot purchase permission to call evil good. Moses' question restores the victims to a discussion that Pharaoh tried to make personal.

**The Enslaved Are the Measure of the Ruler's Claim**

Pharaoh's title to gratitude is tested by the condition of the Israelites. If he were a just guardian, their safety and freedom would be part of the evidence for his rule. Instead, their enslavement reveals that the palace's language of care is selective. A ruler can call himself beneficent while the people outside his household bear the cost of his power.

Moses therefore refuses to let the court define blessing by proximity to privilege. The palace may feel generous to the person inside it, but a society must be judged from the position of those made vulnerable by its order. This is not envy of legitimate care. It is the demand that care be extended according to justice rather than reserved for the ruler's chosen dependents.

**Gratitude Belongs Under God's Moral Order**

Moses' reply does not teach people to despise every favor or to deny the good done by others. It teaches that gratitude has a limit set by God. A created benefactor may be thanked, but he cannot demand obedience in oppression. The first debt is to the Creator, and that debt includes refusing to help a human being violate the rights of another.

This order protects both gratitude and freedom. Without gratitude, people become arrogant and forget the help through which their lives were sustained. Without moral limits, gratitude becomes servitude. Pharaoh wants the second condition: he wants Moses to treat a palace upbringing as a title over his conscience. Moses' answer says that no human favor can make slavery just.

**The Question Exposes the Ruler's Evasion**

Pharaoh's words were meant to shift attention from the Israelites to Moses' childhood. Moses returns the focus to the very people whose condition prompted the mission. He does not allow the court to decide that the messenger's personal history is the only matter worth hearing. The question about a favor is therefore also a question about political accountability: what is the value of a ruler's kindness if his rule is built on another people's suffering?

The answer is not that every good act becomes worthless because the actor has done evil. It is that good acts cannot be used as a shield against judgment. Pharaoh may have cared for Moses in one setting and oppressed Israel in another. The Lord judges the whole pattern. Moses' sentence keeps the whole pattern in view.

**A Ruler Cannot Make Oppression Look Like Generosity**

The most dangerous feature of Pharaoh's argument is its change of names. He calls control a favor, obligation a debt, and resistance ingratitude. Moses refuses those substitutions. Naming matters because a community can be trained to accept injustice when the language around it is softened. Enslavement remains enslavement even when the ruler points to a benefit he once gave.

The verse thus gives the oppressed a vocabulary with which to answer power. Do not allow a selective kindness to erase a whole people's suffering. Do not let a benefactor's reminder become a command to abandon truth. Gratitude can be sincere only when it remains inside justice, and justice begins by refusing to make another person's captivity the price of one's comfort.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:23

> Pharaoh asked, “And what is ‘the Lord of all worlds’?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Turns a Universal Claim Into a Challenge**

Pharaoh's question comes after Moses has invoked the Lord of all worlds. On the surface, it asks for clarification. In context, it also tests whether the messenger's Lord can be made to appear vague, distant, or irrelevant to Egyptian power. The title has already placed Pharaoh under a higher authority, so the question is not harmless curiosity. It is a challenge to the source of the command that he release the Israelites.

The expression Rabb al-ʿālamīn carries more than the idea of a creator who began the universe and then withdrew. Rabb includes the one who owns, sustains, orders, and brings a thing toward its proper state. The worlds are all created realms, not only one nation or one court. Pharaoh asks what this title means because accepting its scope would unsettle his own claim to rule.

**The Question May Be Sincere in Form but Hostile in Purpose**

Exegetes differed over Pharaoh's intention. Some treated the question as a request for the essence or exact nature of God. Others held that Pharaoh already understood enough to know that Moses was challenging his authority, and that he asked only to mock or provoke. The immediate setting supports the second reading more strongly. A ruler who presents himself as supreme is not approaching the title as a humble seeker; he is putting the messenger on trial before his court.

That judgment does not require claiming that Pharaoh had no knowledge of God at all. A person can recognize a claim's force and still resist its authority. Questions can seek understanding, or they can delay obedience by demanding a definition that the questioner has no intention of accepting. Moses' mission exposes the difference between the sound of inquiry and the purpose behind it.

**Rabb Is a Relational Title**

The question also reveals how Pharaoh wants God to be imagined. If the Lord is treated as an abstract object that must be captured in a formula before He can be obeyed, the ruler can keep control while the debate continues. Rabb points in another direction. It names the One whose relation to creation is shown through sustaining, ordering, and judging it. Knowledge of God begins with recognizing what He does and what His lordship requires, not with pretending that the human mind can contain His essence.

This is why the title is especially threatening to tyranny. A ruler can claim mastery over a limited territory, but he cannot be lord in the full sense. His power is received, bounded, and temporary. The title Lord of all worlds removes the possibility that Pharaoh's realm is a closed moral universe in which his word is final.

**A Demand for Definition Can Hide a Refusal to Submit**

There is a legitimate place for questions about divine names and attributes. Revelation itself teaches people how to speak about God and how to avoid comparing Him with creation. But a demand for exhaustive definition can become a tactic for postponing the obvious. Pharaoh does not ask what the title changes in his conduct. He asks what it is as if the messenger must satisfy a hostile court before the court will consider freeing the enslaved.

The difference between inquiry and evasion lies in what follows the answer. A sincere questioner is willing to revise his position when the answer is sound. An evasive questioner keeps moving the standard until no answer can count. The scene prepares us to watch Pharaoh test each description of God's lordship, not because none is meaningful, but because every meaningful description threatens his pretended supremacy.

**The Worlds Are Larger Than Pharaoh's Audience**

The plural worlds also prevents the question from being reduced to a dispute about Egyptian religion alone. God is Lord of all created orders, peoples, and places. His authority does not depend on whether one court recognizes it. Moses is not introducing a local deity who competes with Pharaoh's patron gods. He is announcing the One whose lordship includes every power that claims to be independent.

That universal scope gives the oppressed hope. If God were only the deity of a favored court, the Israelites would remain trapped inside Pharaoh's story. The title says that their lives are visible to a Lord beyond the court and that their enslavement can be judged by an authority Pharaoh cannot absorb into his system. Universal lordship becomes good news when the local ruler has made himself the measure of everything.

**The Question Reveals a Crisis of Authority**

Pharaoh asks what the title means because the title has already had a practical effect. Moses has not merely offered a theory of God; he has carried a command that threatens the structure of power. The ruler must either recognize a superior authority or treat the messenger as dangerous. The question is therefore part of a crisis: who has the right to command Pharaoh?

Moses' answer will describe divine lordship through acts of creation and governance rather than by claiming to map God's essence. That method respects the limit of human speech while giving Pharaoh enough to understand the challenge. The verse leaves the question suspended so that its tension can be felt. A ruler who asks about the Lord of all worlds is being asked, in turn, whether he knows that he is not the lord of even one world.

**The Question Is Also a Test of Pharaoh's Honesty**

A sincere question would place the ruler in the position of a learner. Pharaoh's style keeps him in the position of a judge. He asks Moses to define the authority that has commanded him, yet he does not first admit that his own authority might be answerable. The form of the question therefore tests whether Pharaoh will let an answer change him.

That test remains useful whenever a powerful person demands explanations from a weaker one. Questions can be a path to truth, or they can be a way to keep the weaker person speaking while the powerful person retains the right to dismiss every answer. Moses' mission will not be validated by Pharaoh's willingness to listen. The Lord's claim stands before the question, and the ruler's response will reveal what he intends to do with the answer he requests.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:24

> Moses replied, “˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Moses Answers the Question Through God's Works**

Moses does not try to contain God in a definition of essence. He points to the heavens, the earth, and all that lies between them. This is not a retreat from knowledge. It is a disciplined way to speak about the Creator through the created order that Pharaoh can see and cannot claim to have made. Divine lordship is made known through sustaining and governing the total field of existence.

The answer also avoids making God a rival within the universe. Pharaoh's authority belongs to a place, a court, and a historical moment. The Lord named by Moses is the Lord of the realms above and below and of the interval joining them. He is not one power among other powers. Everything Pharaoh uses to display grandeur already depends on the Lord whose scope surrounds it.

**Heavens and Earth Enclose Every Human Claim**

The pair heavens and earth forms a comprehensive frame. Whatever Pharaoh can point to as evidence of his rule lies inside that frame. His palace, river, army, ancestry, and land are not outside God's ownership. The words do not need to list every created thing because the pair marks the whole visible order, while everything in between closes the gaps that a ruler might try to reserve for himself.

This answer turns cosmology into moral argument. If God owns and sustains the setting in which Pharaoh rules, Pharaoh's authority is delegated and limited. He may administer, but he cannot become absolute. He may possess a title, but he cannot claim the right to enslave people as though their Lord were absent. The extent of creation sets the extent of God's claim over human action.

**Everything Between Removes the Escape of the Middle Realm**

The phrase everything in between is not filler. It blocks a common attempt to divide reality into sacred and neutral zones. Pharaoh might concede that a god created the heavens while treating the earth and human politics as his private domain. Moses denies that division. The Lord's care and authority reach the spaces where people live, labor, worship, and suffer.

That has consequences for religious language. Worship cannot be confined to ritual while injustice is declared outside God's concern. Nor can political rule be treated as a realm where the command of the Creator stops at the palace door. The middle realm belongs to God as surely as the sky and the ground do. Moses' answer brings the oppressed Israelites and the ruling court into the same created field.

**Certainty Is the Required Response**

The closing appeal, if only you had sure faith, identifies the obstacle. Moses has offered a sign of God's lordship through the structure of creation, but Pharaoh's problem is not merely lack of vocabulary. He lacks yaqīn, settled certainty that allows knowledge to govern conduct. A person can repeat that God created the heavens and earth while acting as though his own will is final. Sure faith is the point at which recognition becomes dependable orientation.

The phrase is also a restrained rebuke. Moses does not say that Pharaoh is incapable of understanding. He says that certainty is missing. The appeal leaves open the possibility of a response while making clear that argument alone will not change a ruler who refuses to let the argument judge him. Certainty is not a mood of confidence; it is a moral steadiness rooted in what one knows about God.

**The Answer Does Not Pretend to Exhaust God**

Some theologians and commentators used this exchange to explain why God cannot be reduced to a complete definition of essence. Moses gives signs of lordship without claiming that the human mind can surround the Lord's reality. This is the right balance. God is knowable through revelation and His acts, yet He is not made finite by the descriptions through which creatures come to know Him.

That balance protects faith from two errors. One error makes God so unknowable that no command or worship can be grounded. The other makes God into an object whose nature can be mastered like a physical thing. Moses' answer rejects both. It gives Pharaoh enough truth to understand the moral claim and preserves the transcendence that makes the Lord different from every created ruler.

**Creation Gives the Messenger Common Ground With the Court**

Moses answers in terms that do not depend on Pharaoh accepting Israelite history or Moses' personal authority. The heavens and earth are common to the whole audience. The ruler may reject the messenger's credentials, but he cannot escape the created order to which the answer points. This is wise public reasoning: begin with what can be seen, then draw out the authority it implies.

The verse therefore teaches how a universal claim can be brought into a hostile conversation. Do not begin by flattering the court's assumptions. Name the reality that surrounds the court and sustains it. Pharaoh's power is not denied as a fact; it is placed within a larger fact. The one who rules a corner of the earth must answer to the Lord of the heavens, the earth, and everything between them.

**Creation Is Evidence Against Absolute Human Rule**

The argument does not depend on denying that Pharaoh has administrative power. It denies that administrative power is self-originating or unlimited. A king can command an army, collect wealth, and shape public speech, but he cannot create the heavens, sustain the earth, or bring existence into being. His dependence is not removed by the scale of his palace. It is exposed by the scale of the world around him.

This is why Moses begins with creation rather than with a contest of political strength. If the dispute were decided by force, Pharaoh would appear to have the advantage. By naming the Creator and Sustainer, Moses changes the measure. The strongest ruler remains a dependent creature, and the apparently weak messenger speaks from the authority of the One on whom both ruler and messenger rely.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:25

> Pharaoh said to those around him, “Did you hear ˹what he said˺?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Turns the Court Into an Audience for Ridicule**

Moses has answered with a claim about the whole created order. Pharaoh does not address the claim directly. He turns to the people around him and asks whether they heard what was said. The question is staged for effect. It invites the court to share an expression of disbelief and to treat Moses' answer as an amusing disturbance rather than a demand that requires judgment.

The ruler's movement toward his audience shows how power works in public. A leader does not need to refute a claim if he can control the emotional response surrounding it. By making the chiefs witnesses to his mockery, Pharaoh seeks to establish the proper reaction before they have time to weigh the words. The court is instructed by laughter and amazement, not by evidence.

**Mockery Replaces an Answer**

Pharaoh's question contains no argument about the heavens, the earth, or the meaning of lordship. It signals that he has chosen performance over reply. A speaker can use ridicule when a claim threatens a settled position, because a joke may make the claim feel socially unsafe to consider. The audience then learns that agreement with the messenger would mean joining the target of the joke.

This tactic is different from honest disagreement. An honest critic identifies a premise, offers a reason, and accepts the possibility of correction. Pharaoh instead asks his courtiers to react to Moses' words as though their strangeness were already a refutation. The court is not being invited into inquiry; it is being recruited into a social defense of the ruler's authority.

**The Question Polices the Court's Loyalty**

Those around Pharaoh are not neutral listeners. Their position depends on the ruler, and his question tests whether they will mirror his response. Did you hear what he said carries an unspoken command: hear it as absurd, and show that you belong to the side of Pharaoh. The court's members must decide whether loyalty means repeating the ruler's performance or facing the truth that performance avoids.

This is why tyranny needs an audience. Power is strengthened when people laugh at the same target, repeat the same accusation, and treat the ruler's interpretation as common sense. The question turns private hesitation into public conformity. A courtier may have recognized the force of Moses' answer, but the ruler's framing makes recognition costly. Public mockery can therefore function as a form of coercion even before a formal threat is spoken.

**A Ruler Can Make Surprise Look Like Superiority**

Pharaoh's question also displays amazement. He acts as though Moses has said something so strange that the proper response is incredulity. Yet surprise does not prove that a claim is false. A familiar worldview can make a true statement feel absurd when the statement exposes its limits. Pharaoh's court is accustomed to treating the king as the highest authority; a Lord above all worlds sounds disruptive precisely because it is disruptive.

The scene teaches caution about the language of common sense. What a powerful group calls ridiculous may be the first clear description of its own dependence. A society can normalize a falsehood until truth sounds foreign. Moses' answer does not become less sound because Pharaoh performs shock. The performance reveals the court's investment in its old assumptions.

**The Audience Is Pressured Before It Is Informed**

Pharaoh's sequence matters. He first asks the chiefs to react, and only afterward will he continue the exchange. This order puts social pressure ahead of evidence. Once the court has been invited to mock Moses, any later acknowledgment of truth may look like disloyalty. The ruler is trying to settle the audience's posture before the content of the claim can be considered.

Such pressure appears whenever institutions protect themselves by ridiculing dissenters. The target is not only the speaker. It is everyone who might be willing to listen. The question tells the silent members of the court that they are being watched. Their task is to share the ruler's reaction, not to judge his reasoning. Moses stands before a political theater in which the audience itself is part of the test.

**Silence Can Be a Form of Complicity**

The verse does not record what the people around Pharaoh thought. Their silence may have reflected fear, agreement, or calculation. The omission keeps attention on the ruler's tactic, but it also leaves the courtiers responsible for their response. A person does not become innocent merely because he did not speak the original mockery. He may still strengthen it by laughing, applauding, or remaining silent when silence protects harm.

That does not mean every frightened subject can be judged as though he possessed Pharaoh's power. Responsibility follows knowledge and ability. The court, however, holds influence and is being asked to help define truth for the kingdom. Its members must eventually answer whether they used that influence to serve justice or to protect the ruler's performance.

**A Public Claim Deserves More Than a Public Reaction**

Moses' words concern the Lord of all worlds, so Pharaoh's reaction cannot settle their truth. The question to the court is about reception, not evidence. The verse therefore separates popularity from validity. A room can be made to laugh at a statement without disproving it, and a ruler can make a crowd feel united without making his authority legitimate.

The proper response to such a scene is disciplined attention. Ask what was claimed, what reason answered it, and what the mockery is trying to prevent the audience from seeing. Pharaoh's question shows that a power threatened by truth may attack the social conditions in which truth could be heard. The next exchange will continue that contest over who has the right to define reality.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:26

> Moses added, “˹He is˺ your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Moses Brings Lordship From the Cosmos Into the Family**

After speaking of the heavens and earth, Moses makes the claim personal. The Lord is not only the ruler of distant realms; He is your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers. The words address Pharaoh and his court directly. They cannot place God far away and treat the message as a theory about a remote universe. The One who sustains creation also sustained the people standing in that court and the generations from which they came.

The appeal to forefathers also answers a common defense of power. A ruler may inherit a throne and imagine that inherited status gives his claim a sacred origin. Moses reverses the argument. Pharaoh's ancestors were themselves creatures under God's lordship. Their antiquity does not make them divine, and their relation to the royal line does not elevate Pharaoh above the Lord who gave them life.

**Ancestry Cannot Manufacture Divinity**

The court's respect for lineage may have made the reference to forefathers especially sharp. Pharaoh's rule depends partly on continuity: the present ruler represents a chain of rulers and traditions. Moses does not need to deny the historical chain. He places it in its proper order. Ancestors can transmit customs, property, or political titles, but they cannot transmit ultimate lordship because they never possessed it.

This argument also protects families from becoming idols. Honoring parents and ancestors can be a duty, but inherited practice cannot override the Creator's command. If forefathers were themselves under God's care, then following them is right only when their path agrees with truth. Moses' wording does not attack memory or kinship. It attacks the use of kinship as a shield against judgment.

**The Pronoun Your Removes the Court's Distance**

The word your carries a directness that the universal description alone might not. Moses is not speaking about a lord relevant only to the Israelites. The Lord addresses Pharaoh's life, Pharaoh's ancestors, and Pharaoh's own position. The ruler is included in the created order he pretends to command. He cannot dismiss the message as a foreign theology brought by an outsider.

This is also why the answer can be confronting without being sectarian. Moses does not say that the Lord is merely the patron of one tribe. He says the same Lord is related to the ruler and his forefathers as Creator and Sustainer. The claim creates a shared ground that Pharaoh may reject but cannot honestly call irrelevant. The Lord's authority does not depend on Moses' ethnicity or on Pharaoh's permission to enter the conversation.

**Forefathers Reveal the Mortality of the Throne**

The earlier generations are no longer ruling. Their passing exposes the temporary nature of royal power. A dynasty may speak as though it will last forever, yet every ancestor named in its line has already become part of the past. Moses invokes them not to shame the dead but to remind the living ruler that succession is evidence of mortality, not proof of permanence.

The same reasoning appears in many Qur'anic critiques of inherited pride. A person who boasts of ancestry forgets that the ancestors themselves depended on God and eventually returned to Him. Pharaoh's court can celebrate the past, but it cannot turn the past into a guarantee for the future. Lordship belongs to the One who remains while generations pass.

**The Answer Rejects a Private Definition of God**

Pharaoh's question about the Lord of all worlds could have been answered in a private or philosophical register. Moses continues to describe the Lord through relations visible in life: the Lord of people, parents, and generations. The answer teaches that knowledge of God is not detached from how human beings understand their own origin and dependence.

A ruler may dislike the idea that his own ancestors were dependent creatures, because that idea removes the sacred aura from his lineage. Yet the claim is not an insult to the ancestors. It gives them their true honor as creatures of God rather than turning them into links in a chain of self-worship. Moses' speech makes the royal past answerable to the same Lord who hears the present.

**Personal Address Makes Evasion More Difficult**

When a claim is universal, a person may hide behind abstraction. When it is addressed as your Lord, evasion becomes harder. Pharaoh must decide whether he accepts that his life is received, his authority limited, and his ancestors judged under the Lord named by Moses. The question is no longer only what the title means. It is what the title means for the man who has placed himself above other people.

That is the force of this short verse. It neither adds a new deity nor changes the subject. It presses the universal claim into the ruler's family history. Pharaoh's ancestors did not make him a god. They were evidence that he, like every ruler before him, is a dependent servant before the Lord.

**The Family Reference Also Limits Moses' Own Pride**

Moses does not say that his family possesses a special god unavailable to Pharaoh. He names the Lord as the Lord of Pharaoh's forefathers as well as Pharaoh himself. That universality keeps the messenger from turning revelation into a tribal possession. The Israelites' history matters, but the Lord who sends Moses is not contained by Israel's history or by Egypt's court.

The wording also prevents a messenger from speaking as though he stands outside the judgment he announces. Moses is a descendant of human beings who depended on God. He speaks with authority because he has been sent, not because his ancestry makes him divine. The court can reject his message, but it cannot honestly accuse him of claiming a private privilege for his own family.

A ruler who hears this should recognize that the messenger is not offering a rival dynasty. He is placing every dynasty under one Lord. That is why Pharaoh's inherited status cannot answer Moses. The lineage Pharaoh trusts becomes evidence of dependence, and the family history he uses to support authority becomes a reminder that authority ends with the generations God creates.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:27

> Pharaoh said ˹mockingly˺, “Your messenger, who has been sent to you, must be insane.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Answers a Claim With a Diagnosis**

Pharaoh does not examine Moses' statement about the Lord of the forefathers. He labels the messenger insane. The accusation is a familiar way to avoid an argument: if the speaker can be declared irrational, his words need not be answered. The judgment is presented as though it were obvious, but the verse marks its mocking tone. Pharaoh is not offering a careful account of Moses' condition. He is trying to make the court dismiss the message before it reaches their conscience.

Calling a prophet mad also reverses the moral situation. Moses speaks coherently about creation, ancestry, and authority, while Pharaoh is the one who claims supremacy and defends oppression. The label allows the ruler to make his own extreme position appear normal. A court trained to trust Pharaoh may accept the diagnosis because accepting it protects the order from which the court benefits.

**Your Messenger Creates Distance From the Claim**

Pharaoh says your messenger. The possessive can sound as though Moses belongs to the people around him rather than speaking to Pharaoh. It turns a divine commission into a factional matter: they have their messenger, and Pharaoh has his authority. This wording is a political move. If Moses can be treated as the representative of a troublesome group, his message need not be judged as a claim about every human being.

Yet the phrase also reveals that Pharaoh understands the structure of Moses' argument. He knows that Moses presents himself as sent, not self-appointed. Instead of answering the Sender, Pharaoh attacks the sent person.
