**The Cities Are Drawn Into Pharaoh's Personal Crisis**

The ruler's conflict with Moses could have remained a court dispute. By sending mobilizers everywhere, Pharaoh makes the whole kingdom participate in it. Ordinary people may now be asked to supply information, transport, weapons, or approval. The ruler's personal refusal becomes a national campaign.

The mobilizers also show how quickly a state can turn a moral failure into an official emergency. The departure could have been answered with release, negotiation, or repentance. Instead, Pharaoh gives the cities a mission that assumes his ownership is legitimate. Once the order travels through the kingdom, many people may participate without ever hearing the original demand or seeing the injustice that caused the departure.

The speed of this response cannot be mistaken for moral clarity. An order can move efficiently through cities while carrying a false account of the people being pursued. The dispatchers may know only that Pharaoh wants the fugitives recovered. Their limited view increases the duty to ask what the command is for before helping it reach every road.

That expansion is another form of injustice. A leader who cannot accept correction asks the public to bear the cost of his obstinacy. The Israelites are a small departing community, but Pharaoh's response turns their movement into a matter for every city. The verse begins the description of how tyranny manufactures a crisis large enough to justify its own violence.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:54

> ˹and said,˺ “These ˹outcasts˺ are just a handful of people,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Minimizes the People He Fears**

Pharaoh describes the departing Israelites as a small band. The wording is meant to reduce them before the pursuit begins. If they are only a handful, then their departure can be framed as a minor disturbance that the state will easily correct. The ruler's contempt tries to make his mobilization look proportionate even though the people he is chasing are vulnerable and unarmed compared with his host.

The Arabic term translated outcasts or small band can suggest a remnant separated from a larger body. That sense adds a political edge. Pharaoh speaks as though the Israelites are a leftover group with no independent weight. He does not name them as a people with a history and a divine claim. He defines them by their reduced status within his order.

**Counting People Can Become a Tool of Dehumanization**

Numbers can be used honestly to plan protection, or dishonestly to decide whose lives matter. Pharaoh's handful is not a neutral estimate. It is a rhetorical device that makes the Israelites sound too few to deserve attention and too weak to have legitimate aims. The same population can be called insignificant when the ruler wants to ignore it and dangerous when he wants to justify pursuit.

This double use of numbers is common in political speech. A minority is described as too small to count in one moment and as a threat large enough to fear in another. Pharaoh's statement begins the first version. He minimizes the people so that his court can appear strong, while the very fact that he mobilizes the cities shows that he does not regard them as harmless.

**Outcasts Is a Name Imposed by the Ruler**

The Israelites are not inherently outcasts. Pharaoh's policy has placed them at the edge of power and then uses their marginal position as proof that they do not belong. A ruler can exclude a group from rights, labor, and security, then accuse the group of being foreign because it no longer fits the image of the protected public.

God's command overturns that label by calling them My servants. The contrast is direct. Pharaoh sees a disposable remnant; God sees a people whom He is leading. Political names do not decide human worth. A community pushed to the margins remains visible to the Lord, and its numerical smallness does not reduce His care or its right to justice.

**The Small Band Is Not Without Dignity**

The phrase handful might sound like an insult, but smallness can also describe a people carrying a great responsibility. The Israelites do not need a large army to become the community God has chosen to rescue. Their weakness makes the outcome less likely to be credited to their own military strength and more clearly displays the limits of Pharaoh's power.

This does not romanticize vulnerability. The people face real danger and need protection. It shows instead that numbers do not determine the moral value of a cause. A small group can be right, and a vast host can be wrong. Pharaoh's court assumes that power belongs to the larger force. The story will challenge that assumption without denying the fear such force creates.

**The Ruler's Contempt Is Mixed With Anxiety**

If the Israelites were truly irrelevant, Pharaoh would not need to mobilize the cities. His need to describe them as a handful while preparing a large pursuit reveals anxiety beneath contempt. The ruler wants to reassure his own side that victory is easy because he knows that the act of departure has already weakened his claim.

Contempt often serves as emotional armor. Calling a vulnerable group insignificant makes it easier to pursue them without seeing their suffering. It also reassures the pursuers that they are not facing a moral challenge, only a nuisance. Pharaoh's wording asks the cities to share that emotional distance before they encounter the people themselves.

**A Minority Can Be Made to Carry a Nation's Fear**

The Israelites are a small band, yet Pharaoh speaks as though their movement requires the whole kingdom to respond. This is how a regime magnifies a minority's existence when it needs to justify force. The group is too small to deserve freedom but large enough to explain an emergency. The contradiction benefits the ruler because either description serves control.

The proper question is not only how many people are moving. It is why they are moving and what right the ruler has to stop them. Numbers cannot answer those questions. Pharaoh's statement tries to replace moral reasoning with arithmetic, but the Lord's command has already established the central fact: the people are His servants and are being led away from oppression.

**The Word Handful Cannot Make the Chase Innocent**

A small group can still be pursued unjustly. In fact, the vulnerability implied by handful increases the duty of restraint. Pharaoh's power gives him the ability to let the people go without danger to his kingdom, yet he chooses to chase them. His claim that they are few makes the pursuit look easier, not more lawful.

The verse therefore leaves Pharaoh's rhetoric exposed. He wants the cities to see a weak group and a strong state, then to assume that the state's action is automatically right. The moral order is the reverse. Power carries greater responsibility, and the smallness of the pursued makes the ruler's decision more revealing. His contempt does not diminish the people; it exposes the ruler.

A community's numerical weakness can make its oppressor look strong, but it can also make the oppressor's choice easier to judge. Pharaoh is not defending himself from an equal army. He is pursuing a small and vulnerable people because he cannot accept their freedom. The language of handful becomes a measure of his injustice rather than a measure of their worth.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:55

> who have really enraged us,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Describes the Oppressed as the Offenders**

Pharaoh says that the departing people have enraged him. The sentence shifts attention from what he has done to how he feels. The Israelites' movement away from enslavement is presented as an insult to the ruler, while the oppression that caused the movement disappears from his account. Anger becomes evidence of the victims' guilt rather than a reaction that the ruler must examine.

The phrase exposes a common pattern in tyranny. A powerful person treats resistance to harm as a personal offense. The victim is then accused of provoking the conflict by refusing to remain in the position assigned to him. Pharaoh's anger is real, but its reality does not make its object just. Emotions can reveal wounded pride as easily as they reveal moral danger.

**Enragement Is Not Proof of Wrongdoing**

A ruler may feel anger when his authority is challenged, but anger cannot serve as a legal judgment. The question should be what the Israelites have done and whether Pharaoh has a right to pursue them. Instead, the ruler offers his emotional state as a reason for mobilization. His people are expected to accept that because he is enraged, the departing community must be guilty.

This substitution is dangerous because it removes evidence from the discussion. A person can be sincerely furious and still be wrong. Injustice often becomes more violent when the wrongdoer treats his anger as a moral certificate. Pharaoh's statement asks the cities to join his emotional interpretation before they ask whether the Israelites have committed a crime.

**The Plagues Have Become a Story of Insult**

The anger can refer to the plagues and signs that struck Egypt, as well as to Moses and the Israelites' rejection of Pharaoh's religion. The ruler experiences the consequences of his own refusal as an attack from below. Instead of reading the plagues as warnings, he reads them as provocations. That change of interpretation allows him to pursue the people with resentment rather than repentance.

A warning becomes useful only when it leads to correction. If a person treats every consequence as humiliation imposed by an enemy, he learns nothing from it. Pharaoh's anger shows that the signs have touched his power but not softened his pride. He is enraged that the oppressed have become the occasion for his exposure.

**Tyranny Personalizes a Challenge to Justice**

Moses' demand concerned the rights of the Children of Israel and the lordship of God. Pharaoh reduces that public matter to his personal feeling. The people have enraged us, he says, making the ruler and his circle the main subjects. The plural us expands the ruler's pride into a collective grievance. Officials who benefit from the order are invited to treat the loss of domination as their shared injury.

This language hides the difference between the ruler's interests and the community's interests. Pharaoh speaks as though whatever weakens his control harms everyone. But a state is not identical with its ruler, and a court's anger is not the same as the people's welfare. The verse teaches caution whenever a leader claims that criticism of him is an attack on the nation.

**Anger Can Make Pursuit Feel Like Self-Defense**

A person who is enraged often experiences his own aggression as justified response. Pharaoh's anger prepares the moral cover for the chase. He can tell the mobilizers that they are recovering what has insulted them rather than attacking people who have been commanded to leave. Emotion changes the appearance of the action without changing its nature.

The proper discipline is to separate feeling from fact. What happened before the anger? Who had power? What demand was made? What response would justice require if the ruler were not personally offended? These questions recover the context Pharaoh has removed. His feeling may explain his behavior, but it cannot justify it.

**The Ruler's Anger Is a Sign of Lost Ownership**

Pharaoh does not say that the Israelites have harmed Egypt's people in this verse. He says they have enraged him. The object is the ruler's ego and the court's sense of possession. Their departure proves that Pharaoh's claim over them is no longer accepted. The anger is therefore the emotion of an owner who sees what he calls his property leaving.

God's command has already changed the moral status of the people. They are servants of God, not Pharaoh's possessions. The ruler's anger cannot reverse that truth. It can only reveal how deeply he has confused power with ownership. The more he insists that their freedom is an insult, the more clearly he shows why freedom is necessary.

**A Shared Grievance Can Recruit Ordinary People Into Wrongdoing**

Pharaoh's statement is addressed through mobilizers to the cities. The language of shared anger invites ordinary Egyptians to participate in a ruler's personal crisis. People may join the pursuit because they are told that the Israelites have offended the whole society. Once anger is made communal, violence can feel like solidarity.

The verse warns against that emotional contagion. A community should not inherit a ruler's anger without examining its cause. Solidarity with the powerful is not the same as justice. The Israelites' departure may frustrate Pharaoh, but frustration is not a wrong that authorizes pursuit. The ruler's feelings have been placed before the people's conscience, and the next words will add a claim about the strength of the host prepared to act on them.

The warning is especially sharp because Pharaoh's anger is being converted into a public command. Once officials and soldiers are told that the fugitives have enraged everyone, they may treat cruelty as the expression of a shared emotion. The verse separates the feeling from the duty: anger can be reported, but it cannot be allowed to decide whether a people may go free.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:56

> but we are all on the alert.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Pharaoh Reassures the Court With Military Readiness**

Pharaoh describes his people as a host on the alert. The statement is meant to answer the smallness of the Israelites with the strength of Egypt. A handful may flee, he implies, but the kingdom is prepared to respond. The language turns military readiness into reassurance, asking the court and the cities to feel secure because the ruler has forces, equipment, and command.

The claim is not only a report about soldiers. It is part of the ruler's rhetoric. Pharaoh wants the people to imagine that the outcome is already settled by the balance of power. If Egypt is ready, then pursuit appears reasonable and victory appears certain. The statement encourages the host to trust its preparation rather than question the justice of the order it has been given.

**Alert Means Equipped as Well as Watchful**

The Arabic term can suggest readiness, preparedness, and being equipped. The host is not merely awake. It is organized to move, supplied for pursuit, and confident in its ability to act. That detail explains why Pharaoh can speak so boldly about recovering the Israelites. His confidence rests on a material system that appears overwhelming compared with the departing community.

Readiness, however, has two dimensions. A force can be ready to move and unready to judge. Pharaoh's army may possess weapons and mounts, but it has not been prepared to ask whether the pursuit is just. The verse separates operational skill from moral wisdom. An equipped host can carry out a wrong command more efficiently than an unprepared one.

**The Word All Expands Pharaoh's Claim**

Pharaoh says we are all on the alert. The word all presents the court as united. It leaves no space for hesitation, dissent, or a conscientious official who might ask whether the chase is necessary. A ruler often strengthens a command by describing the whole community as already committed to it. Anyone who questions the pursuit can then be made to look like an outsider.

The claim may also be exaggerated. A leader who speaks for everyone can create the unity he wants people to believe already exists. Some may be afraid, some indifferent, and some opposed. Pharaoh's language erases those distinctions so that the pursuit appears to carry collective consent. The people are made responsible for a decision that began in the ruler's refusal.

**Military Confidence Conceals Spiritual Weakness**

The host is ready in the worldly sense, but it is not ready for what God has decreed. Pharaoh's court measures the coming encounter by numbers, equipment, and speed. Divine planning operates on another level. The host can be organized perfectly and still be unable to prevent the fulfillment of God's promise to the Israelites.

This contrast does not make preparation worthless. The Qur'an does not praise carelessness. It exposes the error of treating preparation as sovereignty. A force can prepare means, but it cannot command outcomes that belong to God. Pharaoh's readiness will make the eventual defeat more revealing because it cannot be blamed on disorder or lack of resources.

**The Host Is Ready to Protect a False Possession**

What is the army ready to defend? Not a city under attack or a people facing invasion, but Pharaoh's claim over servants who have been told to leave. Military language makes ownership sound like national security. The host is described as alert because the ruler has taught it to see freedom as a threat.

This is one of the most dangerous uses of force. Soldiers may think they are protecting the community while they are actually preserving a ruler's control over a vulnerable group. The moral question is therefore prior to the command: what is being defended, and who benefits? Pharaoh's words answer with confidence but not with justice. The host's readiness cannot make the claim legitimate.

**A Ready Host Can Still Be Morally Asleep**

Alertness to an enemy is not the same as consciousness of God. Pharaoh's people may watch roads, prepare weapons, and respond quickly while remaining blind to the Lord's command. The verse's irony lies in that contrast. They are awake to the movement of the Israelites and asleep to the meaning of the signs that led to the movement.

Taqwā would have made them guard themselves from injustice. Pharaoh's alertness instead guards Pharaoh's pride. The difference is not in the amount of attention but in what attention serves. A person can be highly vigilant in protecting status and deeply heedless about the rights of others.

**Confidence in Force Cannot Replace Truth**

The statement ends the ruler's public preparation with assurance, but it does not end the moral issue. Pharaoh has a ready host; Moses has a divine command. The coming pursuit will show that material advantage cannot decide which command is right. A ruler may count soldiers, but God counts deeds and hears the cry of the oppressed.

The verse therefore asks the audience to distrust confidence that rests only on force. Readiness can protect the weak when governed by justice, but it becomes a danger when used to recover people whom the ruler has no right to own. Pharaoh's host is alert. The question is whether it is ready to meet the judgment of the Lord it has refused.

The phrase also strips military readiness of its power to reassure the believer. A host may be prepared for battle and still be moving toward defeat; a community may look exposed and still be under divine protection. The appearance of readiness belongs to the army. The final command over events belongs to God. That difference is the boundary Pharaoh's confidence cannot cross. A ready army is still a dependent army.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:57

> So We lured the tyrants out of ˹their˺ gardens, springs,

**Expanded Commentary**

**God Draws the Tyrants Out From Their Security**

The verse turns from Pharaoh's boast to God's action. The tyrants are brought out from gardens and springs, the settings of luxury that helped sustain their confidence. Their departure is described as something God caused, not as a victory won by the pursuing army. Pharaoh believes he is moving by his own decision, yet the narrative places his movement within a divine plan.

The wording translated lured can also be understood as made to leave or brought out. Commentators considered whether the phrase emphasizes God's direct removal of the Egyptians from their possessions or the desire placed in their hearts to chase the Israelites. Both readings fit the contrast. Pharaoh's army leaves the security of its wealth because it thinks pursuit will restore control, while God is drawing it toward the judgment prepared for its arrogance.

**Luxury Becomes a Trap When It Feeds Pride**

Gardens and springs are signs of provision, but the tyrants treat them as evidence that their power is secure. The beauty and abundance around them create a world in which consequences seem distant. They can imagine that the palace, farms, and water will remain theirs because they have learned to confuse possession with permanence.

God's action exposes that confusion. The same comforts that reassure the tyrants cannot accompany them when they chase the Israelites. Their wealth does not make the pursuit wise, and their gardens do not protect them from the Lord who gave them. A blessing becomes a trap when it produces contempt for the One who provides it and for the people whose labor sustains it.

**The Tyrants Leave Their Own Evidence Behind**

The verse names the possessions from which they are brought out. The list makes their loss concrete. These are not empty people with nothing to lose; they are people surrounded by abundance who still choose oppression. Their wealth cannot be used as proof that their rule is righteous. It may instead increase their responsibility because they possess enough to act justly and still refuse.

The details also prevent a shallow account of judgment. God does not merely defeat an army in an abstract battle. He removes a class of rulers from the spaces that embodied their social power. Gardens and springs represent a way of life built around control of land and resources. The tyrants leave that way of life behind when they make their wealth serve the pursuit of the oppressed.

**The Pursuit Draws Power Away From Its Foundation**

A ruler's strength often depends on remaining within the institutions and resources that support him. Pharaoh's court has cities, advisers, wealth, and military supply. By drawing the tyrants out, God moves them away from the setting in which those advantages appear stable. The pursuit separates them from the comfort that makes their rule look permanent.

This does not mean that God deceives innocent people into danger. The people being drawn out are tyrants whose choices have already placed them in opposition to justice. The movement is judgment on a settled pattern of oppression. Their own confidence supplies the means: they leave safety because they believe force will recover what they have lost.

**Gardens and Springs Cannot Be Carried Into Judgment**

The possessions remain behind because material abundance is tied to a place and a time. A person may own land, water, residences, and treasure in the world, but none of these can be carried as proof of worth before God. The tyrants leave their visible glory behind while pursuing the people they tried to own.

This is not a condemnation of every garden or every form of wealth. Creation is good, and provision can be used gratefully. The judgment falls on those who turn provision into a basis for domination. Wealth should make a person more responsible, not more certain that he can defy the Lord. The tyrants' departure reveals the emptiness of a security that depends on possession.

**The Language of Being Drawn Out Exposes Hidden Direction**

Pharaoh's speeches have made him appear to be the author of the chase. The verse reveals another level of causation. The tyrants choose and God judges; their intention is real, but it operates within a divine plan they do not control. They set out to recover Israel and are drawn toward the consequence of their own wrongdoing.

This balance protects the story from two errors. It does not turn Pharaoh into a puppet with no responsibility, and it does not let Pharaoh imagine that his plan exists outside God's rule. Human pride makes choices; divine sovereignty places those choices within judgment. The gardens and springs are the first visible signs that the tyrants are leaving the world they thought they owned.

**The Wealth of a Tyrant Does Not Make His Pursuit Noble**

A splendid setting can make a ruler look respectable. The verse strips away that visual power by describing the tyrants being brought out from it. Once separated from gardens and springs, their claim to greatness must be judged by what they do to the vulnerable. Their wealth cannot turn a chase into justice.

The passage therefore teaches a way to read political grandeur. Look past the residences and cultivated land to the people whose freedom the ruler denies. If abundance is guarded by oppression, the beauty surrounding the court is also evidence of responsibility. God can remove the tyrant from that beauty and leave the public to see that the tyrant's greatness was never self-sustaining.

The gardens and springs therefore function as witnesses as well as possessions. They show what the tyrants enjoyed, what they believed would remain, and what they were willing to abandon in anger. A life surrounded by provision can still be spiritually poor when it uses provision to keep others captive. God's removal of the tyrants begins by separating them from the signs of abundance they mistook for security.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:58

> treasures, and splendid residences.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The List Moves From Nature to Human-Made Splendor**

The verse completes the list of what the tyrants leave behind: treasures and splendid residences. The earlier gardens and springs represented cultivated abundance; these items represent wealth stored and status displayed. The sequence moves from the resources of the land to the structures and possessions that society builds around them. Pharaoh's world contains every visible sign by which a ruling class measures success.

Yet all of it is named within the story of departure. The treasures do not protect their owners, and the residences do not become refuges. Their grandeur is real as a worldly fact but powerless as a shield against divine judgment. The list asks the reader to distinguish between the existence of wealth and the meaning assigned to it. Possession can be a trust, or it can become a stage on which tyranny performs permanence.

**Treasures Turned Into Evidence of False Security**

A treasure is valuable because people believe it will secure the future. Pharaoh's court has accumulated enough wealth to imagine that nothing essential can be lost. The pursuit of the Israelites exposes that belief. The rulers leave the treasures because they think they can return after recovering the fugitives. Their confidence rests on the assumption that the future belongs to them.

God's judgment interrupts that assumption. Wealth can be left behind in one moment, and ownership can change without the former owners consenting. The treasures that seemed to prove Pharaoh's strength become silent witnesses that strength was temporary. A person who stores wealth without preparing for accountability may discover that the storehouse remains while the owner is gone.

**Splendid Residences Cannot Make a Tyrant at Home**

A residence is more than a building. It represents belonging, rank, memory, and the right to inhabit a place without fear. The tyrants' splendid residences embody the social order they have built. When they are brought out from them, the narrative shows that home is not secure when it is founded on the dispossession of others.

This does not mean that beautiful homes are blameworthy. The moral issue is the relationship between splendor and oppression. A residence becomes part of the indictment when its comfort depends on a system that denies another people freedom. The verse names the buildings because the buildings are not outside the judgment of the order that produced them.

**Worldly Station Is Not a Lasting Rank**

The homes and treasures also mark the tyrants' station. Their architecture announces who commands, who serves, and who may enter. They live high in a hierarchy that treats status as proof of worth. God brings them out of that station, showing that social rank has no permanence when it is used against justice.

A person can be honored by society and condemned by God, just as a person can be marginalized by society and honored by God. The visible arrangement does not reveal the final order. Pharaoh's residences may make him appear secure, but the Lord can remove him from them and give what he valued to people he tried to keep below him.

**Abundance Becomes a Moral Test**

The tyrants possess enough resources to respond to the Israelites with generosity or at least restraint. Their abundance increases the seriousness of their refusal. They are not driven by hunger to seize every possible laborer. They are rulers with gardens, springs, treasures, and residences who still insist on owning a vulnerable people.

Wealth therefore functions as a test. It can widen the ability to do good, but it can also widen the distance between a ruler and the people affected by his decisions. The more a person has, the more easily he can mistake comfort for divine approval. The verse shows that material abundance does not answer the question of whether power is just.

**Leaving Wealth Behind Reverses the Court's Story**

Pharaoh's court had presented the Israelites as a threat to the land. The list now reveals who actually possesses the wealth and status being defended. The tyrants leave their gardens, springs, treasures, and residences because they are pursuing the people. The public can see that the rulers' concern is not a lack of resources but the loss of control.

This reversal is central to the narrative. The court called liberation an attack on national prosperity, yet prosperity belongs to the tyrants who refuse release. God's judgment removes the rulers from the symbols they used to justify their authority. The story refuses to let splendor settle the moral question.

**Possessions Remain While Ownership Changes**

The verse does not say that the gardens, treasures, and residences vanish. They remain as created things even when the tyrants leave. This distinction matters. The world is not evil because tyrants possessed it. The wrong lies in the claim that possession guarantees status and that status authorizes oppression.

When ownership changes, the objects reveal their created nature. They were never eternal extensions of Pharaoh's person. They could serve another community, another order, or another use. The tyrants' departure breaks the illusion that wealth belongs to its possessor by necessity. God gives and removes, and no residence can become a permanent throne.

The list is also a warning to those who inherit comfort without asking how it was made. Splendid residences can conceal forced labor, unequal law, and the fear of people outside the walls. A just use of wealth begins by recognizing those hidden relations. Pharaoh's court sees only what it owns; the divine account includes the people whose lives made that ownership possible. Wealth cannot hide those relations from the Lord who judges both the house and the hands that built it. No wall can outlast divine judgment. Monumental scale is not evidence of permanence; it is another occasion to remember the One who grants and removes power.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:59

> So it was. And We awarded it ˹all˺ to the Children of Israel.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rulers' Former Glory Changes Hands**

The verse states the reversal simply: what the tyrants left was awarded to the Children of Israel. The people whom Pharaoh treated as laborers become heirs to the worldly goods associated with the ruling class. This is not presented as a human coup planned by the Israelites. It is God's judgment on a system that believed its possessions and ranks were permanent.

The word all gathers the earlier list—gardens, springs, treasures, and residences—into one reversal. The meaning is not that every object was immediately carried away by the Israelites or that every detail of later settlement is supplied here. The point is that Pharaoh's people lost the status and resources they treated as proof of superiority, while Israel was raised from subjection into a new position.

**Inheritance Here Is a Divine Transfer of Status**

Commentators differed over how literally to understand the inheritance. Some took it to mean that the Israelites came to possess the Egyptians' actual wealth. Others emphasized a transfer of worldly station and the reversal of power, while some reports connected the wealth with what the Israelites took by God's command when they left. The wording supports a real reversal, but the larger Qur'anic account cautions against forcing every detail into a single material scene.

The strongest conclusion holds together possession and status. God stripped the tyrants of what made them appear secure and gave the oppressed a share in the dignity and resources from which they had been excluded. Whether every residence was occupied immediately is a secondary question. The central truth is that Pharaoh's order was not the final owner of Egypt's good things.

**The Transfer Is Judgment, Not Mere Reward**

The Israelites are not described here as receiving wealth because wealth itself proves their virtue. The transfer occurs within judgment on Pharaoh. The tyrants lose what they used to support domination. The Israelites receive what God's decree assigns them. This is a moral reversal in history, not a doctrine that material possession always marks divine favor.

That distinction matters because the Israelites will later face their own tests in the wilderness. Inheriting goods does not make a community incapable of disobedience, and losing goods does not prove that a people is rejected. The verse describes one act of justice in one historical setting. It should not be turned into a simple formula equating wealth with righteousness.

**God's Gifts Can Expose the Fragility of Ownership**

Pharaoh's court treated ownership as an extension of power. The verse shows that ownership can change when God changes the order. Possession is therefore contingent. A ruler may build residences, control water, and store treasure, but none of these becomes his by an eternal right. God can remove him and award the same goods to people he regarded as beneath him.

This is a warning against pride in property. The good things of the world are real, but they remain gifts. The proper response to receiving them is gratitude and justice, not the construction of a hierarchy that denies other people's humanity. The transfer from tyrants to Israelites exposes how foolish it is to treat a temporary holding as proof of permanent superiority.

**The Verse Uses Succession to Correct Historical Memory**

Pharaoh's narrative presented the Israelites as outcasts who had no rightful place in the land. God's action tells history differently. The people who were excluded from full dignity are now named as recipients. The ruler's story of who belongs is overturned by the Lord who owns the land and its resources.

This does not mean that every political claim made in the name of inheritance is automatically sacred. The verse is about a divine act in a specific prophetic history. It teaches that human rulers cannot write the final account of belonging. A community's imposed low status can be reversed by God, and the possessions that seemed to confirm the ruler's story can become evidence against it.

**A Scholarly Difference Does Not Change the Main Reversal**

The report that the Israelites later returned to Egypt and took possession of the goods has been attributed to some commentators, but that reading sits uneasily with the Qur'an's account of their later journey and the land they were commanded to seek. A more careful reading stays with what the verse plainly establishes: God transferred the former tyrants' worldly standing and possessions to Israel in the course of judgment.

The disagreement is useful because it shows how interpretation should work. One should distinguish the text's central assertion from a later narrative detail that may not fit the wider scriptural sequence. The main point remains firm even when the exact manner of inheritance is discussed: no tyrant can guarantee that his wealth will remain with his house, and no oppressed people is forgotten by the Lord who can reverse the order.

**The Awarded Goods Carry a Responsibility**

Receiving what once belonged to an oppressive order creates a new test. The Israelites must not merely enjoy the reversal; they must learn how to use power and provision without reproducing Pharaoh's injustice. The verse does not develop that duty here, but the structure of the story makes it clear. Deliverance from domination is incomplete if the rescued community adopts domination as its own ideal.

God's award is therefore both relief and responsibility. It gives the Israelites visible evidence that Pharaoh was not sovereign. It also places goods in their hands that can be used well or badly. The true inheritance is not possession alone. It is the chance to live under God's lordship rather than under the rule of a man who called his own control permanent.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:60

> And so they pursued them at sunrise.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pursuit Begins in the Fullness of Day**

The Egyptians pursue the Israelites at sunrise. The timing gives the chase a clear visual setting. The Israelites have left at night under God's command, while the pursuing force moves when daylight makes tracking easier. Pharaoh's host is no longer searching through darkness. It advances with the confidence that visibility, numbers, and speed will return the fugitives to its control.

Sunrise also creates a contrast between the two movements. The Israelites depart quietly under divine instruction; the Egyptians follow openly under the authority of a ruler who has refused to release them. Night protected the vulnerable community, while day reveals the scale of the force behind it. The verse is brief because the pursuit itself is the point: Pharaoh's refusal has become physical and direct.

**Daylight Does Not Give the Pursuers Divine Sight**

The Egyptians can see the route and organize their movement, but physical visibility is not the same as understanding. They know where the Israelites have gone, yet they do not understand what the departure means or who governs its outcome. Sunrise illuminates the road without illuminating the heart of the host.

This distinction continues the chapter's contrast between appearance and truth. Pharaoh's people have watched signs in the court and still chosen a false interpretation. Now they see the fleeing community and read the sight as an opportunity to recover property. The light of day cannot correct a moral blindness that the ruler has taught them to share.

**Pursuit Shows That Pharaoh Has Chosen Possession Over Mercy**

The Egyptians do not follow because the Israelites have attacked them or threatened their homes. They follow because Pharaoh will not accept their departure. The movement of the army therefore reveals the ruler's priority. He values control over the people more than peace with the people. The possibility of letting them go has been rejected, and pursuit becomes the proof.

A ruler may call such pursuit security, but the sequence tells another story. The Israelites were commanded to leave, Pharaoh mobilized the cities, and the host now follows. Each step arises from the refusal to recognize God's ownership. The army's movement is not a neutral reaction. It is the enforcement of an unjust claim.

**Sunrise Makes the Power Imbalance Visible**

At dawn the Israelites can be seen by the pursuing force, but they can also be seen in their vulnerability. The contrast between a departing community and an organized host becomes plain. Pharaoh's side has the apparent advantage of equipment, numbers, and daylight. The verse does not hide that advantage or pretend that deliverance feels easy to those being chased.

This honesty strengthens the meaning of trust. Faith does not require the Israelites to imagine that the army is small or harmless. It requires them to know that visible advantage is not the final measure of power. The scene will soon place the two groups in direct relation, but already the reader knows that the pursuit is moving within the plan announced to Moses.

**The Pursuit Fulfills the Warning**

God had told Moses that the people would be pursued. The sunrise pursuit fulfills that warning. Foreknowledge does not remove fear, but it prevents the people from interpreting the danger as proof that the night departure was mistaken. The event occurs as God said it would, which means the next stage must also be understood within His promise.

A warning can serve mercy by preparing people for what they will face. The Israelites are not promised a journey without resistance. They are told that resistance will come, and they leave anyway. That obedience matters. They do not turn back simply because Pharaoh's host appears behind them. The pursuit becomes part of the path rather than evidence that the path was wrong.

**The Chasers Move Toward the Consequence of Their Choice**

Pharaoh's army believes it is moving toward victory. In the narrative's deeper structure, it is moving toward judgment. The host's confidence does not make its direction false. It has followed the ruler's command into a situation where the resources that protected the tyrants—gardens, springs, treasure, and rank—cannot help them.

This does not turn the Egyptians into helpless objects. They chose to pursue, and their choice carries consequence. Divine sovereignty and human responsibility meet in the movement. God knows where the pursuit leads, while the pursuers remain accountable for why they entered it. Sunrise makes their route visible; it does not make their decision just.

**The Time of Day Highlights the Difference Between Escape and Chase**

Night departure and sunrise pursuit create a rhythm of concealment followed by exposure. The Israelites are allowed to leave before the full force of Pharaoh can gather. The Egyptians follow when the light favors their search. That difference shows the practical care in God's command and the urgency of the ruler's response.

The verse does not praise darkness as a moral good or daylight as a moral evil. It uses time to show how God protects the weak and how the powerful mobilize. The oppressed receive a window in which to move, while the oppressor uses the morning to reclaim them. Both groups are now on the road, but they are not moving under the same authority.

**A Visible Pursuit Cannot Cancel an Invisible Promise**

The Israelites can see the army, while the promise of deliverance must be held in faith. That tension is the spiritual center of the verse. The immediate sight is frightening and seems to contradict freedom. Yet God's command has not been withdrawn. The pursuit is visible; the divine plan is known through revelation.

The line ends before describing the people's reaction, preserving the pressure of the moment. The reader is left with the army at sunrise and the vulnerable community ahead. What follows will show how fear speaks when visible power closes in. For this verse, the essential truth is that Pharaoh's pursuit has begun, but pursuit is not possession and daylight is not victory.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:61

> When the two groups came face to face, the companions of Moses cried out, “We are overtaken for sure.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pursuit Becomes a Visible Trap**

The two groups now meet in direct view of one another. The Israelites have the sea before them and Pharaoh's host behind them. The distance that allowed hope and movement has vanished. The companions see the situation through its immediate physical facts: one route seems blocked, the other is occupied by a powerful army. Their cry expresses the conclusion that those facts appear to demand.

The verse names two groups rather than repeating every identity. The Egyptians are the pursuing host, while Moses' companions are the people who left under God's command. The simple arrangement makes the danger clear without dramatizing it. A community that has escaped oppression is now confronted by the full machinery of the oppressor. The night departure has become a morning crisis.

**Fear Speaks in the Language of Certainty**

They say they are overtaken for sure. Fear often turns an interpretation into a fact. The companions do not say that the army is near or that their options are narrow. They state the outcome as settled. Their bodies are still alive and their journey is still under God's plan, but fear has narrowed their view to the apparent impossibility in front of them.

This response should not be mocked. The danger is real, and the Israelites have reason to be afraid. Faith does not require pretending that a pursuing army is harmless. The problem lies in treating visible danger as the final authority. A person can describe the threat accurately and still misjudge what God can do within it. The companions see one kind of power and forget the command that brought them out.

**Face to Face Means No Human Escape Remains**

The expression came face to face marks the exhaustion of ordinary means. There is no longer a hidden route or a night cover that can solve the problem. The people cannot outrun the army across open ground, and they cannot simply return without placing themselves back under Pharaoh's control. Their fear grows because human planning has reached its limit.

That limit is part of the theological design of the scene. If the Israelites could have defeated the army through superior strategy, the deliverance might be credited to their skill. If they had found an unnoticed road, the event could be explained as luck. The confrontation removes those explanations. The people are brought to a place where rescue must come from beyond their resources.

**The Companions Are Not Yet Speaking From Moses' Certainty**

Moses has received the command to leave and the warning that pursuit would come. His companions may know the command, but they have not yet learned how to hold it against the sight of the army. Their cry shows the difference between hearing a divine promise and possessing settled trust. Community members can travel under a prophet's guidance while still carrying ordinary fear.

This distinction makes the story humane. The Israelites are not a group of perfect believers whose courage never bends. They are people moving through an unprecedented danger. Their weakness creates the setting in which Moses' reassurance can teach them what divine companionship means. A community's fear does not cancel the legitimacy of its earlier obedience.

**The Army's Proximity Looks Like Pharaoh's Victory**

From the viewpoint of the companions, the pursuit seems to have achieved its goal. Pharaoh's host has found them, and the route ahead appears closed. The ruler's mobilization, his claim of readiness, and the sunrise pursuit now gather into one threatening presence. The visible sequence tells a story of Egyptian success.

But the narrative has already shown that Pharaoh's confidence is not sovereignty. The host has been drawn away from its gardens, treasures, and residences. Its arrival at the sea is not proof that its purpose is just. The army has reached the place where its apparent victory will be judged. The same proximity that terrifies the Israelites will bring Pharaoh's force within the range of God's deliverance.

**Fear Can Forget the Meaning of the Journey**

The companions' cry also risks reducing the journey to the present moment. They have seen signs, left at God's command, and watched the tyrants' wealth and power become part of a divine reversal. Yet immediate danger can make earlier evidence feel remote. A person may know that God has helped before and still feel abandoned when the threat appears close.

This is why spiritual steadiness requires memory. The event at the sea does not begin with the army. It begins with a command, a history of signs, and a people led out of captivity. Fear sees the pursuers as the whole story. Faith must remember the Lord who began the story and has not surrendered the people to the power behind them.

**The Cry Opens a Crisis of Interpretation**

The companions have not changed the physical situation by speaking. They have revealed how they interpret it. Their words place a question before Moses and before the reader: does being surrounded mean being abandoned? The answer will not deny the danger. It will reinterpret the danger in light of divine presence.

That makes the verse a truthful beginning for the next response. The Israelites' fear is not the final word, but it is the word that must be answered. A messenger cannot help a frightened community by pretending that its eyes are wrong about the army's nearness. He must show what the eyes have not yet considered: the Lord who guides can create a way where human sight sees none.

Fear describes the closing of human options, not the closing of divine possibility. The two groups stand face to face, but only one group knows why it has been brought there.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:62

> Moses reassured ˹them˺, “Absolutely not! My Lord is certainly with me—He will guide me.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Moses Rejects Despair Without Denying the Army**

Moses begins with an emphatic refusal: absolutely not. He does not accept the companions' conclusion that the pursuit has ended their hope. His answer is not a claim that the Egyptians are far away or that the sea is easy to cross. He rejects the meaning they have attached to the danger. The army may be near, but it is not the lord of the situation.

This is reassurance rather than rebuke. Moses does not shame the frightened people for seeing what he also sees. He speaks into their fear with a stronger truth. The purpose of courage is not to erase facts but to place facts under God's companionship. The sea and the army remain, yet neither is allowed to define the outcome before God has finished guiding His servants.

**My Lord Makes Faith Personal and Relational**

Moses says my Lord. The phrase is personal without being private. He knows the Lord who called him, supported him before Pharaoh, and led the Israelites out at night. That relationship gives him a basis for confidence when ordinary evidence points toward defeat. He does not rely on a general idea that some power might help. He relies on the Lord who has already acted in his mission.

The possessive also helps the companions. Moses is not claiming a special deity unavailable to them. The Lord who is with him is the Lord who brought the people out and who has commanded their journey. His personal trust becomes a public reminder that divine care has not stopped at the edge of the sea. The prophet's certainty is meant to steady the community, not to glorify the prophet.

**With Me Does Not Mean Away From Them**

Moses says that his Lord is with me, yet he is answering a group. The statement does not exclude the companions from divine care. It identifies the point from which Moses speaks. As the messenger responsible for the next command, he has confidence that God will guide him. That guidance will open the way for all who follow the command.

The phrase also avoids a shallow promise of comfort. Divine companionship is not described as removal of every obstacle. Moses stands with the sea before him and the army behind him. The Lord is with him within the crisis, not only after the crisis has become safe. This makes the reassurance stronger. God's presence is proved by His ability to guide through danger, not by the absence of danger.

**Guidance Is the Answer to Being Overtaken**

The companions have concluded that they are trapped because they can see no route. Moses answers with guidance rather than with a map. He does not yet know the visible form the rescue will take, but he knows that the Lord will direct the next step. Guidance means that the people do not have to invent an escape through panic or return to Pharaoh by despair.

This is a different kind of knowledge from predicting every detail. Moses does not announce how the sea will respond or what the Egyptian host will do. He states the principle that will govern the unknown: God will guide. Trust can be firm without possessing the full plan. The servant needs enough light to obey the next command, not a complete view of the road.

**The Prophet's Confidence Is Built on Earlier Evidence**

Moses has already experienced God's help in the court. His staff became a sign, the magicians recognized the truth, and Pharaoh's threats did not cancel the mission. The sea crisis is not his first encounter with overwhelming power. His reassurance grows from a history of divine acts, even though the present danger is new.

Memory gives confidence a rational foundation. Moses is not making a brave sound to keep the crowd calm. He has reasons to trust the Lord who has led him this far. A person may still feel fear while remembering those reasons. Confidence does not require that the heart become incapable of alarm. It requires that alarm no longer dictate the conclusion.

**Absolutely Not Protects the Community From False Certainty**

The emphatic opening interrupts the companions' sentence before it becomes the group's settled belief. In a crisis, one person's fearful interpretation can spread quickly and make obedience seem foolish. Moses stops that spread. He refuses to let the language of inevitable defeat become the community's only account of reality.

His answer offers a new sentence for the group to carry: the Lord is with us through His messenger, and guidance remains possible. That sentence does not solve the physical problem by itself. It changes the posture with which the people will receive the next command. They will need courage to follow when the path opens, and courage begins by refusing despair before the path is visible.

**Guidance Will Make the Impossible Specific**

The verse ends with a promise of guidance, not with a completed rescue. That ending preserves the role of obedience. God will show what to do, and Moses will have to act on what is shown. The community is reassured before it knows the method, because faith often begins at the point where method is still hidden.

The statement therefore holds together trust and movement. Moses does not tell the people to sit and wait for an abstract miracle. He tells them that the Lord will guide him, which means a command will follow and the people must be ready to obey. Despair says the road is closed. Moses says the Guide has not ceased to lead.

The assurance is therefore not a conclusion drawn from the landscape. It is confidence in the Lord who commands the landscape.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:63

> So We inspired Moses: “Strike the sea with your staff,” and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Guidance Becomes a Concrete Command**

The promise that God would guide Moses now becomes an instruction: strike the sea with the staff. Moses is not asked to reason his way through the barrier or to wait for a natural opening. The command joins a familiar instrument to an extraordinary result. The staff that served him in ordinary work becomes the means through which God opens a path for the trapped community.

The action is simple, but the result is beyond ordinary power. The sea splits, and each side stands like a huge mountain. The image does not describe a shallow crossing or a small retreat of water. It presents a passage through a body of water whose walls appear immense. The miracle answers the companions' fear at the exact point where fear saw only an impassable boundary.

**The Staff Is a Means, Not the Source**

The staff appears again, but its repetition should not turn it into a magical object. Moses does not possess an independent power that can command seas. He acts after inspiration, and the staff serves a divine command. The instrument matters because God chooses to use it, not because wood has a hidden authority of its own.

This distinction protects worship from attaching itself to a created means. People may honor the sign and forget the Sender if they focus on the object. The Qur'anic account keeps the order clear: God inspires, Moses obeys, and the sea parts. The staff is a means within obedience. Its ordinary history makes the divine act more visible because the object itself cannot explain the outcome.

**The Sea Is Described Without Being Named**

The Qur'an does not identify the exact body of water. Muslim and Jewish tradition commonly associates the crossing with the Red Sea, but the revealed verse itself emphasizes the miracle rather than the geographical label. Leaving the name unspecified keeps attention on God's power and on the deliverance of the people, not on a detail the text has chosen not to settle.

This restraint is important in interpretation. A traditional identification may help readers imagine the scene, but it should not be presented as though the verse supplied a modern map reference. The certain facts are enough: Moses was commanded to strike the sea, it split, and the divided water stood like mountains. The miracle's meaning does not depend on claiming more geographical precision than revelation gives.

**Mountain Walls Make the Sign Unmistakable**

Some natural processes can move water or change its level, but the image of each part standing like a huge mountain points beyond ordinary retreat. The wonder lies not merely in water being absent from a path. The sea is made into walls that remain separated long enough for a people to cross. The form of the miracle removes the explanation that a temporary shallow or current alone caused the passage.

The comparison with mountains also changes the emotional landscape. A sea that had represented a barrier becomes a corridor bounded by massive structures. What terrifies from a distance becomes the means of escape. The same water can be an obstacle or a path according to God's command. Creation is not independent of the Creator's will, and a barrier can become a road without ceasing to be powerful.

**The Command Requires Action at the Moment of Fear**

Moses had just reassured the people that God would guide him. The next guidance is not merely inward. It requires a physical act. He must strike the sea, and the people must be prepared to enter the opening. Faith becomes effective through obedience to a command whose result could not have been predicted from the object in Moses' hand.

This prevents a passive understanding of trust. Moses cannot say that because God is with him, he need not act. Nor can the people remain at the shore waiting for a path to become familiar. The command creates a route through the impossible, but the servants must respond to it. Divine help does not remove human obedience; it makes obedience fruitful.

**The Two Sides Display a Created Order Under Command**

The sea is not destroyed. It is divided, and each part takes the form of a mountain. The miracle preserves the created substance while changing its relation to the travelers. Water becomes a wall and the seabed becomes a road. This detail shows that divine power does not need to erase creation to govern it.

The same principle appears in other signs. God can use ordinary objects, natural elements, and human actions without being limited by their usual patterns. A believer should not make the mistake of treating regularity as a boundary around God's ability. The ordinary order is real, but it is not a prison for the One who established it.

**A Way Opens Where Human Sight Found None**

Moses' assurance was not an optimistic reading of the landscape. It was trust in the Guide who could create a way. The sea's division vindicates the distinction between visible facts and final possibilities. The people were genuinely surrounded, yet they were not abandoned. Their inability to see a path did not mean that no path existed in God's decree.

The verse is therefore the decisive answer to the cry of being overtaken. It does not tell the frightened companions to deny the sea. It shows the sea obeying a command from the Lord. The barrier becomes evidence that guidance can arrive through the very thing that seemed to make escape impossible.

The miracle also protects the community from believing that fear had been foolish. The sea was a real barrier; God's command made it a passage.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:64

> We drew the pursuers to that place,

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pursuers Are Brought Into the Scene of Deliverance**

The verse shifts attention from the opened sea to the Egyptian host. God draws the pursuers to that place. Pharaoh's army has followed with confidence, expecting to recover the Israelites. It now arrives at the location where the sea has become a path for the oppressed and a test for the oppressor.

The wording exposes a reversal in movement. The Egyptians believe they are acting freely and closing the distance by their own strength. The narrative reveals that their arrival is also within God's action. They are brought to the place of judgment, not because their pursuit is wise or legitimate, but because their own decision to chase has led them there. Divine sovereignty surrounds the choices of the pursuers without removing their responsibility for those choices.

**A Place of Rescue Can Also Be a Place of Judgment**

The same location has two meanings. For Moses and his companions, it is a route opened by God. For the Egyptians, it is the place toward which the consequences of tyranny are drawing them. A physical site does not carry one fixed moral meaning for everyone who enters it. The sea is a path for those obeying God and a danger for those pursuing oppression.

This contrast helps explain why the verse says that the pursuers were drawn there rather than simply saying they arrived. Their movement is being interpreted from beyond their own intention. They think they are following fugitives. In the larger account, they are entering a place where the distinction between divine deliverance and human arrogance will become visible.

**Pursuit Can Lead a Powerful Person Beyond His Safe Ground**

Pharaoh's strength appeared greatest in the palace, among advisers, wealth, and organized forces. The sea removes him from that secure setting. His army must act in an environment where the ruler's usual resources cannot explain what is happening. The pursuit has carried the host away from the foundations of its confidence and into a path determined by another power.

This is a general pattern in the judgment of tyrants. A ruler may control the conditions in which his authority is praised, but his choices can lead him into circumstances that expose its limits. The Egyptians have left the gardens and residences behind. Now they enter the sea's divided space, where the host's readiness must meet the Lord who opened the way.

**Divine Drawing Does Not Excuse the Pursuers**

The phrase We drew does not make the Egyptians innocent victims of a hidden plan. They chose to pursue a people whom God had commanded to leave. Their anger, military preparation, and claim of ownership are part of the moral background. God's drawing of them to the place brings judgment upon a choice already made; it does not create the choice against their will.

This balance matters. One error denies divine sovereignty and imagines that history lies outside God's control. Another uses sovereignty to erase human accountability. The verse holds both together. God governs the place and outcome, while the pursuers remain responsible for entering the path with the intention of recovering the oppressed.

**The Pronoun Others Keeps the Host in Its Moral Category**

The source description calls the Egyptians the others, distinguishing them from Moses and those with him. This simple contrast is not an ethnic judgment on every Egyptian. It identifies the group in the immediate scene: the people who are pursuing rather than the people being delivered. Their category is defined by action and allegiance in this event.

That is important for reading the story without crude collective blame. The judgment falls on a host that has chosen Pharaoh's pursuit, not on every person who shares an origin or language with the army. The narrative's moral line is drawn by oppression and its defense. People are judged by what they do with the authority and knowledge they possess.

**The Place Is Set Before the Final Act**

The verse ends with the pursuers drawn to the place, not yet describing the water closing over them. That pause preserves the tension. The army has reached the opening and appears to have followed successfully. The path that saved Israel is now occupied by those who seek to reclaim Israel.

The scene is therefore arranged for a final contrast. The Egyptians have entered the space created by God's sign, but they have not become participants in the sign's purpose. They see the route as an opportunity for pursuit; the Lord sees it as the place where pursuit will be judged. A path can be open without being safe for every intention.

**God's Deliverance Does Not Require Hiding the Enemy**

The Israelites are not saved by the Egyptians losing their way or failing to notice the opening. The pursuers are brought close enough for the deliverance to be seen in relation to the threat. This makes the rescue public and complete. The oppressor is not merely kept at a distance; his confidence is brought into direct contact with God's act.

That pattern gives the community a deeper assurance. Their safety does not depend on the enemy's ignorance. It depends on the Lord's command over the situation. The pursuers can see the route, follow it, and still be unable to turn it into possession. The place belongs to God's plan, not to the first army that enters it.

The open path is therefore not a prize that belongs to whoever reaches it first. It is a commanded mercy, and mercy cannot be seized by the force that pursues those to whom it was given. The pursuers arrive at God's opening without gaining authority over it. The same command that creates the passage also determines who may pass through it and who is left behind.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:65

> and delivered Moses and those with him all together.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Deliverance Includes the Whole Community**

God delivers Moses and those with him all together. The phrase refuses a narrow picture of salvation in which only the prophet reaches safety while the ordinary people are left behind. Moses is named because he is the messenger and leader, but the act of deliverance embraces the community that followed his command. Divine care reaches the many through the mission entrusted to one servant.

The words all together also emphasize completeness. The Israelites do not escape in a partial or uncertain way, with some families saved and others lost to the pursuit. The deliverance is communal. It creates a people who have crossed from Pharaoh's reach into a new condition under God's protection. Their freedom is not merely Moses' private vindication. It is the rescue of those whose lives were bound to the oppressive order.

**The Prophet's Safety Is Joined to the People's Safety**

Moses is not delivered into a separate privilege. His fate is narrated alongside the fate of those with him. This reflects the nature of prophetic leadership. A messenger's success is not measured by personal survival while the people remain vulnerable. The prophet guides, warns, and moves with the community, and God's rescue confirms the message by protecting those who trust it.

This does not erase differences among the people. Some may have had stronger faith, greater fear, or different responsibilities. The verse gathers them under one act because the crisis was communal and the command was communal. Salvation creates solidarity. Those who crossed together become witnesses that God's promise can include an entire oppressed people.

**All Together Counters Pharaoh's Fragmentation**

Pharaoh's system had classified the Israelites by labor, status, and usefulness. It could divide families and reduce people to separate units of production. God's deliverance gathers them as one body. They are no longer counted according to the categories imposed by the palace. They stand together as servants whom God has rescued.

The phrase also counters the logic that only the strong or useful deserve escape. A community is not saved by selecting its most impressive members. The elderly, children, workers, and those who cannot fight belong to the deliverance. A just liberation refuses to leave the vulnerable as the price of speed. God's act protects the people as a people.

**Deliverance Is a Gift Received Through Obedience**

The Israelites did not create the sea path. They did not defeat Pharaoh's host by their own strength. Yet they had to leave, follow Moses, and cross the route opened by God. The gift does not make their response irrelevant. It makes their response possible and meaningful.

This balance prevents both pride and passivity. The people cannot boast that they rescued themselves, but they also cannot say that obedience was unnecessary. Faith moves when God opens the way. The phrase all together includes the community's shared movement through the danger, not a rescue that happened without their participation.

**The Earlier Warning Becomes Visible Fulfillment**

God had told Moses that He would be with him and guide him. The deliverance is the visible fulfillment of that assurance. Moses' confidence at the shore was not an empty speech. The Lord who accompanied him in Pharaoh's court has now accompanied him through the sea. The people witness the continuity between promise and act.

A parallel account in 2:50 recalls the sea being parted, Israel being saved, and Pharaoh's people drowning before the witnesses. That cross-reference confirms the public and communal character of this deliverance. It is not a private vision known only to Moses. It is an event through which a people learns what God's protection means.

**The Word Delivered Leaves No Room for Partial Victory**

The verse does not say that Moses and some of his companions escaped. It says God delivered them all together. The wording closes the possibility that Pharaoh's pursuit achieved a partial recovery. The ruler's claim over Israel has failed in full. The community is no longer in the hands of the host that chased it.

This completeness also gives the following judgment its proper setting. The Egyptians are not drowning while the Israelites remain mixed with them. The rescued people have been brought out. Divine justice does not require leaving the oppressed in the same danger in order to punish the oppressor. God separates the two groups and establishes the difference between them.

**A Community Saved Together Must Remember Together**

The memory of deliverance belongs to the whole people. No single survivor can treat it as a private achievement. They crossed because they were led, and they were delivered as a body. Shared rescue creates a shared duty to resist the return of the values that made Pharaoh's rule possible.

The verse therefore gives more than a happy ending to a chase. It establishes the community's identity after oppression. They are the people whom God delivered together. Their future must be shaped by gratitude, justice, and obedience rather than by the fear and fragmentation imposed by the tyrant.

The phrase all together also means that no rescued person is treated as an unnecessary remainder. The community's weakest members share in the deliverance, and the community's memory must preserve that fact. Freedom is not complete when only the strong can reach it.

The wording also distinguishes divine deliverance from a private escape by a heroic individual. Moses is saved with the people, and the people are saved with Moses. Leadership and community remain joined. The messenger's honor lies in guiding others to safety, while the community's honor lies in trusting the guidance enough to move together. No one can claim the crossing as a private possession. Deliverance is received as a trust, and gratitude requires remembering the people whose safety was joined to one's own.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:66

> Then We drowned the others.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pursuers Meet the End of Their Own Pursuit**

The verse describes the fate of those who followed Pharaoh into the sea: they are drowned. The sentence is brief because the moral sequence has already been established. Pharaoh refused the command to release Israel, mobilized the cities, called the departing people a threat, and sent a ready host after them. The drowning is not an arbitrary disaster detached from those choices. It is the judgment that overtakes a force committed to recovering the oppressed.

The word others distinguishes the drowned host from Moses and those delivered with him. The separation is complete. The same sea that opened as a path for the Israelites does not become a possession of the pursuers. God's sign has a different consequence for each group according to the purpose with which each entered the scene.

**Drowning Is a Divine Judgment, Not a Victory of Human Force**

The Egyptians are not defeated by an Israelite army. No human host is credited with overpowering Pharaoh. God Himself is the agent of the drowning. That attribution matters because the story is about the limits of tyranny before divine sovereignty, not about one earthly power replacing another.

The Israelites' deliverance does not turn them into conquerors who must destroy Pharaoh by their own strength. They are carried through the sea while God judges the pursuers. This protects the rescued community from pride and keeps the moral source of the reversal clear. The Lord who opened the way also closed the path on those who used it to pursue injustice.

**The Same Water Reveals Two Opposite Relations to God**

The sea is not good for one group and evil for another by nature. Its role changes according to God's command and the people's relation to that command. For Moses and his companions, the water becomes a passage. For the Egyptians, it becomes the place where their pursuit ends. The contrast shows that creation is under divine governance and does not belong to the purposes of whoever reaches it first.

This also gives the event symbolic force without reducing it to symbolism. The oppressed pass through what looked impossible because God commands a way. The oppressor is swallowed by the same setting because he enters in defiance. The physical event carries a moral distinction: obedience finds rescue, while arrogant pursuit meets judgment.

**The Host's Readiness Cannot Defeat the Decree**

Pharaoh had described his people as alert and prepared. The army had equipment, numbers, and the confidence of a state that believed its resources could recover the Israelites. None of that readiness alters the outcome. Preparation is a means, not a guarantee. A force can be organized for victory and still be moving toward its own destruction.

The lesson is not that planning is useless. It is that planning cannot become a substitute for justice or a claim to control the result. Pharaoh's army prepared to defend an unlawful possession. The better equipped it was, the more clearly its defeat exposed the limits of its purpose. Human readiness remains subject to the Lord who gives and removes power.

**Judgment Makes the Earlier Warning Complete**

God had told Moses that the Israelites would be pursued. The pursuit happened at sunrise, and the host was drawn to the divided sea. The drowning now completes the warning's hidden meaning. Pursuit was not proof that the Israelites had been abandoned. It was the route through which the tyrant's claim would be brought to its end.

This sequence gives the rescued community a way to remember danger without glorifying danger. They were not saved because Pharaoh's threat was imaginary. They were saved because God governed a real threat and judged the people who made it. The drowning confirms that the Lord's promise can include a frightening middle stage before deliverance is seen in full.

**The Fate Is a Warning to Every Pursuing Power**

The verse is tied to Pharaoh's host, but its principle extends beyond Egypt. A ruler who chases a people because he cannot accept their freedom may possess a large army and still be moving toward judgment. The power to pursue is not proof of the right to pursue. A state can make an unjust claim appear permanent until God removes its confidence.

This warning should not be used to celebrate the suffering of every defeated opponent. The text concerns a tyrannical host whose pursuit is part of a sustained system of oppression. It teaches that judgment belongs to God and that believers must not assume the role of divine executioner. The proper response is humility before the Lord who alone knows the whole moral account.

**The Drowned Host Leaves No Rival Lord Behind**

Pharaoh had claimed authority over worship and bodies. His drowning strips that claim of its public force. The host that enforced it is gone, and the Israelites are no longer required to measure their future by the ruler's permission. The sea has become a boundary between the old order and the community God has delivered.

The short sentence carries finality. There is no negotiation after the drowning and no recovery of Pharaoh's position through a new threat. The tyrant's claim ends where his pursuit ends. The Lord who saved Moses and those with him has shown that no army can turn oppression into an everlasting right.

The finality also protects the rescued from the fear of return. Pharaoh's host cannot regroup behind them or reclaim the people through another order. The sea has closed the chapter of that pursuit. Deliverance has become a settled fact, not a temporary escape. The rescued need not live as though Pharaoh's army is still one step behind them.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:67

> Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sea Crossing Becomes Evidence for Every Witness**

The verse calls the entire episode a sign. The sign includes the command to leave, the opening of the sea, the rescue of Moses and his companions, and the drowning of the pursuing host. No single detail carries the whole argument by itself. Together the events reveal God's power, His care for the oppressed, and the danger of treating tyranny as permanent.

A sign points beyond the event to its Lord. The sea crossing is not preserved as an adventure story whose value lies in suspense. It tells the audience that creation obeys God, that prophecy is confirmed through divine action, and that judgment can reach a ruler who seems beyond challenge. The event is historical in the narrative and theological in its meaning.

**Most Still Refuse the Meaning of What They See**

The statement that most would not believe follows a miracle of extraordinary public force. That sequence rejects the idea that every person believes once evidence becomes dramatic enough. The event can be clear while the response remains resistant. People may explain it away, refuse its demand, or admire it without surrendering their authority to God.

Most is not all. The wording leaves room for those who respond rightly, including the believers who followed Moses. It also warns against judging truth by majority.
