If God provides food through farmers and guidance through revelation, He can also provide healing through knowledge, skilled care, medicine, and the body's own processes. Means are not rivals to God when they are understood as means.

The proper attitude avoids two extremes. A person should not worship treatment as though success were guaranteed by human technique alone, nor should he abandon responsible care while claiming that trust makes action unnecessary. He may seek competent help, protect the sick, and pray for recovery, knowing that the result remains with the Lord. Reliance and effort belong together.

**Healing Reveals the Difference Between Power and Appearance**

Idols may be surrounded by requests for recovery, but they cannot heal the people who address them. Abraham has already asked whether such objects can benefit or harm. His declaration now gives a positive answer to the question of where benefit comes from. The Lord is not merely less powerless than the idols. He is the One upon whom life, nourishment, and restoration depend.

This contrast makes the idol's appearance irrelevant. A beautifully carved image cannot mend a wound, restore strength, or command the hidden processes of the body. Human beings may honor it, decorate it, and plead before it, but none of those actions gives it healing power. The Lord heals without needing an image to represent His authority.

**The Healer Is Also the Creator**

Because God created Abraham, healing is not an arbitrary intervention by an outsider. The Creator knows the body from its origin and its limits. He knows what is damaged, what can recover, and what wisdom may lie beyond immediate recovery. This does not make suffering easy, but it gives the sick person a foundation for trust that is deeper than the success of any one remedy.

The order of Abraham's words matters here. Creation came first, provision followed, and healing appears within the same relation. The Lord is not a specialist invoked only in emergencies. He is the continuous Lord of the whole person. Sickness reveals a need that was present all along: dependence on the One who gives and sustains life.

**Healing Calls for Humility From the Healthy**

Those who are well may imagine that health is a permanent possession earned entirely by discipline or strength. Abraham's wording corrects that illusion. Health is a mercy, and its continuation is not guaranteed by human confidence. Remembering God as Healer should make the healthy grateful and compassionate toward those whose bodies are suffering.

Such humility should also prevent judgment of the ill. A person's sickness is not proof that God has rejected him, just as health is not proof of superior virtue. Abraham speaks of being sick within the account of divine care. The condition can be a trial, a means of dependence, or part of a wisdom the person does not yet see. The community's duty is support, not contempt.

**Prayer and Treatment Can Share One Direction**

Prayer does not replace care, and care does not replace prayer. Both can be directed toward the same Lord. The patient asks for healing, the caregiver works with skill, and the family offers patience and protection. Each recognizes that ability and outcome are gifts rather than reasons for self-glorification.

Abraham's statement therefore forms a complete posture toward illness. Seek what helps, accept the limits of control, and keep hope attached to God rather than to an object or technique. The Lord who heals is not reduced to a mechanism, and the means He provides are not turned into idols. That balance guards both faith and responsible action.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:81

> And He ˹is the One Who˺ will cause me to die, and then bring me back to life.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Death Belongs to the Same Lord as Creation**

Abraham's account of God moves from creation and provision to death. The transition is deliberate. The Lord who gives life does not lose authority when life reaches its appointed end. Death is not an outside power that interrupts God's rule. It occurs under the command of the One who created the person and sustained him throughout his days.

This conviction changes the meaning of mortality. Abraham does not speak as though death is a rival deity or a meaningless accident. He places it within the relation between servant and Lord. The human being receives life for a time, then returns to the One who gave it. Idols cannot claim that authority because they neither began Abraham's life nor determine its true end.

**The One Who Ends Life Also Restores It**

The verse joins death and renewed life in one sentence. The pairing rejects the idea that death is an absolute disappearance. If God causes death, then death remains within His power; if He brings life again, resurrection is not a problem for the Creator. The second act is not harder for Him than the first. Both belong to the same sovereign command.

Abraham's wording also preserves continuity between the person who dies and the person who is raised. The God who knows and sustains the individual in this life is able to restore him after death. Resurrection is therefore not the creation of an unrelated replacement. It is the return of a servant to the Lord before whom his life already stood.

**Resurrection Makes the Present Life Accountable**

Life would have a different moral weight if death were the final boundary. Abraham's mention of being brought back to life places every choice under a future horizon. Worship, truthfulness, oppression, and repentance are not matters that vanish when the body is buried. The Creator who gives life again will also reveal what the servant made of the life first given.

This is why resurrection belongs in Abraham's argument against idolatry. A powerless object cannot judge the dead or restore them. A shrine may preserve a memory, but it cannot call a person from the grave. Only the Lord who governs life and death can make the moral history of a human being reach its appointed judgment.

**Death Is Not Proof of Divine Abandonment**

People often experience death as loss, silence, and separation. Abraham does not deny that pain. He gives it a theological place. The Lord remains the Lord over the servant even when the servant can no longer act, speak, or protect himself. Death removes human control, but it does not remove divine knowledge.

That belief can produce grief without despair. The dead are not imagined as self-sustaining, and the living are not asked to pretend that parting is easy. They are asked to trust that the One who receives the life of a servant has not ceased to govern it. Death becomes a passage under God's authority rather than evidence that the world has fallen outside it.

**The Personal Pronoun Keeps the Doctrine Near**

Abraham says that God will cause me to die and bring me back to life. He does not hide behind a general statement about humanity. The doctrine touches his own body, his own future, and his own accountability. Personal faith becomes stronger when it includes the self rather than remaining a claim made about other people.

The pronoun also prevents resurrection from becoming a distant theory. Abraham expects to stand within the event he describes. His worship is shaped by the certainty that the Lord's power concerns him directly. Each believer must eventually make the same recognition: the One who gives life to the world will also address me as a particular servant.

**Death Breaks the Illusion of Self-Sufficiency**

Food and drink can make a person feel independent because daily needs are often met through familiar means. Death exposes the limit of that confidence. No amount of wealth, skill, medicine, or social power can make a creature its own source of life. The hour of death reveals what was true from the beginning: the human being is dependent.

Abraham does not use this dependence to demean human effort. He places effort in its proper scale. A person may care for the body and plan for the future, but he cannot grant himself immortality. The Lord alone controls the boundary that no created means can cross. Remembering death therefore turns competence into humility rather than pride.

**The Two Acts Announce a Complete Divine Care**

God's care is not limited to keeping Abraham alive. It includes receiving him at death and restoring him for the final meeting. The full arc of the servant's existence remains in God's hands. This makes divine care larger than comfort in the present. It reaches through the grave and gives the future a meaning that the idols cannot supply.

A parallel prayer in 14:39 praises God for granting Abraham children in old age. That account and this verse share the same outlook: human life is received at every stage, whether beginning, continuing, ending, or being restored. Abraham's worship is therefore grounded in the Lord's complete authority over the servant's journey.

**The Lord of Life and Death Is Worthy of Worship**

The verse completes a direct test of the idols. They cannot create Abraham, guide him, provide for him, heal him, end his life, or restore him. They are surrounded by worship, but they have no share in the acts that define the servant's existence. The Lord alone performs them and therefore alone deserves ultimate allegiance.

Death and resurrection together leave no room for a divided trust. Abraham's people must choose whether their hope rests on powerless objects or on the One who governs the whole passage from life to death and back to life. The choice is not between competing styles of devotion. It is between reality and an object that cannot act.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:82

> And He is ˹the One˺ Who, I hope, will forgive my flaws on Judgment Day.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abraham's Hope Faces the Day of Judgment**

Abraham's description of God ends with forgiveness and the Day of Judgment. The future day gives his hope a definite setting. He is not asking for a vague feeling that everything will be fine. He is looking toward the day when deeds are exposed and the servant stands before the Lord. Hope becomes serious when it is attached to accountability.

The wording keeps both truths together. Abraham trusts God's mercy, yet he does not treat forgiveness as something he can claim by right. He hopes for it. That posture is not weakness. It is the humility of a servant who knows the greatness of the Lord and the limits of his own record. Confidence belongs to God's promise and mercy, not to the servant's ability to declare himself safe.

**Hope Is Not Presumption**

A person may hope for forgiveness while still fearing the consequences of wrongdoing. Hope moves the heart toward God; presumption makes the heart careless. Abraham's words model the first kind. He names the Lord as the One who may forgive, so the request rests on divine generosity rather than on a denial that flaws exist.

The distinction matters because religious language can be used to excuse sin. If forgiveness is assumed without repentance, hope has been distorted into permission. Abraham's hope is spoken by someone who has already separated himself from idols and placed his life under God's guidance. The heart that hopes in mercy also takes the judgment seriously.

**The Language of Flaws Invites Humility**

The translation uses flaws for what Abraham attributes to himself. The source tradition records several ways of understanding this difficult confession. Some interpreters treat it as the language of aspiration and servant humility, not an admission of ordinary moral corruption. Others connect it to episodes that appeared outwardly problematic and explain them within the protection granted to prophets.

Whatever interpretation one prefers, the verse does not turn Abraham into a person who trusts his own perfection. He speaks as a servant seeking God's pardon. That is the point believers can receive without making careless claims about prophetic error. A righteous person can be sincere, obedient, and still stand in need of divine forgiveness in the language of dependence.

**Forgiveness Belongs to the Lord's Character**

Abraham does not seek forgiveness from an idol, an ancestor, or an intermediary. He identifies God as the One who forgives. The earlier verses showed that God gives life, guidance, provision, and healing; this verse shows that divine care also addresses moral failure. The Lord's authority reaches the conscience as fully as it reaches the body.

That relation protects the servant from two opposite mistakes. He must not treat guilt as so small that it needs no pardon, and he must not treat guilt as so great that God's mercy cannot reach it. The Lord is both judge and forgiver. Hope becomes truthful when it bows before judgment without despairing of mercy.

**The Day Gives Hope a Moral Direction**

Hope for forgiveness on Judgment Day is not an escape from moral seriousness. It directs the present life toward repentance, repair, and obedience. A person who expects to meet God cannot be satisfied with the appearance of goodness. He asks whether the heart is turning toward the Lord and whether wrongs are being abandoned rather than merely renamed.

The Day also prevents worldly approval from becoming the final measure. A person may be praised by people and still need forgiveness; another may be criticized by people and still be accepted by God. Abraham's hope relocates the decisive verdict. It will not be issued by an idol, a family tradition, or a crowd, but by the Lord before whom all deeds are known.

**The Prayer Is an Example for Believers**

The exegetical discussion about Abraham's hope also explains why the verse can guide ordinary believers. A person who knows he is answerable should ask God for forgiveness rather than rely on self-congratulation. The prayer teaches a proper balance: hope keeps repentance alive, fear keeps hope from becoming careless, and trust keeps fear from becoming despair.

Abraham's language gives believers permission to speak honestly about their need for mercy. They do not have to pretend that spiritual maturity means never needing pardon. Nor should they use their need as an excuse to remain unchanged. The request is a movement toward God, and movement toward God includes leaving the flaws that obstruct obedience.

**A Parallel Prayer Confirms the Pattern**

In the prayer recorded in 14:41, Abraham asks God to forgive him, his parents, and the believers when judgment is established. That parallel shows that forgiveness is not a marginal concern in Abraham's devotion. It appears within his public hopes for his family and the believing community. Mercy is sought personally and shared with others.

The two prayers also show that hope can be specific without becoming presumptuous. Abraham knows the day of judgment will come, knows that forgiveness belongs to God, and still asks with humility. His certainty concerns God's authority and mercy; the servant's own standing remains a matter for prayer.

**Mercy Completes the Account of Divine Care**

The Lord who feeds the body and heals illness also forgives the servant's flaws. These forms of care are not unrelated. Physical need reveals dependence, and moral need reveals a deeper dependence that no meal, remedy, or social honor can solve. Forgiveness restores the relation that sin damages; it is a mercy more precious than worldly security.

Abraham's hope therefore closes his description of the Lord without closing the door of humility. He will die and be raised, and he will stand before God needing mercy. The proper response is neither pride in one's record nor despair over one's weakness. It is hope directed to the One who alone can forgive on the Day when every false refuge has ended.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:83

> “My Lord! Grant me wisdom, and join me with the righteous.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abraham Asks for Wisdom From His Lord**

Abraham's prayer turns from describing God's acts to asking for gifts. He begins with wisdom. The translation renders the key term as wisdom, while the exegetical tradition also connects it with sound judgment, understanding, and the capacity to decide rightly. The request is larger than information. Abraham wants knowledge governed by truth and action governed by that knowledge.

Calling God my Lord places wisdom inside a relationship of formation. Abraham is not asking for cleverness that will make him independent. He is asking the Lord who created and guided him to deepen that guidance. Wisdom is therefore a form of servanthood. It helps a person see what matters, distinguish truth from appearance, and choose the response that obedience requires.

**Wisdom Is More Than Winning an Argument**

Abraham has just confronted his people about idols. His wisdom is visible in the clarity of those questions, but the prayer prevents us from reducing wisdom to debate skill. A person may defeat an opponent verbally and still lack justice, mercy, or self-control. True wisdom unites clear thought with right purpose.

The request also guards against pride after success. Abraham does not assume that having exposed an error means he has no further need of God. The messenger continues to ask for understanding. Every correct argument must be carried by a heart that knows how to speak, when to remain patient, and how to protect truth from becoming a vehicle for ego.

**The Term Can Be Read as Judgment**

Some exegetes understand the Arabic ḥukm as wisdom and understanding; others connect it with judgment or authority. The first reading emphasizes inward discernment, while the second includes the ability to decide and govern by truth. These meanings support one another. Sound judgment requires understanding, and understanding becomes complete when it directs a decision.

A narrow reading would separate the mind from public responsibility. Abraham's prayer does not. The person who sees truth must also ask how to embody it in relations, leadership, and moral choices. Wisdom is not a private possession that never reaches conduct. It is the light by which a servant judges himself and acts toward others.

**The Request Does Not Mean Abraham Lacked Prophetic Guidance**

The source tradition notes a question about interpreting judgment as prophethood, since Abraham was already a prophet. The stronger lesson is that a prophet can ask for an increase in wisdom without implying that he was previously unguided. Guidance is not a one-time certificate. A servant continues to receive clarity, firmness, and deeper understanding throughout his mission.

This helps believers understand their own prayers. Asking God for guidance does not mean that previous guidance was false. It means that the servant knows his need is continuous. The path may be known in principle while particular choices remain difficult. Wisdom asks God to keep the heart capable of applying known truth to new circumstances.

**Joining the Righteous Is a Request for Company**

Abraham pairs wisdom with being joined to the righteous. Knowledge alone can isolate a person or feed superiority. Righteous company gives wisdom a human setting in which it can be practiced, corrected, and shared. The request is not simply to be called righteous. It is to belong among people whose loyalty to God shapes their conduct.

The righteous may include prophets, those accepted by God, and servants who remain content and faithful through changing conditions. These descriptions differ in emphasis but converge on a life ordered by obedience. Abraham asks for companionship in that order. He knows that a person is influenced by the people with whom he stands and that truth is strengthened by a community that lives it.

**Righteous Company Reaches Beyond This Life**

The wording can include being with the righteous in this world and in the Hereafter. In this life, it means shared work, counsel, worship, and moral support. In the Hereafter, it means acceptance among those whose hearts and actions were sound. Abraham's request therefore joins present belonging to final destiny without confusing the two.

A person cannot earn righteousness merely by attaching his name to a respected group. The company must be joined through truth and conduct. At the same time, no servant should imagine that private excellence makes community unnecessary. Abraham, a prophet and friend of God, still asks to be placed among the righteous. His example makes humility part of righteousness.

**Wisdom and Company Protect Each Other**

Wisdom without righteous company can become self-reliance. Company without wisdom can become blind conformity. Abraham asks for both. Understanding helps a community remain faithful rather than merely traditional, while a faithful community helps understanding remain humble and useful.

This balance answers the earlier defense of idolatry through ancestors. Abraham does not ask to be bound to any inherited group. He asks to be joined with the righteous, a moral category measured by devotion to God rather than by ancestry. The right company is not the oldest or largest; it is the company that makes truth easier to recognize and obey.

**A Related Prayer Extends the Same Concern**

In 14:40, Abraham asks that he and some of his descendants be made keepers of prayer. That parallel shows how his requests combine personal obedience with the formation of a faithful community. He does not seek wisdom as a private distinction. He seeks a life and a lineage ordered toward worship.

The two prayers illuminate this verse without replacing it. Wisdom supplies judgment, while righteous company supplies a setting in which judgment can serve God. Abraham's request is therefore a prayer for the whole shape of faithful existence: to understand rightly, act rightly, and stand with those who do the same.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:84

> Bless me with honourable mention among later generations.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abraham Asks for a True Legacy**

Abraham asks God for honourable mention among later generations. The request is not a demand for fame detached from truth. He asks for a legacy that remains worthy when the generation that knows him personally has passed away. Honourable mention means that his name will be carried with praise because his life pointed people toward God.

The prayer places legacy under divine gift. Abraham does not try to manufacture his reputation through monuments, slogans, or control of memory. He asks the Lord to preserve what is true in the way later people speak of him. That difference matters. Publicity can make a name widely known, but only truth makes remembrance honourable.

**Later Generations Test the Meaning of Renown**

A person's reputation among contemporaries can be shaped by fear, fashion, or political power. Later generations stand farther from those pressures. Their memory can still be distorted, but time exposes the weakness of a reputation built only on control. Abraham asks for a remembrance that survives because the good in his message continues to serve people.

The prayer also gives later generations a responsibility. To remember Abraham honourably is not merely to repeat his name. It is to recognize the monotheism, courage, and submission that define his legacy. A community can praise a prophet while ignoring his challenge to its own idols. True remembrance receives the truth the remembered person carried.

**Honourable Mention Is Not Vanity**

There is a difference between seeking honour for the self and asking God to make one's life a truthful benefit for others. Vanity wants admiration as proof of superiority. Abraham's request seeks a memory that keeps later people connected to faith. The desired honour is not private applause; it is the survival of a good word.

This distinction helps believers think about their own desire to be remembered. Wanting one's children or students to remember good conduct can be a form of responsibility. Wanting every mention to magnify the ego is another matter. Abraham's prayer sets the standard: remembrance is good when it carries truth, encourages righteousness, and leaves the worship of God at the center.

**The Arabic Image Joins Tongue and Truth**

The source tradition notes that the expression behind honourable mention includes the image of a tongue and the meaning of truthfulness or sincerity. That image suggests words spoken about Abraham across time, but it also asks what kind of words they are. A tongue of truth does not preserve flattering myths at the expense of the person's real message.

The phrase therefore joins reputation to moral accuracy. Abraham does not ask for a false portrait that makes him agreeable to everyone. He asks for honour grounded in truth. Later generations may differ in language and culture, yet the remembrance remains sound if it keeps his devotion to the Lord and rejection of false worship visible.

**A Good Name Is Received Through Good Deeds**

Abraham's prayer does not separate honour from the life that can support it. His later reputation is connected to his earlier patience, his refusal of idols, and his willingness to stand alone for truth. The name is not a substitute for character. It is the echo of character after the person has gone.

That principle protects remembrance from empty inheritance. Families may be proud of Abraham while failing to imitate him. Communities may claim his name while preserving the idols he opposed. Honourable mention becomes meaningful only when it directs people back to the qualities that made the mention honourable in the first place.

**The Prayer Envisions a Living Chain of Guidance**

Later generations do not receive Abraham only through books or ceremonies. They meet him through people who keep his call alive. The source tradition includes the possibility that his descendants will uphold truth, and the history of revelation presents his influence across communities. A faithful legacy is therefore active. It produces witnesses, teachers, and servants rather than merely statues.

This is why remembrance can be a mercy. A later person may find courage by seeing that an earlier servant refused the pressure of his society. The distance of time does not weaken the example. It can make the principle clearer, because the immediate social cost is no longer hidden by the success of the messenger's struggle.

**God Controls What Memory Preserves**

Human beings forget, exaggerate, and reshape the past. Abraham's prayer acknowledges that preservation of a truthful legacy lies beyond his own control. God can place a good word in later tongues and protect it from being swallowed by the idols of a new age. The servant acts faithfully; the Lord decides how the faithfulness will travel.

This is a comfort for anyone who serves without seeing the full result. A teacher may not know which sentence remains in a student's heart. A parent may not see how a child carries a practice into adulthood. Abraham's request teaches that a truthful legacy is not measured only by immediate recognition. God can make a small act speak across generations.

**A Verified Parallel Shows the Prayer's Fulfilment**

The parallel account in 37:108 states that Abraham was blessed with honourable mention among later generations. The wording confirms that the request in this verse is not self-display but a prayer whose fulfilment becomes part of the revealed account. Later communities remember Abraham as a model of devotion because God preserved his name together with his truth.

The fulfilment does not turn memory into an object of worship. Abraham's honour directs attention beyond Abraham to the Lord who granted it. That is the proper shape of prophetic legacy: the servant is remembered, but the Creator remains the reason the remembrance matters.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:85

> Make me one of those awarded the Garden of Bliss.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abraham Asks for a Place Among the Blessed**

Abraham asks to be made one of those awarded the Garden of Bliss. The request is personal, but it is not selfish. He does not ask for an isolated reward detached from the righteous. He asks to belong among those who receive the Garden as the outcome of God's mercy and acceptance. Salvation is pictured as a place and a community, not merely as escape from punishment.

The translation's Garden of Bliss renders a word that carries ease, blessing, and settled well-being. The request reaches beyond temporary comfort. Abraham has already recognized that worldly food, drink, health, and reputation are gifts that pass. He now asks for the lasting form of blessed life that belongs to the Hereafter.

**The Garden Is an Award and a Gift**

To be awarded the Garden does not mean that Abraham can purchase it through his own deeds. An award is received, and the language keeps God's generosity in view. Deeds matter because they express faith and obedience, but the servant remains dependent on the Lord's acceptance. The request is therefore a confession of need rather than a claim of entitlement.

This balance corrects two mistakes. A person may imagine that good works force God to reward him, or he may imagine that deeds do not matter because mercy is everything. Abraham's prayer joins effort and dependence. He has struggled for truth and asks God to place him among the blessed. The final gift remains God's decision.

**Bliss Is More Than Pleasure**

The word bliss suggests a condition in which the heart is safe, content, and free from the disturbances that define worldly life. It is not merely a larger collection of pleasures. Worldly pleasure can coexist with fear, rivalry, loss, and the knowledge that it will end. The Garden's bliss is settled because it is received within God's nearness and approval.

A person who asks for this Garden is asking for the completion of every sound desire. He wants peace without anxiety, joy without guilt, and companionship without betrayal. The request also purifies desire. Abraham does not ask for continued possession of idols, status, or domination. He asks for a reward whose goodness comes from the Lord.

**The Request Follows a Life of Examination**

The prayer comes from a servant who has examined worship, rejected powerless objects, and placed his trust in the Lord of all worlds. The Garden is therefore not a decorative ending added to a life of unrelated ideas. It is the destination of the allegiance declared in the surrounding passage. Abraham's hope for bliss grows from monotheism and obedience.

This connection matters for anyone who wants the reward without the path. A person cannot make the Garden a substitute for turning away from false lords. The request is powerful because Abraham has already chosen the Lord over inherited worship. The reward does not replace surrender; it completes the life shaped by surrender.

**Being Among the Awarded Preserves Humility**

Abraham asks to be one of those awarded the Garden, not to be praised as a solitary exception. The plural category keeps the prayer humble and communal. He wants to stand with servants whose faith has been accepted. Righteousness is not a private performance in which one person must outshine everyone else. It is shared belonging under God's mercy.

This also protects the believer from imagining that spiritual rank makes him independent. Even a prophet asks to be joined to a class of the blessed. The request acknowledges that honour in the Hereafter is not self-appointed. God gathers His servants, and the servant hopes to be included among them.

**The Garden Is Described as Near, Not Merely Promised**

The following scene in the chapter will describe the Garden as brought near to the reverent, but this verse should be understood on its own as the prayer for admission to that blessed destination. Nearness in the Qur'anic account conveys welcome and accessibility for those whom God honours. Abraham's request is not for an abstract reward without presence. It is for entry into a real abode of peace.

The parallel description in 37:43 places the blessed in Gardens of Bliss. That cross-reference confirms that bliss is not a vague metaphor for moral satisfaction. It names the lasting home associated with the faithful. The believer may not see it now, but the prayer gives the future a concrete direction.

**A Garden of Bliss Reorders Worldly Ambition**

People naturally seek security, comfort, and honour. Abraham does not condemn those desires; he directs them to their lasting source. The Garden offers what worldly power cannot secure. It cannot be seized by wealth, inherited through family, or guaranteed by public reputation. It is awarded by God to those whose hearts and lives have turned toward Him.

This redirection frees a person from making the world carry the weight of eternity. Work and family remain important, but they are no longer treated as final possessions. The highest ambition becomes acceptance by the Lord. A person can enjoy lawful blessings without worshipping them because he knows that the lasting Garden is better than every temporary form of ease.

**The Prayer Holds Hope and Responsibility Together**

Abraham's request is hopeful, but it does not encourage delay in obedience. A person who asks for the Garden must let that hope shape conduct now. He guards worship, seeks wisdom, joins the righteous, and turns away from the idols that compete with God. Hope becomes practical when it gives present choices an eternal direction.

The Garden of Bliss is therefore the fitting destination of the prayer's earlier movement. The servant began by recognizing God as Creator, Guide, Provider, and Healer. He now asks for the final mercy: to be received among those whose life with God becomes everlasting bliss.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:86

> Forgive my father, for he is certainly one of the misguided.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abraham's Prayer Remembers His Father**

Abraham includes his father in the prayer for forgiveness. The request shows that rejection of idolatry does not erase family feeling. Abraham has challenged his father's worship, but he has not become indifferent to his father's fate. The person who stands against a parent's error may still hope that the parent will receive mercy and leave the error behind.

That hope is not sentimental denial. Abraham calls his father misguided. He does not rename false worship as an acceptable difference in order to preserve emotional comfort. Love and moral clarity remain together. The father is dear enough to be prayed for, yet the practice is wrong enough to be named plainly.

**Misguidance Describes a Path, Not a Worthless Person**

The verse identifies the father as one of those who are astray, a description of direction rather than a claim that he has no human value. To be misguided is to have lost the right path and to need return. Abraham's wording leaves room for the seriousness of error without turning the person into an object of contempt.

This distinction matters in religious speech. A doctrine can be false, and a practice can lead people away from God, while the people involved remain capable of repentance and deserving of honest concern. Abraham's prayer models a firm opposition to idolatry that does not become pleasure in another person's ruin.

**Forgiveness Is Sought From God Alone**

Abraham does not ask his father, his ancestors, or the idols to repair the spiritual damage. He asks God to forgive. The prayer confirms the earlier declaration that the Lord alone governs the servant's final relation to Him. Family loyalty cannot forgive sin, and inherited custom cannot make a person safe before God.

The request also recognizes a limit on Abraham's own power. He can question, warn, and pray, but he cannot force faith into another heart. Forgiveness belongs to the Lord, whose knowledge includes the hidden motives and final choices of the person being prayed for. Abraham's responsibility is compassion and truth; the verdict remains God's.

**A Promise Shapes the Earlier Prayer**

The exegetical tradition connects this request with Abraham's earlier promise to seek forgiveness for his father. The Qur'an later explains that his continued plea was tied to that promise, but that he withdrew from it when the father's enmity toward God became clear. The sequence shows that prayer for a misguided relative is not a permanent endorsement of stubborn opposition to truth.

A promise made in hope can be honored within the limits of obedience to God. Once the moral reality becomes clear, affection cannot require a believer to treat enmity toward God as harmless. Abraham's example therefore balances keeping one's word with recognizing when a spiritual boundary has been reached.

**Filial Care Does Not Mean Religious Surrender**

Abraham's prayer protects family care from being confused with submission to family belief. He does not worship with his father in order to prove love, and he does not soften the truth to avoid conflict. He prays for the father because the father is misguided, not because the guidance is unnecessary.

This is a difficult balance for anyone whose family follows a different path. Respect, service, patience, and sincere concern can remain duties, while worship belongs to God alone. Abraham shows that family affection should become a reason to seek someone's good, not a reason to call falsehood true.

To ask forgiveness for the father is to refuse the assumption that his present condition is his final condition. Abraham sees the error, but he does not claim knowledge of the future that belongs only to God. Prayer keeps open the possibility that a person can turn, even after years of inherited worship.

Hope for repentance should not become naïveté. Abraham's prayer does not deny the father's words or the harm of idolatry. It simply refuses to make despair the only response to error. A warning is most humane when it is spoken while return remains possible.

**A Parallel Prayer Broadens the Family Concern**

In 14:41, Abraham asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, and the believers on the day judgment is established. That parallel shows that his concern is not limited to private emotion. He places family within a wider community of people who need God's mercy. The individual household is important, but it is not the whole horizon of prayer.

The parallel also confirms that asking God to forgive parents belongs within Abraham's devotional language. The request is made to the Lord who hears prayer, not to an ancestor or household power. Its proper end is mercy from God and a community oriented toward Him.

Abraham's concern for his father must not be used to defend false worship or to suggest that love makes every belief acceptable. The verse contains both the request and the diagnosis: forgive my father, for he is misguided. Mercy is sought precisely because the condition is wrong. A prayer that hides the wrong would not be Abraham's prayer.

The passage therefore gives a mature form of compassion. Speak truthfully about misguidance, hope for forgiveness, honor the bond of family, and leave the final judgment to God. Abraham's love is not passive approval. It is the painful concern of someone who wants a beloved person to be rescued from an error that cannot save him. Such concern can remain patient without becoming silent, and firm without becoming cruel. It seeks the person's rescue rather than the satisfaction of proving that the speaker was right.

A family member may therefore keep making sincere prayers and offering honest counsel while refusing to join the error. Abraham's example does not demand emotional distance; it demands that affection serve truth.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:87

> And do not disgrace me on the Day all will be resurrected—

**Expanded Commentary**

**Abraham Asks for Protection From Final Disgrace**

Abraham's prayer turns from his father's condition to his own standing on the Day of resurrection. He asks God not to disgrace him. The request does not suggest that Abraham expects disgrace as a necessary result. It expresses the humility of a servant who knows that the final day belongs to God's judgment and that honour before God cannot be secured by human reputation.

Disgrace is more than private pain. It is exposure before the gathered creation, the collapse of a person's claim to dignity, and the revelation that worldly status could not protect him. Abraham therefore asks for the opposite of being exposed as rejected. He wants to meet resurrection under God's acceptance.

**The Day Is Public in Scope**

The wording all will be resurrected gives the request a universal setting. No family, nation, or social rank will remain hidden behind a private world. Abraham's concern is not the opinion of one audience in one generation. It is his standing when every servant is gathered and the truth of every allegiance is made plain.

That universal setting makes worldly reputation small. A person may be honoured in a palace, praised by a community, or defended by descendants, but none of those judgments controls the resurrection. Abraham asks the Lord who governs that day to preserve him from the shame that follows rejection, hypocrisy, or false worship.

**Righteousness Does Not Produce Self-Satisfaction**

Abraham has just been described as one who rejects idols and seeks the Lord's wisdom. Yet he still asks not to be disgraced. His prayer shows that obedience does not create a right to boast. The servant may act faithfully and still depend on God's mercy for final acceptance.

This humility is not a denial of God's promises to His servants. It is the opposite of claiming security through one's own record. Abraham knows that good deeds are signs of loyalty, but God remains the Judge of hearts and outcomes. A believer can hope in God's acceptance without turning hope into a certificate written by the self.

**Disgrace Is Different From Every Form of Trial**

The request should not be read as a demand for a life without pain, loss, or difficulty. Abraham's story contains struggle, rejection, separation, and danger. The disgrace he fears belongs to the final meeting with God. A person may suffer in the world and still be honoured in the Hereafter; another may enjoy public success and still be exposed as spiritually ruined.

This distinction protects people from judging God's favour by comfort. Illness, poverty, exile, and opposition do not by themselves mean disgrace. Nor do wealth and applause prove acceptance. Abraham asks for final honour, the kind that survives the end of worldly appearances.

**The Prayer Recognizes the Seriousness of Accountability**

Some spiritual language becomes shallow when it treats judgment as a formality. Abraham's request restores its weight. Resurrection is not only a return to life; it is a return before the Lord. The servant's hopes, loyalties, and treatment of truth will matter there. Asking not to be disgraced means asking to be found among those whose allegiance was sound.

The prayer therefore calls the believer to examine the heart before that examination is imposed from outside. Are worship, repentance, and moral action directed toward God, or are they performed for an audience? Human beings can manage an appearance in this world. They cannot manage the final disclosure of what they truly served.

**God's Honour Is the Only Secure Honour**

Abraham's request places honour where it belongs. The Lord grants it, and the Lord can preserve it. A person who tries to secure dignity through idols, lineage, wealth, or power remains dependent on things that pass. The prayer turns the heart from borrowed status to the approval of the Creator.

That turn does not make a believer careless about good reputation. Trustworthiness and honour among people can serve useful purposes. But public respect must remain a means, not the final goal. Abraham asks for honour before God because every other form of honour ends at the grave or changes with the crowd.

**A Parallel Supplication Explains the Fear**

The believers' prayer in 3:192 also links being admitted to the Fire with disgrace and the absence of helpers. That parallel confirms that disgrace is a spiritual consequence of rejection, not simply an emotional embarrassment. Abraham's request is therefore a plea for God's protection from the final state in which no created support can repair the loss.

The connection also shows why his earlier prayer for forgiveness matters here. Mercy and honour belong together. The servant asks for pardon because he wants to meet the Day of resurrection as one accepted by God rather than as one whose public identity conceals a rejected heart.

The verse ends with a dash after naming the Day of resurrection. The pause holds the believer before the event rather than allowing the mind to move quickly past it. Abraham's prayer remains unfinished in the sense that every servant must carry it into his own life. The day is certain, but the personal outcome is not something to treat casually.

His words teach a disciplined hope. Work for truth, reject false worship, seek forgiveness, and ask God for final honour. The goal is not to escape every hardship or preserve a flattering image. It is to be raised among those whom the Lord does not disgrace. The prayer asks for a verdict that remains good when every temporary reputation has fallen away. It is a request for lasting dignity, not for escape from the honest consequences of a servant's choices.

That concern can shape the present without creating panic. The believer corrects the heart now because the final day will reveal what the heart became.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:88

> the Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Day Exposes False Security**

Abraham explains the Day of resurrection by naming two of the strongest forms of worldly security: wealth and children. Neither will be of any benefit then. The statement does not deny that money and family can be blessings in this life. It denies that either can purchase acceptance, carry a person through judgment, or replace a heart turned toward God.

People often measure safety by what they possess and whom they can call upon. Wealth supplies options, while children supply affection, continuity, and social strength. On the final day, those supports reach their limit. The servant stands before God not as the owner of a protective network but as a morally responsible person.

**Wealth Cannot Be Taken Into the Final Account**

Money can solve some worldly problems, but it cannot buy forgiveness or alter the truth of a deed. It may pay for comfort, education, medicine, or influence, yet its power ends where God's judgment begins. Wealth has no independent value before the Lord if it was used to deny Him or to injure His creation.

This does not make wealth evil. Abraham's words concern its inability to benefit on the Day of resurrection, not its lawful use in the world. Wealth can be a trust used for charity, family care, justice, and worship. Its limitation is precisely what makes responsible use important: it is a means for a short life, not a shield against the final meeting.

**Children Cannot Carry Another Person's Faith**

Children are among the deepest sources of hope and pride. Parents may imagine that a respected family name, a large household, or a child's achievement will secure their own standing. The verse separates love from this illusion. Children can be loved, taught, and supported, but they cannot take responsibility for a parent's heart or substitute for the parent's obedience.

A family can help a person toward righteousness, but assistance in the world is not the same as intercession before God. Each person remains accountable. This gives children dignity as moral agents and gives parents a serious duty: family affection should guide people toward truth, not turn them into objects used for status.

**The Verse Does Not Denigrate Family or Provision**

Because the line speaks of wealth and children as unable to benefit, it must not be read as contempt for ordinary blessings. Abraham himself prays for family, and the Qur'anic account presents provision as a mercy. The problem is not possession. The problem is relying on possession as though it could decide the soul's final fate.

A believer may enjoy wealth and raise children with gratitude while remembering that both belong to God. The heart should hold blessings without making them idols. Wealth is a trust, and children are an entrusted responsibility. Neither should become the object of ultimate fear, hope, or obedience.

**The Final Day Reorders Social Rank**

Worldly societies rank people by money, family, connections, and influence. The Day of resurrection removes the protective force of those rankings. The rich person cannot make wealth answer for him, and the parent cannot present children as proof of righteousness. The categories that organize public honor are exposed as temporary.

This reordering is not arbitrary. It reveals what those categories could never prove. Wealth may show opportunity or fortune; children may show family continuity. Neither demonstrates a sound heart. God's judgment reaches the person behind the social role and measures what the person did with every trust.

**A Checked Parallel States the Same Limit**

The parallel warning in 3:10 expressly joins wealth and children with the inability to benefit those who reject God. The repetition across the Qur'an makes the point a stable principle rather than a detail limited to Abraham's prayer. Worldly security becomes dangerous when it persuades a person that no higher account will be required.

The parallel also keeps the verse balanced. It does not tell the poor that lack automatically saves them or the childless that they possess automatic spiritual advantage. Wealth and children are not the cause of ruin by themselves. The decisive issue is whether the servant uses blessings in submission or lets blessings replace submission.

**The Verse Protects the Vulnerable From Envy**

A person who hears that wealth and children will not benefit on the final day might be tempted to envy those who possess them or to glorify deprivation. Abraham's statement gives no basis for either response. The poor still need justice, and the wealthy still carry responsibility. The verse removes the illusion of ultimate security, not the need to treat worldly needs seriously.

Knowing that possessions cannot save also frees the heart from measuring its worth by comparison. A person with little can seek God without believing he is spiritually inferior. A person with much can give without imagining that generosity makes him owner of salvation. Both stand in the same need for a sound heart.

**The Heart Is the Decisive Possession**

The verse prepares the reader to see that what matters on the Day is not the size of a person's estate or household but the state of the person before God. Wealth and children are external supports. They can surround a person without changing the direction of his heart. The final account reaches the inner allegiance that possessions often conceal.

This is why Abraham's prayer for protection from disgrace is connected to the failure of wealth and children. If external supports cannot help, then only God's mercy and a faithful heart remain. The servant should use worldly blessings responsibly, but he must bring to the final day something wealth cannot buy and family cannot lend: sincere submission to the Lord.

**Worldly Blessings Become Tests of Gratitude**

Once wealth and children are seen as unable to save, their proper role becomes clearer. They are tests of gratitude, patience, justice, and care. The wealthy person is tested by how he earns and spends. The parent is tested by how he raises, protects, and releases children into moral responsibility. The blessings matter because of the choices they make possible.

Abraham's sentence therefore does not empty worldly life of meaning. It prevents worldly life from claiming final meaning. Wealth and children can serve obedience, but they cannot replace it. On the Day of resurrection, the servant will not be asked how impressive the gifts looked. He will be asked what relation he formed with the Giver.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:89

> Only those who come before Allah with a pure heart ˹will be saved˺.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sound Heart Is the True Provision**

After removing wealth and children as final supports, Abraham identifies what saves: coming before Allah with a pure heart. The heart is not a passing mood or a private feeling separated from conduct. It is the center of intention, trust, worship, and moral direction. A sound heart arrives before God free from the loyalties that make created things rivals to Him.

The verse's condition is exact. External possessions cannot save, but neither can a religious appearance that leaves the heart divided. A person may have little wealth and no influential family while still carrying pride, envy, hypocrisy, or attachment to false powers. Salvation is tied to the inner state that directs the life, not to a social profile.

**Purity Means Freedom From Idolatry**

The immediate setting makes the first meaning clear. Abraham has spent the passage exposing idols and turning worship to the Lord of all worlds. A pure heart is therefore one that does not assign God's rights to created objects. It is free from the worship of images, ancestors, status, desire, or any other rival raised to ultimate authority.

This purity is not achieved by refusing every created means. A person can work, love family, seek treatment, and accept help while knowing that none of these is a lord. The heart is sound when it uses means without worshipping them. It receives blessings without making blessings the center of hope and fear.

**A Sound Heart Knows What It Will Meet**

The source tradition connects the sound heart with recognition that God is real, that the Hereafter will come, and that God will resurrect what is in the graves. This knowledge gives the heart a stable direction. It does not merely accept a doctrine; it lives as though resurrection and accountability are true.

Such a heart cannot make the present world its final home. It may enjoy lawful life, but it measures decisions by the coming meeting with God. Wealth and children lose their power to deceive because the heart knows they cannot cross the boundary into final judgment. Awareness of resurrection makes sincerity practical rather than decorative.

**Purity Is Sincerity Without Hidden Rivals**

A heart can perform good actions while seeking admiration, influence, or control. The act may look correct, but its inner direction remains divided. A pure heart seeks God without making the approval of people its real reward. Sincerity does not mean that a person never notices praise or feels pain from criticism. It means those reactions do not govern worship.

The demand is high, but it is not an invitation to obsessive self-inspection. The servant asks God to cleanse the heart and then works against the attachments he recognizes. Purity grows through repentance, truthful intention, and repeated return to God. It is a living condition, not a label a person awards himself.

**The Heart Can Be Spiritually Healthy or Sick**

The Qur'anic image of a sound heart allows a comparison with illness. A sick heart may still recognize truth in some measure but resist it through doubt, envy, pride, or desire for false authority. Spiritual illness affects how a person interprets signs and chooses actions. It is not identical to every emotional struggle or intellectual question.

A healthy heart can face fear and uncertainty without surrendering its central trust. It can be corrected because it values truth more than self-defense. The heart Abraham describes is not a heart that never feels pain. It is a heart whose pain does not turn into rebellion against God and whose desires do not become competing gods.

**Coming Before Allah Requires Movement**

The verse speaks of those who come before Allah with a sound heart. The image is active. The heart is brought to the meeting through a life of choices, not discovered suddenly as a hidden possession. Worship, repentance, justice, and patience are the ways in which the inner state becomes visible. A person cannot claim purity while deliberately feeding the attachments that corrupt it.

At the same time, the servant comes rather than presenting himself as self-made. The heart's soundness is a gift sustained by God. Human effort matters, but effort is a response to guidance. Abraham's prayer for forgiveness and his request for wisdom show the posture that protects purity: dependence, hope, and honest awareness of need.

**A Verified Parallel Places Abraham Beside the Sound Heart**

The parallel account in 37:84 describes Abraham as coming to his Lord with a pure heart. That wording confirms that the quality in this verse is not an abstract virtue detached from Abraham's life. It describes the inner foundation of his rejection of idols and his single-minded worship.

The parallel also guards against reducing purity to outward calm. Abraham's heart was sound while he confronted his people and endured their opposition. A pure heart can be courageous and forceful against falsehood. Its gentleness is not surrender; its firmness is not hatred. Both are governed by devotion to God.

**The Criterion Is Available to Every Servant**

The verse does not say that only the famous, wealthy, or socially protected can come before God with a sound heart. Wealth and children have just been stripped of final power, leaving a criterion that is inward but not exclusive. Every servant can seek sincerity, abandon false worship, repent from corruption, and ask God for a heart that is sound.

This gives the Day of resurrection both seriousness and hope. No external advantage can save a divided heart, but no person is barred from seeking purification while life remains. Abraham's prayer leads the reader away from what cannot help and toward the one condition that matters: arriving before Allah with worship, trust, and allegiance undivided.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:90

> ˹On that Day˺ Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Paradise Is Brought Near as a Welcome**

The verse depicts Paradise being brought near to those who fear God. The image turns reward into an approaching welcome. The Garden is not described as a distant idea that the righteous must force themselves to imagine. It is brought near to them by God's command, making the promised destination present before their eyes.

Nearness carries emotional as well as spatial force. A person who has travelled toward a goal is strengthened when the goal comes into view. The verse gives the God-fearing that moment of recognition. Their long obedience has not led into emptiness. The place prepared by God is now near, and its nearness announces acceptance.

**God-Fearing Means Living Under Taqwa**

The God-fearing are those whose awareness of God shapes choices. Taqwa is not panic that makes a person unable to act. It is a guarding of the self from what displeases God, joined to hope in His mercy. The people described here have treated accountability as real, so their conduct was not governed only by immediate appetite or public approval.

This quality is deeper than a reputation for caution. A person may appear restrained while hiding arrogance or false worship. Taqwa reaches the heart and the ordinary decision. It guides speech, wealth, family duty, private conduct, and the use of power. Paradise is brought near to people whose inner awareness has become a practical form of obedience.

**Nearness Is an Honour Granted by God**

The verse does not say that the God-fearing seize Paradise through their own strength. It is brought near. That passive form directs attention to divine generosity. The righteous act, repent, and persevere, but the arrival of Paradise is still a gift from the Lord. Their nearness to the Garden reflects His acceptance rather than a right they can impose.

This language protects good works from becoming a source of pride. A servant may work hard without imagining that the reward is owed as a commercial payment. Every capacity to obey, every chance to repent, and every moment of restraint is itself sustained by God. Nearness to Paradise is therefore received with gratitude and humility.

**The Scene Answers the Prayer for Bliss**

Abraham asked to be among those awarded the Garden of Bliss. This verse shows the kind of fulfilment his prayer seeks. Paradise is not only named as a future location; it is brought near to a class of people whose hearts were guarded by reverence. The prayer's hope now appears as a scene of divine welcome.

The connection also clarifies the relation between hope and conduct. Abraham's request for the Garden was not a wish detached from the life of faith. The God-fearing are those who turn their fear of God into obedience and their hope of the Garden into patience. The destination belongs to a path, even though the final gift remains God's mercy.

**The Garden Comes Near Before the Servant Enters**

The wording emphasizes approach. The righteous are allowed to see the Garden's nearness before the full experience of dwelling there. Anticipation is part of the reward. A promise that was trusted without sight becomes a reality placed before the servant, and the distance between hope and fulfilment collapses.

This movement also honors patient faith. The God-fearing lived without possessing the unseen reward in the world. They organized their lives around a promise that could not be handled or displayed. When Paradise is brought near, faith is not shown to have been naïve. It is shown to have been a truthful response to God's word.

**A Parallel Describes the Same Nearness**

Quran 50:31 describes Paradise as brought near to the righteous and not far away. The parallel confirms that nearness here expresses readiness and welcome rather than a human journey that forces open the Garden. The righteous find the promised home close because God has prepared the way to it.

That parallel also keeps the verse from being reduced to a metaphor for a good feeling. Paradise is a real reward in the Qur'anic account. Its nearness is part of the resurrection scene, where God's promises become visible. The God-fearing are not merely told that they were morally successful; they are brought before the home of lasting bliss.

**Taqwa Turns Fear Into Movement**

Fear of God can be misunderstood as a static emotion. This verse shows its destination. Taqwa moves a person away from false worship and harmful conduct and toward the Garden. It is fear that guards because it values closeness to God more than the pleasure of disobedience. Hope then gives the guarded life a positive direction.

A servant who fears God properly does not spend the whole life imagining rejection. He fears losing the Lord's acceptance and hopes for the mercy that brings Paradise near. The two feelings work together. Taqwa prevents false security, while hope prevents paralysis and despair.

**The Verse Makes the Future Present Enough for Obedience**

The God-fearing cannot see Paradise during worldly life, yet this verse lets the future enter present decisions. A person can refuse an idol, restrain an injustice, or forgive an offense because the coming welcome is more real than the immediate reward of wrongdoing. Nearness in the resurrection begins as a direction in the heart now.

The scene therefore honors those whose obedience looked costly or unnoticed. Their true audience was God, and their true destination was not the praise of people. When Paradise is brought near, the hidden value of their choices becomes clear. The Lord has not forgotten the hearts that guarded themselves for His sake. Their restraint was not wasted, and their hope was not directed toward an empty promise.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:91

> and the Hellfire will be displayed to the deviant.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Hellfire Becomes Visible to the Deviant**

The verse describes Hellfire as displayed to the deviant. The image is not of a punishment hidden from those who are about to face it. It is brought into view. People who spent life turning away from truth are confronted with the destination their choices had made difficult to believe. The display strips away the comfort of denial before the consequence reaches its full force.

The translation's deviant refers to those who departed from the straight path. The word is moral, not merely geographical. They were not lost because they lacked a route; they adopted a direction that led away from God. Hellfire is displayed to people whose error has become a settled orientation of worship, loyalty, and conduct.

**Seeing the Fire Is Part of the Judgment**

A person can fear an unseen consequence without allowing that fear to shape action. On the Day of resurrection, the unseen becomes visible. The deviant no longer has to be persuaded that judgment is real. The Fire itself stands before them as evidence, and the distance between warning and reality disappears.

This visibility carries psychological force. Denial depends on keeping the consequence abstract or remote. Display removes that refuge. The people who dismissed warnings must now look at what the warnings meant. The verse therefore presents judgment as an unveiling of truth, not as an arbitrary change in God's treatment of them.

**The Display Fits the Heart's Chosen Direction**

Hellfire is not shown to people who were sincerely seeking God and occasionally stumbled. The verse names the deviant, those whose relation to truth was defined by turning away. Their destination corresponds to their chosen direction. They made false worship, arrogance, or disobedience into a road, and the road now ends in a reality they cannot deny.

This does not reduce judgment to impersonal fate. The people chose and persisted. Divine knowledge does not cancel human responsibility, and the certainty of the displayed Fire does not mean that the deviant was forced to love error. The scene reveals the consequence of an allegiance that was freely maintained.

**Hellfire Is Displayed Before Excuses Can Work**

In worldly life, people can blame circumstances, ancestors, leaders, or social pressure. Some explanations may be relevant to how a person was shaped, but they cannot erase the person's response to truth. The display of Hellfire makes every excuse stand in a new light. The question is no longer whether the warning was clear but whether the person answered it.

The verse does not list the speeches of the condemned. Its economy is severe. The Fire is displayed, and the deviant sees. The scene has no need for a long argument because the object before them embodies the seriousness of the path they chose. What was disputed as a possibility is now present as a fact.

**Display Is Both Terror and Recognition**

The Fire terrifies, but it also clarifies. The deviant sees the truth about idols, false hopes, and disobedient loyalties. Recognition has arrived, but too late to function as repentance. That timing is part of the warning for the living. Understanding the consequence after the life of choice has ended is not the same as understanding it while return remains open.

A believer should therefore not seek proof by waiting for the final unveiling. The purpose of revelation is to make the unseen known enough for a responsible response. The displayed Fire shows what faith already took seriously. It is not the first moment at which the truth becomes meaningful; it is the moment at which denial can no longer protect the denier.

**The Scene Preserves the Difference Between Fear and Despair**

Fear of Hell can guard a person from arrogance, but it should not become despair of God's mercy. The verse addresses the deviant who has reached judgment, not every person who fears that he may fail. During worldly life, fear can produce repentance and repair. After the display of the Fire, the opportunity described by that fear has passed.

This distinction keeps the warning useful. A person should not read the verse and conclude that his flaws make return impossible. He should read it as a call to turn before the consequences are displayed. The frightening image is mercy for those still able to change, even while it describes justice for those who persisted in deviation.

**A Parallel Links the Fire With Confession**

The account in 67:11 records the residents of the Blaze confessing their sins. That parallel shows the relation between seeing the punishment and recognizing the moral failure behind it. The confession does not make the display unnecessary. It confirms that the condemned understand what they refused to understand earlier.

The present verse keeps the emphasis on the first sight. Hellfire is displayed to the deviant before the later words of dispute and regret are heard. The visual encounter already judges the false story they told themselves. Their former objects of hope cannot make the Fire disappear, and their former confidence cannot turn its display into a warning for someone else.

**The Display Exposes the Failure of False Worship**

Abraham's argument began with idols that could not hear, benefit, harm, create, guide, or forgive. This verse shows the end of trusting such objects. The deviant now faces a reality the idols cannot avert. False worship promised security but delivered no protection at the moment protection mattered most.

The contrast is not between two equal powers. Hellfire is displayed by God's command, and the deviant stands as a servant before the Lord. The idols had public names, ceremonies, and inherited authority, but none of that survives the unveiling. The Fire reveals what the heart had chosen when it treated created things as rivals to God.

**The Verse Makes the Final Scene Present in the Mind**

The displayed Fire is a future event, yet the verse places it before the present reader in language that can be imagined. That is the force of warning. It allows a person to test his direction now rather than wait for the destination to be shown. Are wealth, family, reputation, desire, or idols being trusted as final supports? If so, the road needs correction before its end is visible.

The verse is brief, but its warning is not small. Hellfire displayed to the deviant is the collapse of every denial that protected false allegiance. The wise response is not fascination with the scene. It is repentance, worship of God alone, and a life that turns away from the path that leads there.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:92

> And it will be said to them, “Where are those you used to worship

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Judgment Begins With a Question**

The condemned are asked where those they used to worship are. The question is not for information. God does not need to locate the idols, and the speakers already know that the objects have no power. The interrogation exposes the absence of the supposed gods at the moment their worshippers most need them.

A question can reveal a false claim more sharply than a direct statement. During life, the idolaters said that their objects deserved devotion. On the Day of judgment, they must face the objects' disappearance as sources of help. The question returns their own practice to them and makes them confront what they placed at the center of hope.

**Where Is a Worshipped Object When Judgment Arrives?**

The verse asks where the objects are, not where the people kept them or how they decorated them. Their physical location is not the real issue. The issue is their absence from authority. They are not present as protectors, advocates, or lords. The community's ceremonies could make them appear important, but ceremony cannot create a power that stands before judgment.

That absence reveals the difference between a symbol and a god. A symbol can remain as an object of memory, while a god must possess actual authority over the worshipper's fate. The idols fail the second test. They were addressed in life, but they cannot answer the question placed before them now.

**The Past Tense Makes Habit Accountable**

The wording refers to those they used to worship. The past tense gathers their former life into one phrase. Their worship was not an isolated mistake that can be separated from their identity. It was a repeated practice, sustained long enough to become the way they understood dependence and security.

Yet the past tense also shows that the practice has ended. The idols are no longer treated as objects of worship in any meaningful sense. Their former worshippers have been brought to a scene where the illusion cannot continue. A habit that seemed permanent in the world has become an accusation in the Hereafter.

**The Question Addresses the Whole Group**

The verse speaks to them collectively. False worship may be practiced by individuals, but it also gains strength from crowds, families, institutions, and public agreement. The question therefore reaches the social world that protected the idols. What did the community gather around, and what remains when the gathering stands before God?

Collective responsibility does not erase individual responsibility. Each person chose how to respond, but the group also made false worship normal and dissent costly. The public question strips away the comfort of saying that everyone did the same. A crowd can make an error feel safe without making it true.

**Where Is the Promise of Protection?**

Worshippers often remain attached to false objects because they expect protection, blessing, or mediation. The verse does not repeat every promise they associated with the idols. It asks one short question that includes them all. If the object was a protector, where is its protection now? If it was an advocate, where is its advocacy?

The absence is not a surprise to God. It is a demonstration for the worshippers. They are made to see that their expectations rested on an object incapable of fulfilling them. The question is painful because the answer is visible in the silence. No inherited title can turn a created thing into a source of salvation.

**A Parallel Exposes the Same Absence**

The Qur'an describes those invoked besides God as unable to create and as themselves created in 16:20–21. That parallel gives the present question a clear theological background. An object that did not create life cannot be expected to control the final destiny of life. Its worshippers may grant it a name, but they cannot grant it creative or saving power.

The parallel also shows why the question is directed at worshippers rather than at the idols. The idols have no capacity to answer. The moral conversation belongs to the people who chose them. The question calls them to account for a dependence that had no real object behind it.

**The Interrogation Removes the Comfort of Distance**

People can speak about idolatry as a theory and avoid seeing its consequences in their own lives. The question removes that distance. It does not ask what some other society worshipped. It asks those people about what they themselves used to worship. Their own history becomes the evidence.

This has a present lesson without reducing the verse to a slogan. Modern people may reject statues while giving ultimate loyalty to wealth, leaders, nations, or desire. The question can still be heard: where is the thing you trust as a final lord when you stand before God? A created support cannot answer for the allegiance given to it.

**The Broken Sentence Holds the Hearer in Suspense**

The translation ends with an open quotation because the question continues. The pause is rhetorically powerful. The audience is made to wait before hearing the test that will be applied to the absent objects. That waiting mirrors the exposure of the condemned, who cannot escape the subject even though the answer is already apparent.

The verse stands complete as an indictment of misplaced worship. It turns a former boast into a question of absence. The worshippers once gathered around their objects; now the objects cannot stand beside them as powers. The Lord's interrogation has already shown that false worship leaves its adherents alone at the moment of final need. The question does not create their helplessness; it reveals the helplessness that had always been there.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:93

> besides Allah? Can they help you or even help themselves?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Tests the Idols' Ability to Help**

The interrogation becomes specific. Can the objects worshipped besides Allah help their devotees, or can they even help themselves? The two parts expose the same failure from different angles. A claimed god must possess power for the worshipper and stability for its own condition. These idols possess neither.

The question is framed in terms of help because worship is usually tied to need. People turn to a supposed power for rescue, protection, provision, or relief. Abraham's earlier question already tested whether the idols could hear and benefit. This verse places the test at the final crisis, where the difference between appearance and power cannot be hidden.

**A Helper Must Possess What the Worshipper Lacks**

The idolaters treated created objects as sources of help, yet a carved object depends on people for its position, care, and public importance. It cannot supply itself with life or protection. A thing that needs worshippers to maintain its presence cannot be the ultimate rescuer of those worshippers.

This does not deny that people can help one another by God's permission. A doctor, parent, teacher, or neighbor may provide real assistance within created limits. The question concerns objects raised to divine status. Such objects are not simply weak helpers. They have no independent agency on which ultimate trust can rest.

**The Second Question Makes the First Ironic**

If the idols cannot help themselves, the worshippers' dependence on them becomes visibly absurd. The people had placed their own fate in the hands of objects unable to preserve their own standing. The question therefore uses the idolaters' expectation against itself. Their supposed protectors are shown to require protection.

This irony is not mockery for its own sake. It is a final exposure of a dangerous error. False worship persuades people to reverse the proper relation between Creator and creature. The dependent object is treated as lord, while the actual Lord is ignored. The judgment scene restores the order that idolatry had inverted.

**Help in the Hereafter Cannot Be Claimed by Ceremony**

Rituals can be repeated until they feel like guarantees. The verse denies that feeling. Ceremony does not create a saving power in the object toward which it is directed. The question asks what the idol can actually do, not how often people bowed before it or how impressive the shrine appeared.

This warning also applies to religious forms that have lost their inner truth. A person may collect symbols, titles, and public acts while neglecting sincere worship and repentance. The issue is not that forms are worthless, but that forms cannot help when they are severed from faith. On the final day, an empty performance cannot become a helper.

**The Lord Is Not Placed Beside the Idols as an Equal**

The phrase besides Allah identifies the central error. The question is not whether people recognize God in some distant way. It is whether they assign another object a share in the dependence that belongs to Him.
