Entitlement is dangerous because it turns a gift into a claim against both God and people. The entitled person expects provision to continue while refusing the duties attached to it. Fear of Allah restores proportion: enjoy what is lawful, acknowledge its source, and do not use it as an excuse to disregard the Giver or harm His creation.

**Provision Does Not Confirm Every Choice**

ʿĀd could argue that its prosperity proves that God approves its way of life. Hūd's warning rejects that conclusion. A blessing can be granted as an opportunity, a test, or a temporary respite. Continued wealth is not a certificate that a society's worship and violence are right.

This point protects the reader from judging truth by immediate material success. Some people prosper while acting unjustly, and some righteous people endure hardship. The Provider gives in wisdom, while accountability concerns the response. The proper question is not merely, “What do we possess?” but, “What are we doing with what we possess?”


Hūd's reasoning is relational. Fear Allah because He has provided what you know. The command is not an arbitrary demand from a distant ruler. It is a call to respond rightly to the One whose care has sustained the people from the beginning.

If ʿĀd acknowledges God as Provider, it must abandon the fantasy of self-sufficiency. It must recognize that its buildings, attacks, and social order are answerable to the source of its life. Provision becomes a doorway to worship when the people let gratitude govern their power.

**A Blessing Remembered Becomes a Sign**

The good things around ʿĀd are signs not because they force belief mechanically, but because they invite reflection. They reveal dependence, order, and generosity. The person who looks with humility sees a reason to fear God; the person who looks with vanity sees only material for further self-display.

Hūd asks the people to choose the first way of seeing. Their cattle, children, gardens, and springs will soon be named, but the central lesson is already given: what they know and enjoy comes from the Lord. To remember the Provider is to let every blessing lead back to obedience.

The reminder also teaches the difference between possession and ownership. A person may hold a thing in trust and be responsible for it, but he cannot make himself its ultimate source. This humility leaves room for gratitude, generosity, and repentance when a blessing has been misused.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:133

> He provided you with cattle, and children,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Provision Becomes Specific**

Hūd moves from the general reminder of provision to two familiar forms: cattle and children. The examples bring theology into daily life. The people do not have to search for a hidden miracle before recognizing dependence on God. Their food, labor, wealth, family life, and future are all tied to gifts they did not create from nothing. Quran 16:5 links cattle with warmth, food, and other benefits, while 16:72 names children among God's good provisions; those parallels illuminate why Hūd chooses these ordinary signs.

The verse places animals and children together without reducing either to property. Both are blessings that involve responsibility. Cattle may support food, work, transport, or livelihood; children carry the hope of continuity and require protection, formation, and care. The gifts enlarge a people's capacity, but they also enlarge its accountability.


A society can count animals as units of prestige and economic power. Hūd asks the people to see beyond the count to the Provider. Each benefit drawn from an animal—food, clothing, labor, or means of exchange—reminds the community that its prosperity depends on life it did not manufacture.

This recognition should produce humane stewardship. If animals are treated only as instruments for increasing status, the blessing becomes another expression of the vanity already criticized. A grateful people uses what it has with restraint and care, acknowledging that dominion over creatures is limited and answerable to God.

**Children Are a Gift and a Trust**

Children are named as provision, but they are not possessions by which parents may boast. They are lives entrusted to families and communities. The gift includes the duty to feed, protect, teach, and prepare them for moral responsibility. A society that celebrates its population while neglecting the vulnerable has misunderstood the blessing.

The mention of children also exposes the emptiness of seeking permanence through descendants alone. Earlier, ʿĀd built as if it would live forever. A family line may continue after an individual dies, but it cannot make a person immortal or excuse the deeds for which he will answer. Continuity is not the same as salvation.


Cattle and children connect private life to public life. Animals may support households and markets; children depend on parents, relatives, teachers, and neighbors. God's provision therefore creates networks of obligation rather than permission for isolated accumulation.

A powerful group that hoards resources while weaker households struggle contradicts the meaning of the gift. The Provider is not honored by turning provision into a weapon. Gratitude seeks fair dealing, protection of dependents, and generosity toward people who cannot return the benefit immediately.

**The Gifts Challenge Self-Made Identity**

ʿĀd may have defined itself through strength and ancestry. Hūd names gifts that reveal dependence. No person chooses the circumstances into which he is born, and no society creates every condition that allows its herds and families to flourish. Recognizing this weakens the boast that success is entirely self-produced.

This does not erase human effort. Caring for animals and raising children require work, skill, and patience. It places those efforts in their proper frame. Human beings cultivate what they receive; they do not become the ultimate source of life. The Provider deserves acknowledgment precisely because effort operates within gifts already given.


Cattle can finance oppression, and children can be used as symbols of status. A gift does not remain morally neutral after it enters human hands. The people must decide whether their abundance will deepen gratitude or strengthen the very arrogance Hūd has condemned.

The Qur'anic warning is therefore not nostalgia for a simpler economy. It addresses the heart's tendency to turn every increase into proof of superiority. More animals and more descendants do not make a people closer to God. They make the test more extensive because more lives and resources fall under its care.

**Family Continuity Must Be Joined to Truth**

Parents naturally desire their children to inherit security and honor. Hūd's call asks them to give a better inheritance: recognition of God and responsible conduct. Material provision without moral guidance can pass vanity from one generation to the next.

A child is not saved by the pride of his family, just as a parent is not justified by the success of his children. Each person remains accountable before God. The right response to family blessing is to guide with compassion, protect without possessiveness, and model obedience rather than merely demand it.


The verse gives no exotic example. Cattle and children are precisely the things a prosperous people may take for granted. Hūd makes the ordinary spiritually visible. Daily familiarity should not dull gratitude; it should provide repeated occasions to remember the Lord.

When the people see their herds and families in this way, prosperity can become a path away from vanity. They may still possess abundance, but they will no longer mistake abundance for independence. The gift points back to the Giver and forward to the responsibility of using it well.

The order of the examples also widens the reader's understanding of abundance. Provision is not merely what fills a storehouse. It includes living creatures that require care and human relationships that require patience. A society can be rich in numbers and still poor in mercy if it treats both animals and children as instruments of its pride.

When gratitude governs these gifts, wealth becomes a means of service. Herds can feed people without becoming occasions for cruelty, and children can be raised with dignity rather than displayed as proof of status. Hūd's reminder turns the inventory of prosperity into an examination of character.

The best response is therefore neither possessiveness nor neglect. It is grateful care: receiving the gift, meeting its duties, and remembering that God can ask how every dependent life was treated. Such care turns abundance into worship rather than a reason to boast. Gratitude becomes visible.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:134

> and gardens, and springs.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Landscape Itself Is Named as Provision**

Hūd completes his immediate list with gardens and springs. The gifts are not confined to objects owned by a household. They include a living landscape: cultivated growth and the water that makes growth possible. ʿĀd's prosperity is therefore surrounded by signs of sustaining care.

Gardens display the fruit of time, soil, labor, and water. Springs suggest a source that continues to feed life beyond a single moment. By naming them, Hūd asks the people to look at the environment that supports their comfort and to recognize that its order is not an achievement of their pride alone. Quran 16:10–11 similarly connects rain with drinking water, grazing, crops, and fruit, presenting the chain of provision as a sign for reflection.


A garden can be enjoyed, cultivated, and shared, but it cannot be treated as an endless possession. Its fertility depends on conditions outside the gardener's total control. A grateful society protects water, soil, and access to nourishment instead of exhausting the land for immediate display.

This is not a technical rule about one agricultural method. It is a moral principle. What sustains life is a trust. The people who receive gardens should ask whether their use leaves the land capable of benefiting others and future generations. Vanity consumes resources to make the present look powerful; gratitude preserves them as gifts.

**Springs Point to Dependence**

A spring gives a visible image of provision that precedes human labor. People can channel water, build around it, and distribute it, but they do not command the source into existence. The spring reminds the people that their skill works with a gift already present.

That reminder should temper claims of ownership. Control over access to water can make rulers feel indispensable, but the source remains God's. A just community manages the means of provision for life rather than turning necessity into a tool of humiliation or domination.


When gardens remain green and springs continue to flow, a generation may assume that prosperity is automatic. The more stable the blessing appears, the easier it is to forget the One who sustains it. Hūd's list restores the origin of what the people see every day.

Forgetfulness is not corrected merely by repeating the word “gift.” The people must let the recognition affect their conduct. They should show gratitude in worship, restraint in consumption, fairness in distribution, and mercy toward those whose access to provision is less secure.

**The Gift Is Collective, Not Only Private**

Gardens and springs shape the life of a whole people. Their benefit can pass through families, workers, travelers, and neighbors. The image therefore challenges an economy in which a small group claims the entire blessing while everyone else serves its display.

A community that fears God treats common goods with public responsibility. It does not allow the powerful to make abundance a reason for exclusion. Nor does it assume that shared provision removes individual duty. Each person must act honestly, while leaders must prevent the strong from consuming what belongs to the community's welfare.


A garden is useful and beautiful. The verse does not ask the people to despise pleasure or to regard cultivated beauty as vanity by definition. The problem lies in forgetting the Provider and converting beauty into a proof of superiority. Enjoyment becomes honorable when it is joined to gratitude and does not require oppression.

This balance protects against an austere misunderstanding of piety. Fear of Allah does not require people to destroy every attractive thing. It asks them to enjoy created beauty without worshipping it, hoarding it, or using it to announce that they are beyond accountability.

**Provision Does Not Excuse the Oppression of Others**

The gardens and springs cannot justify the attacks mentioned earlier. A prosperous land is not a license to take neighboring people's resources or to treat outsiders as obstacles. If ʿĀd's abundance leads to cruelty, the gift has become evidence in the case against them.

God's provision should widen compassion. A person who knows dependence can recognize the dependence of others. He does not ask only whether his own garden is watered; he asks whether his power is blocking another person's access to life. Gratitude is measured by that widening of concern.


The cultivated garden can awaken hope for a greater, lasting reward, but it can also make people cling to the temporary world. Springs flow and seasons change; even the richest landscape remains within time. The beauty is real, but it is not final.

Hūd's reminder asks ʿĀd to use present provision without making it an idol. Let gardens encourage gratitude, and let springs teach dependence. When the people fear the Provider, the land becomes a sign that leads them to worship. When they forget Him, the same land feeds their illusion of self-sufficiency.


Cattle, children, gardens, and springs form a picture of sustenance at several levels: living creatures, family continuity, cultivated food, and water. Hūd is showing the people that mercy has surrounded them in ordinary forms. Their refusal is not a response to deprivation but to a call they hear amid abundance.

The proper response is not to abandon the gifts. It is to return them to their right meaning. Everything they know and enjoy comes through the generosity of the Lord, so it should lead to reverence, justice, and obedience rather than vanity.

The list also joins nourishment with beauty. Gardens give sustenance and delight, while springs make continued life possible. A faithful community can appreciate both dimensions without confusing enjoyment with entitlement. It receives pleasure as a reason to praise God and shares the conditions of that pleasure as a responsibility toward others.

The land's generosity should make the people more aware of dependence, not more contemptuous of those who have less. If the same water and soil are used to concentrate privilege or support aggression, abundance has been severed from its moral purpose. Hūd's reminder restores that connection before he warns of the coming day.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:135

> I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous day.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Hūd's Warning Comes From Fear for Them**

After recalling the gifts given to ʿĀd, Hūd explains why he has urged reverence and obedience. He fears for them because their rejection places them before a tremendous day. The sentence reveals the emotional source of the warning: not envy of their prosperity, but concern about what their choices will bring.

A messenger who sees danger and remains silent would not be trustworthy. Hūd has already stated that he seeks no payment. Here he shows that his motive is protective. He wants the people to escape a consequence that their vanity and violence are making more likely.


The word tremendous gives the coming day a scale that exceeds ordinary human disputes. ʿĀd may think only in terms of rivals, buildings, and present security. Hūd places their lives before a judgment larger than any authority they recognize on earth. Their wealth cannot make that day small.

A serious warning should not be softened into a vague suggestion that every choice has harmless effects. Some actions destroy lives and corrupt communities. God is merciful, but mercy does not make accountability unreal. The fear Hūd expresses protects the people from treating moral consequence as an empty threat.

**Fear and Hope Are Not Opposites**

Hūd's warning occurs amid a reminder of provision. This pairing matters. The people are told both that God has cared for them and that He will judge their response. Hope in divine generosity should lead to gratitude, while fear of judgment should prevent gratitude from becoming complacency.

A balanced heart needs both directions. Fear without hope can produce despair, and hope without fear can produce presumption. Hūd speaks to a people in danger of presumption. Their abundance has made them feel secure, so he restores the seriousness that their comfort has erased.


Hūd does not say that the punishment is desirable or that he takes pleasure in imagining it. He says he fears for them. His words carry urgency because delay is dangerous, but they do not celebrate the people's destruction. The true guide can oppose a people's conduct while still wanting its repentance.

This distinction matters when warning is delivered in public life. Correcting wrongdoing is not permission to despise the wrongdoer or enjoy his downfall. Hūd's fear keeps the warning morally clean. He wants justice to be avoided through return, not witnessed as entertainment.

**A Verified Parallel Shows the Same Warning**

Quran 46:21 describes Hūd warning ʿĀd at the sand-hills and saying that he fears for them a tremendous day's punishment. The parallel confirms that this fear belongs to the heart of his mission. It is not an exaggerated phrase added only after the people's destruction; it is spoken before the outcome is visible.

That passage also situates Hūd among warners who came before and after him. The warning is therefore part of a recurring mercy: God sends guidance before judgment so that a people can recognize its danger while a response remains possible.


ʿĀd's horizon has been narrowed to what it can build, defend, and command. Hūd opens it again. The tremendous day makes present decisions transparent. A monument, a castle, or a victorious attack cannot be considered apart from the account that follows life.

This wider horizon does not make earthly duties irrelevant. It makes them more serious. The way people use provision, treat dependents, and respond to warning will matter beyond the applause of their contemporaries. A society that remembers the final day will not be satisfied with looking successful while harming others.

**Fear Is a Form of Mercy**

Many people regard fear as the opposite of care. Hūd shows that appropriate fear can be protective. A child warned away from fire is not being denied love; he is being preserved by it. In the same way, the warning of punishment is mercy when it turns a person away from a path of ruin.

The warning becomes harmful only when it is detached from truth, proportion, and hope. Hūd's message has all three. He identifies the Lord, recalls real blessings, names the people's conduct, and points to the consequence. His fear is disciplined by revelation rather than by personal anger.


Hūd speaks of the future day before it arrives. That timing is crucial. A warning after judgment would confirm the sentence but would not offer the same opportunity to change. The present verse stands at the threshold where ʿĀd can still exchange pride for gratitude and tyranny for justice.

The people may think that continued prosperity proves there is no danger. Hūd teaches the opposite: time before punishment is a chance to repent, not proof that accountability has been cancelled. The longer the warning is resisted, the more serious the refusal becomes.

**The Warning Includes Every Gift They Have Received**

Cattle, children, gardens, and springs are not unrelated to the tremendous day. They are part of the evidence that the people were cared for and part of the trust for which they will answer. Blessings increase responsibility because they give a society more capacity to do good.

ʿĀd cannot say that it lacked means to live differently. It had provision, strength, and guidance. Hūd's fear arises because a richly supplied people is using its gifts against the purpose for which gratitude would have directed them. The warning calls the gifts back to their Giver before they become witnesses against their owners.


Hūd has spoken as a brother, a trustworthy messenger, and a servant who seeks no reward. Now he speaks as one who foresees danger. The combination should make ʿĀd pause. Their familiar countryman is not flattering them, and he is not inventing a threat to gain money. He is asking them to take God's judgment seriously.

For the reader, the verse asks whether warnings are heard only when consequences become visible. The wise response comes earlier. Fear the tremendous day by living gratefully now, obeying the Lord before the opportunity to change is gone.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:136

> They responded, “It is all the same to us whether you warn ˹us˺ or not.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Indifference Is Their Answer to Warning**

After Hūd recalls the Provider and warns of a tremendous day, ʿĀd responds that warning and silence are the same to them. Their words present themselves as calm, but they reveal a hardened moral posture. The issue is no longer that they failed to understand the message. They claim that understanding would make no difference.

A warning matters only if the hearer allows it to affect judgment and action. By declaring that all outcomes are equal, the people try to remove the force of consequence before they have examined the truth. They protect their habits by pretending that no voice can require a response from them.


A person may say that two options are the same because he lacks information, but ʿĀd has already heard Hūd's call, his claim of trustworthiness, and his explanation of their blessings. Their statement is not an honest admission of uncertainty. It is a refusal to let the warning disturb the order they prefer.

True indifference would involve no passionate defense of the old way. Yet a people that insists that warning is useless is often protecting something. Pride may appear as boredom, but it still has an object: the desire to remain answerable to no one.

**Warnings Are Meant to Preserve Choice**

Hūd warns before the punishment becomes visible. That timing is a mercy because it leaves the people room to change. They treat the warning as irrelevant, but the very fact that it has arrived shows that their choice still matters. A person who can repent does not stand in the same position as one who has already met the consequence.

The answer of ʿĀd attempts to reverse this mercy. By saying that warning and no warning are equal, they make opportunity sound pointless. The Qur'anic account shows the opposite: the warning is evidence that God has not abandoned them to their chosen path. Quran 2:6 uses a closely related formulation for people who persist in disbelief, showing that the problem lies in the hearer's refusal, not in any weakness of the warning.


Humility listens even when a message is unwelcome. Arrogance decides in advance that no correction deserves attention. The people of ʿĀd have made their own judgment the measure of every warning, so they can dismiss Hūd without responding to his reasons.

This posture is dangerous in public life. Leaders who treat criticism as irrelevant cannot distinguish between malicious insult and necessary correction. They surround themselves with agreement, then call the resulting confidence proof that no change is needed. Hūd's people show where such confidence can lead.

**The Messenger's Duty Does Not Depend on Acceptance**

Hūd cannot force the people to fear God. His duty is to convey the truth clearly and warn them of the consequence. Their statement does not make the message useless, even though it reveals that they are refusing its benefit. The value of a warning is not measured only by the immediate response of those who hear it.

This protects the messenger from despair and the believer from a false measure of success. Faithful counsel may be rejected for a time. The servant remains responsible for honesty and compassion, while God judges the hearer's decision and the eventual result.


The people speak as though Hūd's words add nothing. But silence would leave them without a clear invitation to repent, while warning gives them knowledge of what is at stake. The two situations cannot be equal for a community that still has the capacity to respond.

A society also has a duty to welcome truthful warning. If it punishes every critic or mocks every reminder, it creates the very blindness it later calls inevitable. Hūd's speech is a public service because it keeps accountability audible. Rejecting it does not erase the danger; it only removes a means of preparation.

**The Familiar Can Make Warning Seem Ordinary**

Hūd is their brother, and his words may have become familiar through repetition. Familiarity can make a warning seem less urgent, especially when no immediate punishment follows. The people confuse delay with cancellation and repeated mercy with proof that nothing will happen.

The wise listener does the reverse. Repeated warning increases the need to respond because it shows both the seriousness of the matter and the generosity of the opportunity. A message should not be dismissed merely because it has been heard before.


A reader may condemn ʿĀd's indifference while treating present reminders in the same way. The verse asks whether warning changes anything: does it affect worship, the treatment of others, the use of wealth, and the way power is restrained? If not, the heart may be repeating the people's answer even without saying the words aloud.

Hūd's warning is therefore not merely a historical exchange. It places the hearer before a choice. Take the message seriously and return to God, or declare by conduct that warning and silence are the same. The consequence of indifference is that a mercy offered in speech is refused in practice.

Indifference also changes the way a person remembers the past. He may hear that an earlier people was warned and destroyed, then place the account safely outside his own life. That distance is another form of saying that warning and silence are equal. The wise reader lets the story interrupt complacency before a familiar habit becomes a settled verdict.

Hūd's words remain useful even when a hearer does not feel immediate fear. Moral seriousness is not measured by emotion alone. A person can begin by admitting that the warning deserves obedience, then allow that admission to reshape desire and conduct. What matters is that the message is no longer treated as irrelevant. Even a small act of obedience can prove that the warning has been heard.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:137

> This is simply the tradition of our predecessors.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The People Appeal to Precedent**

ʿĀd explains its indifference by appealing to the tradition of its predecessors. The statement shifts responsibility from the present generation to those who came before. What they do feels safe because it is inherited. Yet age and familiarity do not turn a practice into truth, and an ancestor's decision cannot answer for a descendant's judgment.

The appeal is powerful because communities receive language, rituals, social rules, and stories through generations. Inheritance gives people identity, but it can also make examination feel like betrayal. Hūd's call requires ʿĀd to ask whether loyalty to its past has become resistance to God.


The Arabic expression can carry the sense of an inherited way, custom, religion, or claim repeated from earlier people. The ambiguity itself is instructive. Quran 25:5 records a related dismissal in which opponents reduce revelation to tales of the past, showing how an appeal to antiquity can be used to evade the truth being heard now. ʿĀd may be defending its worship, its conduct, or the stories that make its conduct appear respectable. In each case, the appeal to the past is being used as a shield against correction.

A tradition deserves respect when it preserves truth and wisdom, but it does not become authoritative merely by being old. The people must distinguish between memory that helps them obey God and habit that asks God to approve whatever they already do.

**Ancestors Are Not the Final Measure**

Honoring ancestors can include gratitude for their sacrifices and care for their good example. It cannot mean assuming that they were incapable of error. If every predecessor were beyond question, no generation could ever repent of inherited injustice or recover a truth that its elders neglected.

Hūd does not ask ʿĀd to despise its forebears. He asks the living to answer the Lord with their own conscience. The dead cannot carry the responsibility of the present people, and their existence in the past cannot cancel the warning now being delivered.


A practice may survive because it is true, but it may also survive because power protects it, fear repeats it, or people never examine it. Longevity is evidence of transmission, not proof of righteousness. ʿĀd mistakes continuity for confirmation.

This error appears whenever a society says, “We have always done this,” as though history itself were a revelation. The statement avoids the real questions: Does the practice honor God? Does it protect justice? Does it withstand truthful examination? Hūd's message brings those questions back into view.

**The Past Can Be Used to Silence the Present**

Those who benefit from an established order often invoke ancestors to prevent reform. A person who questions the order is labeled disloyal, even when the order has become cruel. The past then functions as a political tool rather than a source of wisdom.

The people of ʿĀd have already shown their readiness to use force against others. Their appeal to predecessors may therefore protect more than worship; it may protect a whole arrangement of prestige and domination. Hūd's warning threatens the arrangement because it says that no custom stands above the Lord's judgment.


Divine guidance does not require people to forget every earlier generation. It gives them a criterion by which inherited practices can be kept, corrected, or abandoned. A beneficial custom can remain beneficial after being submitted to truth, while a corrupt custom loses its claim even if it is ancient.

This balance avoids two extremes. Blind traditionalism treats every inheritance as sacred, while blind novelty assumes that anything new is better. Hūd calls for neither. He calls ʿĀd to obey God, which means honoring what is true and relinquishing what opposes Him.


The people do not say that their predecessors were right for a particular reason. They simply point to the fact of inheritance. That brevity reveals how little examination they have performed. The custom is defended by its origin rather than by its moral content.

A serious believer can state why a practice accords with revelation and justice. He does not need to rely on ancestry as a substitute for evidence. When a person cannot explain the good of an inherited way but refuses to leave it, attachment has replaced conviction.


Every generation receives something and passes something on. The question is whether it transmits wisdom or merely repeats appetite. A responsible heir examines what he has received so that he does not pass harm to his children under the name of heritage.

ʿĀd's example warns that a people can inherit strength and still inherit a blindness about strength. Its predecessors may have begun a custom, but the present generation chooses to continue it. The response to Hūd therefore belongs to them, not to the ancestors behind whom they hide.

**The Reader Must Test Familiar Claims**

The verse is especially challenging because inherited language often feels natural. A reader may accept a belief, social ranking, or habit simply because it was present before he could question it. Hūd's encounter invites a pause: is this truly guidance, or only the oldest explanation available?

The right response is not contempt for one's roots. It is gratitude joined to discernment. Keep what leads to God, correct what departs from justice, and refuse to make the past an idol. Tradition can be a vessel of truth, but only God is its final authority.

This discernment is an act of loyalty, not betrayal. A community honors its worthy inheritance more faithfully when it removes what contradicts justice and preserves what leads to God. Otherwise, it passes an unexamined burden to children and calls the burden identity.

The appeal to predecessors should therefore prompt investigation rather than surrender. Ask what the earlier practice was meant to protect, whom it served, and whether its present form still serves that good. Honest examination can recover the wisdom of the past without becoming captive to its errors.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:138

> And we will never be punished.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Denial Reaches Its Extreme**

ʿĀd's appeal to the past ends with a confident denial of punishment. They do not merely say that they have no evidence of consequence. They say that punishment will never come. The word never reveals a certainty that exceeds their knowledge and turns a hope of escape into a creed.

Their earlier indifference now has a foundation. If no punishment exists, warning can be ignored, inherited custom can govern without review, and power can act without fear. Denial of accountability is not a small theoretical error; it changes the moral atmosphere of a whole society.


The claim can coexist with acknowledgment of a creator while denying that people will be held to account after death. Whether expressed through that distinction or through complete rejection, the practical result is similar: God's claim over conduct is emptied of consequence. Quran 46:26 makes the parallel point that hearing, sight, and understanding do not benefit a people who persist in denying God's signs.

A person may admit that life has a source and still resist the idea that life has a destination and judgment. Hūd's warning joins the two. The Provider who gives cattle, children, gardens, and springs is also the Lord before whom the recipients will answer for their use of those gifts.

**Denial Protects the Powerful From Moral Cost**

If there is no punishment, the strongest person can interpret success as permission. A blow against another becomes merely a victory, a seized resource becomes deserved, and a monument becomes proof that the builder is right. The denial is convenient because it removes the cost of choices that benefit the powerful.

This does not mean every person who doubts accountability is consciously defending oppression. But a society without a serious expectation of judgment is vulnerable to impunity. Its laws may restrain some harm, yet those who control the laws can begin to regard themselves as beyond the standard imposed on others.


Some wrongs are punished in this life, but many are hidden, delayed, or left apparently successful. If the present world were the entire measure, victims could conclude that injustice has no answer and oppressors could mistake delay for approval. The promise of a tremendous day completes the moral picture.

Hūd does not ask ʿĀd to believe in punishment because every consequence is immediately visible. He asks them to trust the Lord's truth about what lies beyond their limited observation. The absence of instant judgment is not proof that no judgment exists.


Cattle, children, gardens, and springs have filled the people's horizon with evidence of favor. They interpret those gifts as security from punishment. Hūd's message reverses that interpretation. Blessings are opportunities to obey, and their misuse can increase responsibility.

A prosperous society may assume that continued success means God has endorsed it. The verse exposes that assumption as dangerous. Time and abundance can be mercy before a person changes, not a guarantee that his conduct will never be judged. The people are warned precisely because their confidence has become unjustified.

**“Never” Converts a Claim Into a Barrier**

To say that punishment will never come closes the door before evidence can be considered. The people are not simply asking for clarification; they are announcing that no future event could correct them. Such language makes repentance appear unnecessary and turns the heart against every warning.

Humility leaves room for correction. It can say, “I do not yet understand,” or, “I need to examine this.” Arrogance says, “This cannot be true,” even when the speaker lacks authority to make that judgment. Hūd's people choose the second posture and make their certainty part of their guilt.


Belief in accountability should protect the rights of people whom worldly power can ignore. If ʿĀd is convinced that no punishment awaits, the suffering of those it attacks can be dismissed as an unfortunate part of dominance. Hūd's warning gives the victim a future before God even when earthly society refuses justice.

That future is not a license for private revenge. It is a reason for the oppressed to trust God's judgment and for the powerful to restrain themselves. The certainty of accountability should make every person more careful with authority, property, speech, and force.


Hūd has identified their Lord, recalled their provision, and expressed fear for their future. The people answer with denial. Their problem is not that no argument was offered. They refuse the framework in which an argument could matter: the framework of revelation, gratitude, and judgment.

A warning can be rejected in many forms, but this is the most complete. They do not merely continue an old practice; they deny the consequence that would make repentance urgent. Their confidence is now directed against the Lord's promise rather than only against Hūd's counsel.

**The Reader Should Not Borrow Their Certainty**

The verse asks the reader to notice the difference between honest doubt and defiant assurance. Not knowing every detail of the unseen is not the same as declaring that accountability is impossible. Faith requires humility before what God reveals, while arrogance turns limited human experience into a boundary for reality.

ʿĀd's statement therefore remains a warning against building a life on the assumption that nothing follows death. The proper response is not panic but preparation: use provision gratefully, correct inherited wrongs, and live as someone who will meet the Lord who knows every hidden deed.

Accountability also gives meaning to private choices that no public court observes. The promise of judgment assures the wronged that silence does not erase their claim and reminds the wrongdoer that concealment is not escape. A society shaped by this knowledge will seek justice even when enforcement is difficult.

ʿĀd's certainty says that punishment will never come; faith answers that no deed is lost. That answer should make the heart cautious, not self-righteous. The unseen belongs to God, and the servant prepares by acting well within what he can see.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:139

> So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ We destroyed them. Surely in this is a sign. Yet most of them would not believe.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Rejection Becomes a Verdict**

The account now moves from speech to consequence. ʿĀd rejected Hūd, and God destroyed them. The connection is not a claim that every worldly difficulty is a direct punishment that humans can confidently identify. Here the Qur'an itself explains the judgment within a prophetic account: the people had received warning, persisted in rejection, and then met the consequence announced to them.

Their destruction is therefore neither random nor a victory of one tribe over another. It is the outcome of a moral refusal before the Lord. The verse brings the people's confident words into contact with reality. Their claim that punishment would never come does not become true through repetition.


Quran 46:24–25 describes ʿĀd seeing a dense cloud approach their valleys, mistaking it for rain, and then facing a fierce wind whose command destroyed what God willed. It also says that the remains visible were their dwellings. This parallel confirms the seriousness of the present verdict without requiring speculation about every historical ruin.

The scene is morally striking because the people interpret the approaching danger through their expectation of benefit. They see rain where punishment is coming. A community that has trained itself to assume security may misread even a final warning until the opportunity to change has passed.

**Destruction Is Not the Only Sign**

The verse calls the event a sign, but the sign includes more than the physical end of a people. It includes the failure of their arguments, the exposure of their pride, and the contrast between their imagined permanence and their disappearance. A sign is understood when the event is read as evidence about God and human responsibility.

The landmarks and castles were signs of ʿĀd's power to its own eyes. Their destruction becomes a sign of the limits of that power. The people could raise structures and attack others, but they could not command the wind or make themselves immune to the Lord's decree.


Hūd did not threaten destruction to gain wealth or status. He warned because he was trustworthy and feared for the people. When the announced consequence arrives, the truth of his mission becomes visible. The messenger is not made true by the event; the event reveals that the message he faithfully carried was true.

This distinction protects the role of prophecy. Hūd is not a magician controlling punishment, nor a ruler who triumphs through private force. God judges, and the messenger has conveyed the warning. The servant remains a servant even when the promise of judgment is fulfilled.

**The Saved Lesson Is Not a License for Arrogance**

A reader who sees ʿĀd destroyed might feel superior to them. That response would miss the sign. The purpose is not to make later people boast that they would have listened, but to make them examine how they treat warning, custom, strength, and provision.

History can humble the believer or feed another form of pride. The humble reader says, “Let me not repeat their certainty.” He does not assume that belonging to a later community or possessing different technology makes him safe from the pattern exposed here.


The refrain says that most would not believe even after such a sign. This does not mean the event lacked clarity. It shows that people can resist the moral meaning of history. They may treat destruction as an isolated ancient story, blame only unusual circumstances, or admire the remains while ignoring the warning.

The word most also leaves room for those who respond rightly. Truth is not measured by the number of people who accept it. A small group can believe, repent, and be saved from the spiritual pattern even when a dominant society refuses to change.

**The Sign Includes the Collapse of False Security**

ʿĀd's security rested on visible strength, inherited confidence, and the denial of punishment. The destruction strips these supports away in one movement. What they thought would continue forever is shown to be temporary, and what they thought could not reach them reaches them by God's command.

False security does not always look like arrogance. It may appear as routine, wealth, institutional stability, or a reputation for being untouchable. The verse warns that created arrangements can end quickly. True security is found in obedience, not in the appearance that no consequence is near.


The destruction of ʿĀd closes one prophetic episode, but the refrain does not allow the reader to stop at spectacle. Another people will soon receive the same kind of call. The repeated structure teaches that the pattern is not limited to one vanished nation.

A messenger warns, a society responds, and God judges with wisdom. The names and temptations change, but the fundamental test remains. Will a people let revelation govern its strength, or will it turn blessings into proof that it cannot be corrected?


The verse stands as a pause for reflection. The people of ʿĀd have gone, but their assumptions can survive in later hearts. The reader is given the benefit they refused: the chance to see the result before making the same claim.

The proper response is belief joined to conduct. Recognize the Lord's power, accept the messenger's warning, and use provision without vanity. The sign is not fully received until it changes the way a person prepares for the judgment that ʿĀd denied.

A society can preserve the memory of a disaster and still miss its meaning. It may study the wind, admire the old remains, or tell the story as proof of its own sophistication. The Qur'anic sign asks for more: humility before God, repentance from injustice, and readiness to let warning govern the present.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:140

> And your Lord is certainly the Almighty, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Refrain Interprets the Destruction**

After stating that ʿĀd were destroyed, the verse closes with the names of the Lord: the Almighty, Most Merciful. The judgment is therefore not a chaotic disaster outside divine wisdom. It occurs under the power of the One who sent warning and made repentance possible. The names tell the reader how to understand both the severity and the care in the account.

Power explains why ʿĀd's castles, attacks, and confidence could not protect them. Mercy explains why Hūd came to them as a brother, why he asked for no payment, and why he continued to warn them before the final consequence. Quran 46:24–25 likewise places the approaching punishment after Hūd's warning and describes the remains of ʿĀd's dwellings, reinforcing the contrast between divine power and human security. The refrain holds these meanings together.


ʿĀd measured greatness through landmarks, fortifications, physical strength, and the ability to strike others. The title Almighty dismantles that measure. No created power can compete with the Lord who gives existence to people, land, water, and time.

This does not make human strength meaningless. It makes it dependent. A strong society can act beneficially when it knows that its strength is borrowed and accountable. It becomes dangerous when it treats borrowed power as a rival to the One from whom it came.

**Mercy Came Before the Sentence**

The judgment should not be isolated from the warning that preceded it. Hūd did not arrive after the people had been destroyed; he came while they could still respond. His calls to reverence, obedience, gratitude, and restraint were openings of mercy.

Mercy can be present even when a people refuses it. The fact that ʿĀd rejected the warning does not turn the warning into cruelty. It shows that divine care had been offered and that the people chose to close themselves against it. Their destruction confirms the seriousness of that choice.


Some imagine that mercy requires allowing powerful people to continue harming others. The story gives a fuller account. Mercy toward the oppressed and toward the moral order can require ending the power of those who persist in tyranny. The Almighty's judgment protects the truth that violence is not entitled to continue forever.

Yet human beings must not claim God's complete knowledge for themselves. The refrain calls them to oppose injustice with lawful means and humility, not to declare every personal enemy condemned. Divine mercy includes wisdom about hidden circumstances that no human tribunal fully possesses.

**The Names Correct Two Errors**

One error sees only power and imagines God as a distant force whose judgment gives no room for hope. The other sees only mercy and assumes that no wrongdoing will have a final consequence. The refrain rejects both distortions. God is mighty enough to judge and merciful enough to invite return.

For the believer, this balance produces courage without cruelty. He does not fear tyrants as though they were ultimate, and he does not enjoy judgment as though he were its owner. He trusts the Almighty and seeks the mercy that every servant needs.


The same pair of names closed Noah's account and now closes the account of ʿĀd. The repetition teaches that the Lord of different peoples is one Lord with one consistent moral character. He saves, warns, delays, judges, and forgives in wisdom; the changing communities do not change Him.

The pattern also helps the reader compare responses. Noah's people rejected and were drowned; ʿĀd rejected and were destroyed. The forms of judgment differ, but the lesson is stable: a messenger's warning is mercy, and persistent denial cannot make the Almighty powerless.

**The Refrain Guards Against Worshipping the Story**

A reader might become absorbed in the vanished civilization, the wind, or the ruins. The final names redirect attention. The true subject is not ʿĀd's grandeur but the Lord whose power exposes its limit and whose mercy gave it an opportunity to repent.

This redirection matters because historical fascination can become another form of vanity. People may admire ancient strength while repeating its spiritual error. The refrain asks them to leave the story praising God, not envying the people who were judged.


It is not enough to say that God is Most Merciful while refusing the guidance He sends. Mercy appears in the messenger, the reminder, the provision, and the time given before judgment. The hearer's response is gratitude expressed through obedience.

The title Most Merciful also gives hope to someone who recognizes the pattern in his own life. A person need not wait until security collapses to return. He can abandon vanity, repair harm, and seek forgiveness while the door of repentance remains open. Fear of the Almighty should move him toward the mercy already offered.

**Power and Mercy Meet in Divine Justice**

Divine justice is not a compromise between power and mercy. It is the wise action of the Lord who knows what every person has done and what opportunity each received. ʿĀd's destruction is not evidence that mercy failed; it is evidence that mercy does not erase truth or permit unending oppression.

The human task is to live under both names. Be firm against wrongdoing without becoming tyrannical, and hopeful for repentance without excusing harm. Remember power so that pride falls, and remember mercy so that correction remains compassionate.


The account of ʿĀd ends, but the reader remains. The next community may have different buildings, technologies, and customs, yet it will still receive gifts from the Lord and face the temptation to treat them as proof of independence. The final refrain places every age under the same reality.

Your Lord is Almighty: no false security can resist Him. Your Lord is Most Merciful: no sincere return is meaningless while life remains. To understand the story is to carry both truths into worship, stewardship, and the way power is used.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:141

> The people of Thamûd rejected the messengers

**Expanded Commentary**

**Thamûd Is Introduced by Its Response**

The account of Thamûd begins with a verdict about how the people received revelation: they rejected the messengers. The verse does not first praise their settlements, skill, or resources. It puts their moral response before their material description. A people may be remembered for what it builds, but the Qur'an asks first whether it accepted the truth sent to it.

This opening also connects Thamûd to the communities already mentioned. Noah's people and ʿĀd had heard warning and refused it. Thamûd now enters the same sequence, not because every historical detail is identical, but because human pride keeps returning to the same decision. The names change; the test of submission remains.

**The Plural Includes the Shared Prophetic Call**

Ṣāliḥ is the messenger immediately associated with Thamûd, yet the verse says messengers in the plural. Rejecting one messenger who brings the true call is treated as rejection of the prophetic mission as a whole. The messengers do not compete over separate gods or incompatible foundations. They call people back to the Lord who created them and judges them.

The plural therefore prevents Thamûd from reducing the matter to a disagreement with one local man. Ṣāliḥ stands within a line of warning that began before him and continues beyond his people. The community's refusal becomes a refusal of the authority represented by every faithful messenger, not merely a personal dislike of Ṣāliḥ.

**The Community Has a History, Not an Excuse**

Thamûd is a named people with its own memory and way of life. That specificity matters. Revelation does not condemn an imaginary type called “the arrogant”; it addresses a real community whose habits can be examined. Naming the people makes the warning concrete and prevents the reader from treating rejection as a vague flaw found only in legends.

At the same time, a historical name does not place the story safely in the past. Every community develops reasons for trusting its own customs and achievements. Thamûd becomes a mirror when a later society recognizes the same instinct in itself: defend inherited confidence first, and ask about God's command only afterward.

**Rejection Comes Before the Famous Sign**

The verse records the response before the narrative describes the she-camel. This order matters. The people do not begin with an innocent search for evidence and then reluctantly reject an unmistakable sign. Their basic stance toward revelation is already resistant. The later sign exposes that stance; it does not create it from nothing.

Quran 7:73 likewise presents Ṣāliḥ as Thamûd's brother and describes the she-camel as a sign from their Lord. That parallel shows that the miracle was placed within a prior call to worship Allah. The community's central problem was not a shortage of marvels but a refusal to let evidence govern its allegiance.

**Material Skill Does Not Settle Spiritual Truth**

Thamûd is associated with skilled settlement and mountain dwellings in the verses that follow. Such ability can create a powerful sense of self-sufficiency. A society that can shape difficult terrain may begin to think that every limit is merely an engineering problem. The prophetic message asks a different question: who has given the ability, and for what will it be used?

Achievement deserves gratitude and careful use, but it cannot decide whether worship belongs to God. A strong economy cannot prove that its gods are real. A beautiful settlement cannot prove that its rulers are just. Thamûd's rejection shows the danger of allowing visible competence to become a substitute for submission.

**The Messenger Comes From Among Them**

The next verse identifies Ṣāliḥ as their brother, so the opening verdict should be read with that closeness in mind. Thamûd was not confronted by a stranger who knew nothing of its language or circumstances. The messenger belonged to the people and understood the world whose assumptions he challenged.

That familiarity removes one common excuse but creates another temptation. People may dismiss a truthful neighbor because they have known him as an ordinary person. They can accept his honesty in daily dealings yet reject the authority of the message he conveys. Thamûd's response must therefore be judged as resistance to guidance, not as a justified complaint about distance.

**The First Sentence Sets the Moral Scale**

The verse is short, but its placement sets the scale for everything that follows. Watch the community's prosperity, its buildings, its demand for proof, and its treatment of the sign through the opening verdict. None of these details can be evaluated apart from the fact that Thamûd chose rejection.

For the reader, the sentence is a warning against admiring a civilization without asking what it worshipped and how it responded to correction. A society can be capable, established, and culturally rich while remaining answerable for denial. The real measure of Thamûd is not what it could carve, but whether it would bow to the Lord behind every gift.

The opening verdict also separates collective reputation from individual responsibility. A people can be called by a single name, yet each person still chooses whether to support, question, or resist the community's direction. The verse warns against hiding behind a group identity. A society's refusal is built out of many personal refusals, and a person's faith is not invalidated merely because the crowd rejects it.

Thamûd's story therefore begins with a decision that cannot be buried under later detail. The reader is invited to hear the word rejected as a moral act, not as a label for an unfortunate outcome. Revelation was placed before the people, and they chose a posture toward it. The coming account will show what that posture did to their understanding of their own gifts.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:142

> when their brother Ṣâliḥ said to them, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺?

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ṣāliḥ Speaks as Their Brother**

The verse places brotherhood before the question of fear. Ṣāliḥ is one of Thamûd, sharing its language, environment, and human concerns. His warning is not an abstract announcement delivered from outside the community. It comes through someone whose life is woven into theirs and whose knowledge of their condition cannot be dismissed as ignorance.

Brotherhood gives the appeal tenderness without weakening its force. Ṣāliḥ does not flatter Thamûd or approve its direction simply because he belongs to it. He speaks as a person who wants his people rescued from a danger they cannot see clearly. A loving warning may sound severe when the threatened harm is serious.


The question asks whether they will fear Allah. Taqwa is not mere fright before an approaching disaster. It is an active awareness of God that makes a person guard his choices. Ṣāliḥ calls Thamûd to let that awareness govern worship, ambition, property, and treatment of others.

A community can acknowledge that God exists and still live as though it has no duty toward Him. Taqwa closes that gap. It turns belief into caution, gratitude, and obedience. The question is therefore larger than an emotional response. It asks whether God will have a practical place in the way Thamûd conducts its common life.

**The Messenger Is Close Enough to Be Known**

A local messenger carries a special kind of evidence: the people can compare his claim with the character they have observed. Ṣāliḥ is not asking them to trust an unknown adventurer. They know his family and his conduct. If they reject his warning, they must explain why the message is false rather than simply inventing a reason to distrust his motives.

Quran 7:73 also presents him as Thamûd's brother and describes his call to worship Allah alone. The parallel confirms that the family language is part of the mission's meaning. God sends guidance through a human being who can speak plainly to a human community, not through a voice detached from ordinary life.


Some people hear religious fear as a demand for constant anxiety. Ṣāliḥ's question has a different purpose. Fear of Allah restrains the hand before it harms, the ruler before he abuses authority, and the wealthy person before he turns provision into domination. It is a moral guard placed before the deed, not only a reaction afterward.

This is why the question is addressed to a people known for prosperity. Abundance can reduce a sense of dependence and make restraint seem unnecessary. Taqwa reminds Thamûd that every advantage remains under the Lord's judgment. The secure person is not the one who feels untouchable, but the one who remembers that God sees how security is used.

**Brotherhood Does Not Mean Tribal Loyalty**

Ṣāliḥ's belonging does not mean he will defend Thamûd's customs at the expense of truth. Genuine brotherhood seeks the good of the people, and their good cannot be separated from worshipping God. A messenger may oppose the practices of his own community while continuing to speak with concern for it.

This distinction prevents two distortions. Loyalty must not become silence about injustice, and correction must not become hatred of the people corrected. Ṣāliḥ's question holds both sides together. He remains their brother while asking them to abandon the arrogance that is endangering them.


The question has social force because Thamûd's choices are not private. The people manage land, water, homes, animals, and relations among families. If they fear Allah, they cannot treat every resource as the property of the strongest. They must ask whether their decisions preserve justice and acknowledge the rights of those with less power.

The religious call therefore does not withdraw from practical affairs. It supplies the standard by which practical affairs are judged. A settlement can be well planned and still be corrupt if its prosperity depends on cruelty. Taqwa makes technical ability answerable to moral purpose.

**The Question Leaves Room for Return**

Ṣāliḥ asks rather than announcing that Thamûd is beyond hope. A question invites recognition and leaves the hearer responsible for the answer. The community can still move from confidence in itself to reverence for God. Warning is therefore an opening before it becomes a record of refusal.

That opening should not be mistaken for weakness in the messenger. Ṣāliḥ knows that judgment is real, but he does not rush to it. He gives his people a clear chance to reconsider. His brotherhood makes the opportunity personal: the one asking them to fear Allah is one of their own.


Thamûd could answer with a word of agreement and continue its old practices. Taqwa must be visible in changed decisions. The question reaches beyond speech to what people build, consume, protect, and permit. Fear is genuine when it limits the actions that pride once treated as normal.

For the reader, the verse asks whether closeness to a reminder has become a reason to discount it. Ṣāliḥ's familiarity should have made listening easier, not less necessary. The Lord's claim arrives through a brother, and the decisive issue is whether that appeal will produce reverent conduct.

A community does not honor its own people by silencing the one who warns it. It honors them by judging the warning fairly and allowing truth to correct inherited confidence. Brotherhood is therefore a bridge to accountability, not a shelter from it. The question remains compassionate because Ṣāliḥ wants Thamûd to live, but compassion would be empty if it concealed the danger.

A warning from within a community can be harder to hear than one delivered by a stranger. The familiar voice knows where pride is strongest, and its closeness makes evasion less comfortable. Thamûd must not confuse personal discomfort with evidence against the message. The question is gentle in its aim, but firm about the Lord's right to be feared.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:143

> I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Trustworthiness Supports a Difficult Claim**

Ṣāliḥ identifies himself as a trustworthy messenger because the people are being asked to accept a message that will unsettle their worship and confidence. Trust is not decorative praise. It addresses the question of whether the speaker is delivering God's command faithfully or using religion to pursue influence, wealth, or revenge.

A community can test a messenger's character through the life it has seen. Ṣāliḥ has grown among Thamûd, so his statement invites them to compare his conduct with his claim. The message should not be dismissed by assigning him a hidden motive without evidence. They must engage what he says and why it follows from God's authority.


The word messenger places Ṣāliḥ in a precise position. He is neither an ordinary adviser speaking only from personal experience nor a divine being who possesses independent power. He receives and conveys guidance. His trustworthiness includes honesty about the source of his authority and humility about his own place before God.

That balance protects the people from two mistakes. They must not reject the message because Ṣāliḥ is human, and they must not turn Ṣāliḥ into an object of worship because he is a messenger. A reliable envoy points beyond himself. His success is measured by whether people obey the Lord he represents.

**The Same Standard Appears Across the Stories**

The phrasing repeats the declaration made by the earlier messengers in this sūrah. Noah and Hūd likewise identify themselves as trustworthy messengers before calling their people to obedience. Repetition does not make the claim empty; it shows that truthfulness and fidelity are essential to every prophetic mission.

The continuity also prevents Thamûd from treating Ṣāliḥ as a private religious innovator. His call stands within a known pattern: a messenger from the people, a summons to fear Allah, and freedom from the desire to profit by the message. The community is being asked to recognize a familiar form of guidance.


A messenger may be sincere yet still fail if he alters the message to suit the audience. Ṣāliḥ's claim includes faithful delivery. He cannot soften the warning merely because Thamûd is wealthy, nor can he intensify it to satisfy personal anger. He must convey what God has entrusted to him without adding a private agenda.

This makes prophetic courage a form of trust. The community's approval is not the measure of accuracy. Ṣāliḥ must tell people what they need to hear even when their admiration turns to hostility. A message adjusted to preserve popularity would be easier to receive but less worthy of trust.

**The People Are Not Asked for Blind Admiration**

Trustworthy speech deserves a fair hearing, not a personality cult. Ṣāliḥ does not ask Thamûd to abandon understanding. His claim can be considered alongside the clarity of his call, the coherence of his worship, and the signs God provides. The messenger's character opens the door to listening; it does not replace the truth of what he conveys.

This protects religious life from manipulation. A charismatic speaker can be persuasive while being false, and an honest person can be unpolished while speaking truth. Ṣāliḥ's trustworthiness matters together with his message. The people should neither follow appearances alone nor use the human form of the messenger as an excuse to reject him.


The objection that Ṣāliḥ is one of them will appear explicitly later. This verse answers it in advance by presenting ordinary human familiarity as part of the proof. A messenger who shares the people's world can explain their habits and address their excuses in a language they understand.

Quran 18:110 states the same basic relation for the Prophet Muhammad: the messenger is a human being who receives revelation and calls to one God. Humanity is not a defect in an envoy. It is the condition that makes imitation, instruction, and moral accountability possible for those who hear him.

**Freedom From Personal Gain**

Trust is weakened when a teacher turns guidance into a private business. Ṣāliḥ's declaration prepares for the recurring prophetic statement that he seeks no reward from his people. He is not asking Thamûd to buy access to God's favor or to enrich him in return for spiritual advice.

This does not mean that every person who serves a community must refuse lawful support. It means that the messenger's authority cannot be purchased. His reward and accountability are with God, which allows him to address rich and poor by the same standard.


Once Ṣāliḥ has identified himself as trustworthy, Thamûd cannot fairly dismiss him without examination. The people may still choose rejection, but they will be rejecting a warning delivered by one whose character and mission demand attention. Their response becomes a moral decision rather than a casual preference.

The reader also receives a test for evaluating guidance. Look for truthfulness, fidelity, independence from manipulation, and a call that directs worship to God rather than to the speaker. Ṣāliḥ's short declaration establishes that the messenger can be trusted precisely because he remains a servant of the Lord.

Trust also requires consistency between the messenger's private conduct and public call. A person who condemns greed while pursuing it secretly would undermine his own warning. Ṣāliḥ presents a different model: the message limits him before it limits anyone else. He stands under the same Lord he names, and that shared submission keeps his authority from becoming a claim of personal superiority.

This is also why the messenger's humanity is not an embarrassment to the message. Human beings can understand a human example, witness patience under pressure, and see that obedience is possible in ordinary circumstances. The envoy's weakness points to God's strength rather than competing with it.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:144

> So fear Allah, and obey me.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Trust Must Become Obedience**

Ṣāliḥ has said that he is a trustworthy messenger. This verse states what the people should do with that claim: fear Allah and obey the messenger. The command does not ask Thamûd merely to respect Ṣāliḥ's honesty. It asks the community to let his guidance govern its choices.

The order keeps the messenger's role clear. Reverence belongs first to Allah, while obedience to Ṣāliḥ follows because he conveys God's command. The people do not replace direct worship of the Lord with attachment to a human leader. They follow the messenger as an act of submission to the One who sent him.


Fear of Allah gives obedience its right motive. A person may comply with a leader because of force, custom, or the promise of reward. Taqwa is different. It makes the servant aware that God sees the hidden intention and the public action. Obedience then grows from reverence rather than from fear of social consequences alone.

This inner foundation matters for Thamûd because its outward prosperity can hide inward independence. The people may obey one another's customs while refusing the Lord. Ṣāliḥ calls them to a deeper loyalty, one that remains present even when no human authority is watching.

**Obedience Reorders a Prosperous Society**

Thamûd's resources are not condemned simply because they are abundant. Obedience changes what abundance means. Land, crops, homes, and water become trusts instead of proof that the community may rule without limits. The strong must restrain themselves, and the community must protect those who can be overlooked.

A society can repeat the words of submission while preserving the same injustice. Genuine obedience reaches its institutions and habits. It influences whose claims are heard, how shared goods are used, and whether the powerful are allowed to turn prosperity into a license for harm.


Ṣāliḥ's command does not establish a rival kingdom for himself. He calls the people to Allah, not to his own name. A true messenger's authority is inseparable from his refusal to collect worship, wealth, or absolute loyalty for his person.

That distinction also protects obedience from becoming tribal politics. Thamûd is not asked to exchange one human master for another. It is asked to submit to God and to accept Ṣāliḥ's guidance only within that submission. The messenger's strength comes from the message, not from personal domination.

**A Repeated Prophetic Formula Carries Continuity**

The same call was directed to Noah and Hūd in the preceding accounts. Their peoples heard a combination of reverence and obedience because the core of prophetic guidance is stable. Thamûd cannot claim that Ṣāliḥ has invented a new demand simply because it challenges its own practices.

Quran 7:73 presents Ṣāliḥ calling Thamûd to worship Allah alone and identifying a clear proof from their Lord. That parallel shows the command is attached to a call to divine oneness, not to blind loyalty. Obedience to Ṣāliḥ is meaningful because it leads the people away from idols and back to God.


To follow Ṣāliḥ means more than attending to his speech. It includes stopping when the messenger identifies a boundary. Later, the community will face a test involving a protected sign and a shared resource. The present command establishes the principle before that test arrives: God's instruction must control appetite and power.

This is a general measure of obedience. A person who claims to follow revelation but refuses every limit has followed his desire instead. Taqwa becomes visible when a person can leave something alone even though he has the ability to take it.

**The Command Is Mercy, Not Humiliation**

Thamûd may hear obedience as a loss of status. Ṣāliḥ presents it as the way to preserve the community from its own pride. A people is not diminished by recognizing its Creator. It is freed from having to defend the illusion that its achievements make it independent.

The command also offers an honorable path for leaders. They can use their authority to implement justice rather than surrendering to the appetites of the strongest. Obedience to God does not erase responsibility; it gives responsibility a standard higher than popularity.


Ṣāliḥ's sentence is direct because the decision is direct. Either Thamûd will allow reverence for Allah to govern its conduct, or it will continue treating custom and ability as final authorities. The people cannot claim to honor the messenger while keeping his command outside the areas that matter most.

For the reader, the verse asks whether obedience is selective. God is feared truly when His guidance reaches wealth, family, public decisions, and private desire. Ṣāliḥ's call is simple, but it demands a whole life: fear Allah, then follow the messenger who faithfully brings His word.

The command also gives a standard for evaluating claims of religious leadership. A guide who asks for obedience while directing praise, wealth, and fear toward himself has reversed the order of Ṣāliḥ's words. The authentic messenger makes God's supremacy clearer and his own status smaller. His obedience is not a path into human domination but an escape from it.

In daily life, this means that reverence must survive when no dramatic sign is being discussed. It appears in fair contracts, careful use of land, restraint in conflict, and willingness to stop at a revealed limit. Thamûd is not being asked for a momentary gesture. It is being asked to let the command become the shape of its common life.

That common life includes the way a community responds when obedience costs it an advantage. Anyone can praise submission while the command agrees with existing interests. The test comes when truth limits a profitable custom or protects someone without influence. Fear of Allah gives the people a reason to accept that loss without treating justice as defeat.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:145

> I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ṣāliḥ Removes the Motive of Profit**

The messenger has asked Thamûd to fear Allah and obey him. The people might answer that he is pursuing wealth or a position of influence. Ṣāliḥ removes that suspicion: he seeks no reward from them for delivering the message. His call is not a bargain in which acceptance purchases his favor.

This matters because his audience is divided by status and resources. If guidance could be bought, the wealthy would receive the best access and the poor would be left outside. Ṣāliḥ presents a message that cannot be priced by the people. Every person hears the same claim of God's authority.


Ṣāliḥ does not describe his work as unpaid labor with no value. He locates its reward with the Lord of all worlds. That answer changes the direction of his hope. The approval of Thamûd is temporary, and its wealth is limited; God's knowledge and recompense encompass every people and every hidden intention.

A messenger who expects his reward from God is not free from concern for his audience. He wants Thamûd guided and fears its destruction. But love for the people is not the same as dependence on their praise. He can continue warning when they turn against him because his service is not sustained by their applause.

**No Payment Keeps the Message Open**

Ṣāliḥ's refusal of a reward prevents religion from becoming a private gate controlled by money. A poor family does not need to purchase the right to hear, and a chief cannot purchase a milder standard. The message is public and universal because its source is the Lord of all worlds, not the household of the messenger.

This principle does not forbid lawful support for ordinary teachers, workers, or community servants. Their human labor may be compensated. The verse concerns the messenger's motive and authority. Acceptance of revelation is not a financial transaction, and God's favor cannot be sold by any human being.


The title Lord of all worlds is especially important in a local dispute. Ṣāliḥ is not appealing to a private deity who belongs only to Thamûd or to his own family. He speaks of the Lord who owns every people, land, and generation. The community's customs cannot limit God's claim.

That title also explains why the reward is secure. A tribe may withhold wealth or honor, but it cannot withhold God's recompense. The messenger's real audience is not confined to the people standing before him. His work is part of a divine order that reaches beyond one settlement and one age.

**A Messenger Must Not Sell Silence**

A paid advocate may adjust his speech to preserve his contract. Ṣāliḥ cannot do that. He must identify idolatry, entitlement, and the misuse of the land even when the truth threatens powerful interests. Refusing payment protects the independence needed for truthful warning.

The absence of a fee does not make his task easy. He pays through patience, rejection, and the risk of being misunderstood. His statement separates worldly compensation from faithful service. He gives the message because God entrusted it to him, not because Thamûd has promised to make the work comfortable.


If Ṣāliḥ asks nothing from the people, their rejection cannot be explained by the cost of conversion. The issue is not a demand on their treasury. It is whether they will surrender the right to define worship and conduct for themselves.

This is why accusations of hidden motives can be convenient. They shift attention from the truth of the warning to a suspicion that has not been proved. Ṣāliḥ's declaration asks Thamûd to be fair. Examine the message, the messenger's character, and the evidence rather than protecting pride through an invented financial explanation.

**A Parallel From Hūd Clarifies the Pattern**

Quran 11:51 records Hūd telling ʿĀd that he asks no reward and that his reward is with the One who created him. Ṣāliḥ's statement follows the same prophetic ethic. The repetition establishes that the messengers do not come to create personal empires. They direct all reward and worship back to God.
