The judgment is therefore not outside divine care. It is the act of the Lord who knows what the people heard, what sign they received, and what limit they crossed. Mercy does not mean that the camel's destruction is ignored. Power does not mean that the warning was unnecessary. The two names explain the whole sequence.


Thamûd carved mountains and cultivated a prosperous land. Its skill was impressive but bounded. The Almighty is the One who created the people, the stone, the water, the crops, and the forces that can overturn human plans. No monument can claim equality with the Lord who gives the material and the ability to shape it.

That truth does not require despising craft. It requires placing craft beneath worship. A skilled community can use its ability for protection, food, and beauty, but it cannot use ability as evidence that it owes no obedience. The refrain strips power of its false independence while leaving room for responsible work.

**Mercy Was Present in the Warning**

Ṣāliḥ spoke as a brother, declared his trustworthiness, asked no payment, and repeated the call to fear Allah. Each part of his mission was an opening of mercy. The community had time to listen before the punishment overtook it. Its refusal does not turn the opportunity into cruelty.

The mercy also appears in the clarity of the sign. The she-camel was not a hidden riddle available only to a small elite. It stood within the people's daily life and came with a clear limit. The people were given a practical path to obedience, not an impossible demand to discover an unseen code.

**The Two Names Reject Two Distortions**

One distortion sees only power and imagines God as a force whose judgment leaves no hope. Another sees only mercy and assumes that no wrongdoing can bring a final consequence. The refrain rejects both. God is Mighty enough to judge and Merciful enough to warn, delay, and accept a sincere return.

A believer needs both truths. Fear of the Almighty prevents pride, while hope in the Merciful prevents despair. Thamûd's story especially corrects presumption, the idea that abundance and delay prove safety. The mercy they received was an invitation to repent, not permission to continue violating the command.


The final names direct attention away from the spectacle of a ruined people. A reader who delights in the punishment has not understood the Most Merciful. The event should produce sober recognition that justice is real and that God's care includes protecting the truth from being erased by powerful refusal.

This also disciplines human judgment. People can resist oppression and seek lawful justice, but they should not claim to know every hidden reason behind a calamity. God's power is complete because His knowledge is complete. Human beings must act with evidence, restraint, and humility.


Quran 7:77–78 records the killing of the camel followed by an overwhelming earthquake that left the people lifeless in their homes. That parallel confirms the severity of the judgment described here. It also preserves the order that makes the judgment intelligible: a clear sign and command came before the community's defiance.

The refrain therefore keeps the parallel from becoming a mere disaster report. The Lord's power is shown in the punishment, and His mercy is shown in the warning and sign that preceded it. The event is morally legible because both names remain present.

**Mercy Does Not Cancel the Rights of the Victim**

The she-camel's protected share represented a right assigned by God. To ignore that right in the name of mercy would leave the vulnerable exposed to whoever has the greater appetite. The Most Merciful is not indifferent to the creature and community harmed by transgression.

This gives divine mercy a moral shape. It includes forgiveness and opportunity, but it also includes the restoration of order and the ending of aggression. A society cannot demand mercy for its own pride while refusing mercy to the beings and people its power harms.


The reader is not asked to stand with the crowd because it is large, or with the builders because their work is impressive. Stand under the two names. Trust God's power more than human security, and seek His mercy before a choice becomes irreversible.

This posture is neither passive fear nor confident self-righteousness. It is active obedience. Use gifts carefully, accept limits, repair harm, and keep the heart open to correction. The Lord who judged Thamûd is still Almighty, and the Lord who sent Ṣāliḥ is still Most Merciful.


The refrain closes Thamûd's episode but not the Qur'an's concern. A new community will be mentioned next, and the same pattern will invite comparison. The reader must not treat the refrain as a formula that belongs only to a vanished nation.

Every generation receives signs, provision, and warnings in forms suited to its condition. The question is whether it sees them as mercy from the Almighty or as obstacles to its own authority. Thamûd's end is a sign because it gives the living time to choose differently.

A refrain at the end of judgment is also a safeguard for memory. It prevents later generations from treating the event as fate without a Lord, or as a triumph of one human group over another. The correct memory keeps both divine power and divine mercy in view.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:160

> The people of Lot rejected the messengers

**Expanded Commentary**

**A New People Enters the Repeated Pattern**

The account turns from Thamûd to the people of Lot with another opening verdict: they rejected the messengers. The change of community does not change the central test. A people hears a warning and decides whether revelation will govern its desires, customs, and treatment of others.

The repeated wording teaches the reader to compare rather than isolate the stories. Thamûd's setting involved land, cultivation, skill, and a sign. The next account will have its own circumstances, but its first moral fact is the same. Rejection is the community's response to the messenger, and that response places every later detail under accountability.


Lot is the messenger associated with his people, yet the verse uses the plural messengers. As in the accounts of Noah, ʿĀd, and Thamûd, rejecting one true messenger is treated as rejection of the shared prophetic call. The messengers do not invite different forms of worship based on tribal preference. They call people to the Lord who owns every community.

The plural also prevents a people from reducing revelation to a personal dispute. Lot is not merely an individual whose lifestyle or temperament the community dislikes. He stands within the line of warning that has already been heard by earlier nations. To reject him is to resist the authority of the message he carries.

**The People Are Named Before Their Practice**

The verse calls them the people of Lot before the account develops their behavior. Identity is introduced through relation to the messenger. This keeps the reader from approaching the community as a collection of strange acts without moral history. They are people who receive guidance and then choose how to answer it.

That order also protects against reducing an entire people to a single description. God knows individuals, motives, and degrees of responsibility. The collective verdict concerns the community's response to the messenger, while divine judgment remains more precise than human stereotypes. A later reader must learn the moral lesson without pretending to possess God's complete knowledge of every person.


To reject a messenger is not merely to disagree with one sentence. It is to protect a pattern that the messenger's warning threatens. A community may prefer its inherited pleasures, social power, or idea of freedom to the limits of revelation. The opening verdict identifies that preference before the narrative describes its public consequences.

This is why the same wording can appear across very different stories. The surface temptations differ, but rejection has a common structure. The people want to keep authority over worship and conduct for themselves. The messenger says that God has the final word, and the community responds by treating the messenger as the problem.

**Lot's Message Is Not a Private Innovation**

The plural messengers places Lot within continuity. His call must be heard alongside the prophetic summons already described in this sūrah: worship God, fear Him, obey the messenger, and do not let appetite rule the community. The setting changes, but divine oneness and moral accountability remain central.

Quran 7:80 introduces Lot's rebuke to his people within a broader sequence of prophetic warnings. That parallel confirms that the narrative is not inviting curiosity about an isolated scandal. It is exposing what happens when a society is warned about wrongdoing and chooses to defend the wrongdoing instead.


A reader may become accustomed to the refrain and stop hearing it. Repetition can dull attention, but it can also reveal that human beings repeatedly need the same correction. The verse insists that a new society is not exempt merely because another society has already failed.

Each community has its own reasons for believing it is different. It may point to its culture, its intelligence, or its freedoms. The repeated verdict asks a more serious question: when a truthful messenger challenges the community, will it submit to God or make its own preference the measure of truth?

**Collective Identity Cannot Carry a Person to Safety**

Being associated with a people does not determine a person's final standing. The community may reject while an individual believes, and a person may belong outwardly to a group without sharing every intention within it. The verse names the collective because collective choices matter, but God's judgment does not erase individual accountability.

This distinction prevents both contempt and complacency. Do not despise every person because of a group's rejection, and do not assume that belonging to a group protects you from its moral direction. Each hearer must decide whether to support falsehood, remain silent before it, or follow the guidance God sends.


The verse is a threshold. It does not yet detail every claim made by Lot or every response of his people; it establishes the fact that rejection governs the story. The reader should carry forward the earlier lessons: prosperity, custom, and majority opinion cannot replace submission to God.

A messenger's presence is mercy because it gives the community an opportunity to change before judgment. If the people reject that mercy, the outcome will not be a mystery of fate. Their own response will reveal what they chose to protect. The opening sentence asks the reader to listen before the next exchange begins.


The phrase “the people of Lot” can tempt later readers to look at another society with distance. The Qur'an places the verse here to prevent that escape. Every community has desires it protects and boundaries it resents. The question is whether it will accept correction when revelation confronts those desires.

The safest response is humility. Hear the messenger, test claims by God's guidance, and do not treat a familiar social order as an authority above Him. The people of Lot rejected the messengers; the account is a warning to anyone who believes that a community's insistence can make its chosen way immune to judgment.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:161

> when their brother Lot said to them, “Will you not fear ˹Allah˺?

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lot Speaks From Within the Community**

Lot is introduced as their brother before his question is heard. He is not a stranger who has arrived to mock the people from a distance. He shares their human world and addresses them as someone who knows their society from the inside. His warning therefore carries both intimacy and authority.

Brotherhood does not mean approval of every practice in the community. Lot's concern for his people requires him to challenge what is wrong rather than protect their reputation. A truthful relative can be more loving in correction than a flattering ally who leaves a people to its ruin.


Lot asks whether they will fear Allah. The question connects his story to the calls of Noah, Hūd, and Ṣāliḥ. Prophetic guidance begins with recognition that human desire is not the highest authority. Taqwa places conduct before God and prevents a society from calling every appetite a right simply because it is desired.

Fear here is not panic or hatred of the self. It is moral awareness. The people are asked to remember that God sees what is public and private, and that pleasure does not erase accountability. Lot's question invites them to pause before defending a practice that revelation has condemned.

**A Local Messenger Removes an Excuse**

The people cannot claim that Lot knows nothing of their circumstances. He belongs to them and can speak their language. The closeness makes their response more responsible: they are hearing a warning from someone who has shared their environment and understands the social pressure around the conduct he addresses.

Quran 7:80 also introduces Lot's rebuke to his people in the context of a shameful practice. The parallel confirms that the question is a moral summons, not a private dispute between a prophet and a few individuals. Lot is calling the community to examine its public direction before harm becomes normalized.


A distant rule can be discussed abstractly. Lot's question is carried by a person whose relationship to the community can be felt. He has family ties, memories, and a stake in what happens. His warning is not delivered from superiority; it comes from concern for people with whom he is connected.

That human closeness also makes rejection more revealing. The people know that Lot is not attacking them because he is an outsider who hates them. They reject a moral claim because it threatens what they have chosen to protect. Their resistance cannot be explained simply as a clash of unfamiliar cultures.


Sexual desire, social custom, and public approval can reinforce one another. A person may participate because he wants the act, because others praise it, or because he fears being excluded if he objects. Lot's question places every one of those pressures beneath God. The crowd is not allowed to turn agreement into moral truth.

A society that fears Allah must protect the ability to refuse wrongdoing. It cannot force every person to celebrate what he believes is forbidden, nor can it make public approval a substitute for conscience. Taqwa creates space for truthful correction even when the dominant mood is hostile.

**The Warning Is About Conduct, Not Mere Existence**

Lot's rebuke concerns what the people do. It does not authorize contempt for a person merely because he experiences a temptation or struggles with desire. Moral accountability concerns chosen acts, public encouragement of wrongdoing, and the harms associated with a practice. The prophet's question calls for restraint and repentance, not dehumanization.

This distinction matters because a community can condemn sin while becoming sinful in how it speaks about sinners. Fear of Allah requires justice, privacy, and refusal to turn correction into cruelty. Lot's own position, as shown by his concern for his people, keeps moral seriousness joined to human dignity.

**The Question Is an Opening Before Judgment**

Lot asks rather than announcing that the people cannot change. A question gives the hearer a moment to recognize the Lord's claim and turn back. The opportunity is real, even though the practice has become established and defended.

Mercy often begins with an interruption. A society may be moving confidently along a harmful path, and a messenger breaks the momentum by asking whether it fears God. The question does not flatter the people, but it gives them a way to stop before their habits become a public identity from which they no longer wish to depart.


They can respond with a slogan and continue unchanged, or they can let fear of Allah reshape their conduct. Taqwa is visible in restraint, repentance, protection of others, and willingness to accept revealed limits. It is not proved by saying that God is great while treating His command as optional.

For the reader, Lot's opening question is both intimate and demanding. A familiar messenger speaks to a familiar community, and the Lord's claim is clear. The right answer is not merely an emotional reaction to the story. It is a life that refuses to make desire, custom, or crowd approval more authoritative than God.

The question also guards the dignity of moral correction. Lot does not treat his people as beyond recovery, and he does not make the practice a reason to abandon every person within the community. He separates the wrong from the worth of the human being who can repent. That balance is difficult, but it belongs to prophetic compassion.

A society that hears such a question should examine the atmosphere it has created. Can a person admit wrongdoing without being mocked? Can a family seek guidance without being forced to defend the community's reputation? Taqwa grows where truth can be spoken honestly and where repentance is valued more than public pride.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:162

> I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lot Establishes the Basis for Hearing Him**

Lot describes himself as a trustworthy messenger. The declaration comes after he has asked his people to fear Allah, so it explains why his warning deserves a serious hearing. He is not offering a private preference about the community's behavior. He is conveying a command entrusted to him by God.

Trustworthiness includes truth in speech, fidelity to the message, and freedom from a hidden plan to profit at the people's expense. The community knows Lot as one of its own, which gives it the chance to compare his claim with the character it has observed. It cannot dismiss the warning by inventing a motive without evidence.


Lot is both trustworthy and a messenger. The first quality concerns his integrity; the second identifies the source and scope of his duty. He is not merely a respected moral critic, and he is not a ruler claiming power over the people. He serves as an envoy of the Lord.

This distinction protects the community from two errors. It should not reject the message because Lot is human, and it should not elevate Lot into a divine figure. A true messenger directs worship and obedience to God. His personal reliability matters because it shows that he will not distort the Lord's command for his own benefit.

**A Messenger From Among the People Can Be Known**

Lot's closeness to the community is part of the moral situation. The people have seen his conduct, family life, and manner of dealing with others. They cannot say that the messenger appeared without a history. If they disagree, they must address the message rather than pretend that Lot's character is unknowable.

Familiarity, however, can be used in the opposite way. People may say that they know Lot too well to accept a special calling from him. They mistake ordinary human familiarity for evidence against revelation. A messenger's shared humanity makes his example accessible; it does not cancel the trust he carries.


A messenger who wants popularity would avoid the subject that threatens the community's pride. Lot does not do that. He speaks about conduct the people have normalized and asks them to fear God. His courage is not a desire to humiliate them. It is the cost of being faithful to a warning that could save them.

The trustworthy person tells the truth even when silence would be easier. He does not soften the command until it loses its meaning, and he does not sharpen it with insults to satisfy anger. Lot's position shows that moral clarity and compassion can inhabit the same speech.

**The Messenger Does Not Own the Message**

A false religious leader may treat a message as personal property, demanding loyalty to himself and using revelation to build an empire. Lot's wording resists that pattern. He is a messenger, which means that the truth precedes him and continues beyond him. The people must follow God, not Lot's ego.

This also means that Lot cannot bargain away the difficult part of the warning. He is not free to edit divine guidance because his audience is powerful or because rejection is painful. Trustworthiness is measured by fidelity to the Lord, not by the comfort his words create.


Lot remains a human being with fear, grief, and limited control over the people. Trustworthiness does not mean possessing every power or knowing every hidden event. It means conveying what God has given him and acting honestly within his duty.

Quran 18:110 presents the same principle for the Prophet Muhammad: human nature and revelation are not opposites. A messenger's humanity shows dependence on God, while the revelation he receives gives him an authority no personal invention could supply. Lot's people must distinguish the messenger's human form from the divine source of his call.

**A Trustworthy Warning Protects the Hearer**

The people may regard Lot's message as an intrusion into their freedom. Yet the warning is protective because it identifies a practice that has become morally destructive and asks them to return to God. Silence would leave them confident while they move toward judgment.

Trustworthy counsel often feels severe to the person who wants approval. Its value lies in the danger it reveals, not in its ability to preserve a pleasant mood. Lot's concern for his people gives the warning its human warmth; God's command gives it its binding force.


Lot has identified his role clearly. If the people reject him, they cannot claim that they misunderstood whether he was speaking for himself or for the Lord. The declaration makes their decision accountable. They may dislike the message, but they know the basis on which it is presented.

For the reader, the verse offers a standard for receiving moral guidance. Look for truthfulness, fidelity, humility, and independence from personal gain. A trustworthy messenger does not invite worship of his personality. He points beyond himself to the Lord who sent him and asks the hearer to obey God rather than desire.

The messenger's trustworthiness also protects the vulnerable from being made responsible for the powerful person's appetite. A leader who uses religion to excuse exploitation is not carrying the trust of God. Lot's warning places every person under one moral authority and refuses to let social influence decide who may be harmed.

For this reason, a trustworthy messenger can be both gentle and unyielding. He knows the hearer's weakness, but he does not rename wrongdoing as harmlessness. He offers a way back through repentance and obedience, while keeping the revealed boundary clear enough that no one can mistake compassion for approval. This clarity is part of the trust placed in him: he neither hides the command nor uses it as an excuse for cruelty.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:163

> So fear Allah, and obey me.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning Requires a Response**

Lot has identified himself as a trustworthy messenger. He now gives the response that follows from that trust: fear Allah and obey him. The command is not an invitation to admire Lot's sincerity while retaining the community's chosen practice. Trust becomes meaningful only when it produces obedience.

The order also keeps the messenger in his proper place. Fear belongs to Allah, and obedience to Lot is required because he conveys God's command. Lot is not asking the people to replace divine worship with loyalty to a human leader. He is calling them through a human voice to submit to the Lord.


The people of Lot are being confronted with a form of desire that has become public and defended. Taqwa teaches that desire is real but not sovereign. A person is not morally free merely because he wants something or because others around him approve it. He remains answerable to the One who created him and knows the consequences of his choices.

Fear of Allah does not mean despising the body or pretending that temptation never exists. It means refusing to let temptation dictate action. Taqwa gives the heart a higher loyalty than impulse and gives the community a reason to protect moral boundaries even when doing so is unpopular.

**Obedience Is More Than Private Belief**

A person may affirm that God is Lord while keeping God's command outside intimate conduct, public entertainment, or social policy. Lot's sentence refuses that division. Obedience reaches the areas people most want to reserve for themselves. Faith has consequences for the way desire is disciplined and the way a community treats those who are vulnerable.

This does not authorize intrusive policing of every private struggle. Human beings must act with justice and avoid slander. It does mean that a society cannot demand celebration of what revelation forbids and call the demand neutral. Obedience includes refusing to make sin a public virtue.


When appetite rules without restraint, the powerful may turn other people into objects. The moral issue is not only the desire itself but the way it can erase another person's dignity, consent, safety, or right to live without coercion. Lot calls his people back to a standard in which no appetite is allowed to govern without accountability.

Taqwa therefore protects both the person who must restrain himself and the person who might otherwise be used. It refuses the idea that the strong may define morality by what they can obtain. Fear of God limits desire before desire becomes a social order.

**The Messenger's Obedience Is the Pattern**

Lot does not stand outside the command he gives. He fears Allah and obeys the Lord by delivering a difficult warning. His authority is not based on claiming that he is above human moral responsibility. He is the first servant of the message he brings.

This makes prophetic obedience visible. The messenger's life should direct people toward God rather than toward a private code reserved for others. Lot's call is credible because it is a call to submission, not an opportunity for him to enjoy control over the community.


The same wording has appeared in the calls of Noah, Hūd, and Ṣāliḥ. The repetition shows that the moral center of prophecy does not change when the social problem changes. Worship God, fear Him, and obey the messenger. A community cannot declare that its custom is exempt because its temptation has a different form.

Quran 29:36 records Shuʿayb calling Midian to worship Allah, hope for the Last Day, and avoid corruption. The parallel shows how reverence for God becomes a public ethic. Fear is not an escape from society; it is what keeps society from turning desire and power into corruption.

**Obedience Does Not Mean Human Domination**

Because Lot says “obey me,” the people might imagine that he seeks personal rule. The first part of the sentence prevents that reading. Obedience is directed through him to Allah. A true messenger does not make the people dependent on his personality or claim a right to be worshipped.

The distinction is important for every community. Religious obedience must be measured by the revealed call, not by the unchecked preference of a leader. Lot's mission curbs human domination; it does not establish a new form of it.


Lot could have pronounced the people hopeless, but he calls them to fear and obey. The command is an opportunity to stop defending a harmful way of life and return to God. Warning is severe because the danger is real, yet it remains merciful while repentance is possible.

The reader should hear the sentence as more than a refrain. It asks whether divine guidance is allowed to govern desire, speech, and public pressure. Taqwa is not an abstract feeling. It is the courage to obey God when the surrounding culture insists that obedience is unnecessary.

The phrase also teaches the messenger's community how to resist coercion. If a leader commands people to praise what God forbids, refusing that command is not rebellion against truth. It is loyalty to the higher authority. Such refusal should remain principled rather than abusive, because the servant who fears Allah must not become another source of domination.

Lot's call therefore joins personal restraint with public responsibility. The person disciplines his own desire, and the community refuses to build laws, celebrations, or pressures around desire's unchecked rule. Obedience begins in the heart but becomes visible in the moral shape a people agrees to protect. It asks the community to make reverence stronger than pressure, fashion, and the fear of standing alone. A community cannot call itself obedient while punishing every person who honors God's boundary.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:164

> I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lot Denies a Financial Motive**

Lot has asked his people to fear Allah and obey him, a request that challenges a settled public practice. They could accuse him of seeking money, influence, or a position above the community. He answers that he asks no reward from them. His warning is not a transaction in which moral approval can be bought.

That independence matters because a paid advocate may be tempted to protect the interests of the person who funds him. Lot places his reward with God, so the community cannot purchase his silence or demand a softer version of the message. His concern for them is real, but it is not a strategy for personal enrichment.


Lot names God as the Lord of all worlds rather than as a tribal patron. The authority and recompense behind his mission extend beyond the people in front of him. Their approval is limited, their wealth is temporary, and their power cannot determine the value of faithful service.

This title also means that Lot's message is not an attempt to impose one family's private code on a rival group. He speaks for the Lord of every people. The community is being asked to answer to a universal Creator, not to submit to Lot because he wants to win a local dispute.

**A Messenger Can Be Compassionate Without Being Dependent**

Lot wants his people saved, and his later prayer shows how deeply their conduct troubles him. Yet love does not make him dependent on their acceptance. He can grieve their refusal without altering the command to gain their approval. His reward from God gives his compassion a stable foundation.

A leader who needs applause may confuse popularity with success. Lot's mission has another measure: faithful delivery of the truth. If the people turn back, he is grateful; if they resist, he remains responsible for warning them. The final assessment belongs to God, who knows both the messenger's motive and the hearer's response.


When a messenger asks no payment, the poor are not excluded and the wealthy cannot buy privilege. The same warning reaches the household with influence and the person with little social standing. Lot does not establish a religious market in which access to God's favor is exchanged for money.

This principle does not mean that every teacher or worker must refuse lawful support. Human services can be compensated. The messenger's declaration concerns the source of his authority and the purity of his mission. Acceptance of revelation is not a fee-based arrangement, and divine mercy is not a commodity under human control.

**The Message Cannot Be Bought Away**

A community might attempt to preserve its practice by offering Lot status, wealth, or a place within the ruling order. His statement closes that path. He cannot be bribed into silence because his true reward is not held by the people whose conduct he challenges.

This independence also exposes a common accusation. When a truthful critic refuses to flatter the powerful, the powerful may claim that he seeks influence. Lot's lack of demand makes that claim empty. The real dispute is over the authority of God's guidance, not over a benefit Lot wants to extract.


Noah, Hūd, and Ṣāliḥ made the same kind of declaration before calling their people to obedience. The repetition identifies a mark of prophetic speech: the messenger is trustworthy, independent of payment, and focused on the Lord of all worlds. Lot's mission belongs to that same line.

A community that rejects such a messenger cannot say it was confronted by a commercial scheme. The message was offered without a price, yet it still demanded a costly change in conduct. The cost was not money paid to Lot; it was pride surrendered to God.

**Reward With God Protects the Messenger's Heart**

A servant who expects the deepest reward from God can continue serving when the visible outcome is disappointing. He does not measure the worth of truth by the applause of the audience. Lot can speak with grief and firmness because his hope is not dependent on the people treating him well.

This protects against two opposite failures. The messenger does not become harsh merely because he is rejected, and he does not become silent merely because he wants to be liked. Dependence on God allows both courage and compassion to remain present.


Once Lot removes personal gain from the discussion, the people must face the warning rather than the messenger's supposed motive. They can accept God's authority or defend their practice, but they cannot fairly explain the call as a plan for Lot's enrichment.

For the reader, the verse offers a way to assess religious counsel. Ask whether the speaker directs worship to God, refuses to sell divine favor, and remains faithful when approval is withheld. Lot's reward is with the Lord of all worlds, so the community's decision cannot change the truth he was sent to convey.

The statement also protects a listener from judging guidance by the speaker's worldly circumstances. A messenger may have little wealth and no political office, yet his lack of worldly leverage can make his independence clearer. Truth is not measured by the size of the platform from which it is spoken.

Lot's refusal of payment leaves the people with a clean decision. They cannot say that he is selling them a private advantage. They must decide whether God's command is true, whether their practice can stand before Him, and whether they will exchange the safety of pride for the mercy of obedience. No payment can answer those questions for them. The messenger's lack of demand leaves the conscience face to face with revelation, without a bargain to hide behind.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:165

> Why do you ˹men˺ lust after fellow men,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lot Names the Direction of Desire**

Lot's question identifies the conduct he is challenging rather than hiding behind a vague reference to wrongdoing. The people are directing sexual desire toward men, and the prophet asks why they have chosen that direction. A question can expose a practice without pretending that the practice is too difficult to describe.

The wording also gives the community a chance to examine desire before it is defended as destiny. Lot does not ask whether desire exists. He asks what the people do with it and why they have made a forbidden object central to their public way of life. Moral responsibility begins where desire meets choice.


A society may decide that a widespread practice should be accepted because many people participate in it. Lot's question refuses that measure. Popularity cannot settle what God permits. The community must answer to the Creator who made human beings and knows the purposes and limits of their bodies.

This does not give individuals permission to act as investigators of other people's private lives. Moral seriousness must be joined to justice, privacy, and avoidance of slander. Lot is a messenger addressing a public practice and a people who have made it part of their collective conduct. His warning should not be turned into a license for personal cruelty.

**Desire Does Not Become Right Through Intensity**

The force of an appetite can make it feel authoritative. A person may reason that because a desire is strong, fulfilling it must be necessary or good. Lot's question exposes the gap between intensity and moral truth. Feelings can be real without becoming commands that God has authorized.

Taqwa gives the servant a place to stand when desire presses hard. It does not require pretending that temptation is absent. It requires recognizing that the self is not its own lawgiver. A desire must be disciplined by revelation, wisdom, and concern for the consequences imposed on oneself and others.


Quran 29:28–30 records Lot rebuking his people for male-male desire and also mentions their abuse of travelers and misconduct in public gatherings. That parallel shows that the present question belongs to a wider moral disorder. The problem is not presented as an isolated private feeling but as part of a community's public conduct.

The parallel also explains why Lot's warning carries social urgency. When a practice is reinforced by intimidation, public celebration, or harm to outsiders, it affects more than the people who choose it. A community has to examine the culture it creates around desire and power.


The verse condemns a practice without instructing believers to treat every person associated with it as worthless. A sinner remains a human being who can repent and whose basic rights must not be violated. Lot's role is to warn and invite return, not to authorize humiliation or violence.

This distinction is essential because moral correction can be corrupted by hatred. A person who despises a forbidden act may still behave unjustly toward the one who commits it. Fear of Allah requires the critic to obey God's limits while calling others back to them.


Lot speaks to men as a group because the conduct has become a defining part of the society he addresses. A private struggle can be met with counsel and repentance; a public order that pressures people to accept wrongdoing requires a public warning. The prophet challenges the standard the community is building around desire.

A culture can make resistance difficult by mocking those who refuse, excluding families who seek guidance, or teaching the young that restraint is shameful. Lot's question interrupts that formation. It tells the people that a society does not have the right to redefine God's command simply because it has organized itself around disobedience.

**The Question Restores Created Purpose**

The phrase “fellow men” is set against the created order referenced in the following line. Lot's argument is not that men lack dignity or that women are objects. It is that sexual desire has been directed away from the marital purpose God created and toward a practice the revelation condemns.

The question therefore joins bodily creation to moral responsibility. Human beings are not self-invented creatures free to assign every desire its own purpose. They receive life, body, and capacity from God, and they must ask how those gifts are to be used with justice and restraint.

**A Messenger Challenges the Community's Self-Description**

The people may describe themselves as liberated, advanced, or merely following their nature. Lot's question refuses to let a slogan settle the matter. It asks them to compare their chosen practice with God's guidance and with the harms already connected to their public behavior.

A community may become so used to a sin that naming it sounds like hostility. The hostility, however, is not in the clear warning. It lies in the refusal to allow any authority above the community's appetite. Lot speaks because a people needs more than self-description; it needs truthful judgment.


The verse is not a command to search for scandal in strangers. It is a prophetic challenge to a society that has normalized a forbidden sexual practice and connected it with wider corruption. The reader should take the moral claim seriously without inventing permissions for gossip, abuse, or vigilantism.

Lot's question asks whether desire will rule the people or whether the people will fear God. The answer requires repentance, restraint, and protection of human dignity under divine law. A clear moral boundary can be held without abandoning compassion for those who need guidance.

The question also prevents the community from hiding behind silence. If everyone knows what is being practiced and no one may name it, the absence of criticism becomes a false sign of peace. Lot breaks that silence so that desire can be judged by revelation rather than by the comfort of the crowd.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:166

> leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you? In fact, you are a transgressing people.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Identifies What Is Being Abandoned**

Lot continues by pointing to the wives God has created for the people. His argument is not a statement that women exist merely to satisfy men. It is a reminder that God created a lawful marital path for sexual intimacy, family life, and mutual responsibility, yet the community is turning away from that path toward what revelation forbids.

The verb leaving exposes deliberate refusal. The people are not being described as lacking any lawful relation or as unable to understand the created order. They are choosing to abandon an authorized channel while pursuing another. Lot asks them to see the moral direction of that choice rather than treating it as a neutral preference.


Speaking of wives as created by the Lord does not reduce women to instruments. A marriage governed by God includes rights, duties, affection, protection, and accountability. The lawful path cannot be used to excuse coercion, betrayal, or abuse. Lot's contrast is about the moral framework of sexuality, not a permission for men to treat women as possessions.

A person who invokes marriage while violating a spouse's dignity has not honored the created order. The same God who establishes lawful intimacy commands justice. Moral teaching is coherent only when it protects the human beings within the institution it praises.


Exegetes have discussed the scope of the two verses. Some read the first line as a direct condemnation of male-male sexual acts and the second as a statement that the men avoid women; others consider whether the wording includes forms of the practice involving both men and women. The immediate contrast with wives gives the passage its central direction: the people have rejected the lawful marital path in favor of a forbidden one.

That contextual reading is stronger for this verse because Lot's question is structured around what the people leave and what they pursue. The point is not to settle every possible detail of their private conduct. It is to expose a community's deliberate reversal of the sexual order revealed by God.

**The People Are Called Transgressors**

Lot does not describe the conduct as an innocent variation that becomes right through social approval. He calls the people transgressors, meaning that they have crossed a boundary. The term places their behavior within a larger pattern of refusing God's limits, not merely within a debate over taste.

Transgression also includes the social harms described in the parallel account. Quran 29:29 associates the people with abuse of travelers and public immorality alongside their sexual wrongdoing. That context shows why the community's condition is not a private matter detached from justice. A people that celebrates desire while violating others has crossed several boundaries at once.


Calling a people transgressors does not erase their human status. The warning leaves room for repentance, and the messenger's concern shows that he wants them rescued rather than humiliated. A believer can say that an act is forbidden while refusing to mock, assault, expose, or dehumanize the person who commits it.

This discipline is especially important when a society is polarized. Moral truth should not be weakened to avoid offense, but the delivery of truth must not become an excuse for cruelty. Lot's sentence is severe because the matter is severe, yet its purpose is to stop the community and return it to God.


The mention of wives can also remind the reader that lawful sexuality is not only about a permitted object. Marriage carries obligations toward another person. It requires consent, faithfulness, care, and responsibility for consequences. A person cannot claim to honor God's design while using a spouse for appetite and neglecting her rights.

That broader responsibility keeps the verse from being reduced to a slogan. The lawful path is morally meaningful because it is ordered, relational, and accountable. Lot challenges the people to leave transgression, not simply to exchange one form of selfishness for another.

**The Community Has Made Reversal a Public Identity**

Lot addresses a people, not merely an isolated offender, because the conduct has been woven into its public life. The community's identity is being built around what it refuses to restrain. When wrongdoing becomes a badge of belonging, the pressure on individuals grows and the need for a prophetic warning becomes more urgent.

A person who recognizes the wrong but fears the crowd may need protection and patient counsel. A leader who celebrates the wrong bears a different responsibility. Divine judgment distinguishes among people, but the collective culture still matters because it can make repentance difficult and transgression attractive.

**The Verse Connects Desire to Accountability**

Desire is not self-justifying. The Lord who created the body also sets its boundaries and knows what will preserve dignity and life. Leaving God's guidance for an appetite does not create freedom; it places the person under the appetite's rule and under the judgment of the One whose command was rejected.

Lot's words therefore call for a return to ordered freedom. The people can repent, restore justice, and refuse to let public approval define good and evil. The warning is not meant to produce despair. It is meant to make transgression visible before the consequence becomes unavoidable.


A reader should not soften the verse into a claim that nothing is forbidden. Nor should he use the verse as a warrant for personal abuse. The text calls the practice transgression and calls the people back to God; it does not transfer divine judgment to every angry individual.

The faithful response is principled restraint: uphold the revealed boundary, protect people from harm, avoid slander, and leave repentance open. Lot's warning is strongest when it is carried with the same moral seriousness it demands from the people—submission to God rather than indulgence of one's own anger.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:167

> They threatened, “If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be expelled.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Community Answers Correction With Threat**

Lot has warned his people about a practice they have made part of their public life. Instead of answering the moral claim, they threaten him with expulsion. Their response reveals how a society protects wrongdoing: it treats the person who names the harm as the danger and seeks to remove him from the community.

The threat is not an argument. It is an attempt to make the cost of truth so high that Lot will become silent. A people confident in its conduct should be able to answer a warning with reasons. The resort to exile shows that the community's confidence is more fragile than its public posture suggests.


To threaten removal is to say that belonging depends on agreement with the dominant practice. The people are not merely rejecting Lot's theology; they are trying to control who may remain among them. Exile becomes a warning to everyone else: speak as Lot speaks, and you too may lose home, family ties, and safety.

Such pressure can be more powerful than a direct blow. It makes neighbors police one another and persuades the uncertain to remain quiet. A community can claim to value freedom while denying it to the person who refuses its moral demands. Lot's threat exposes that contradiction.

**The Messenger's Place Is Not Granted by the Crowd**

Lot belongs to the community by human relation, but his mission comes from God. The people may control access to their town, yet they cannot decide whether God's command is true by voting on it. Their threat can endanger Lot's worldly residence, but it cannot cancel his status as a messenger.

This distinction gives courage to anyone who loses social approval for obeying God. Belonging to a place is valuable, and expulsion is painful, but no community is the final owner of a servant's conscience. The believer seeks to remain just and peaceful, yet he cannot purchase membership by surrendering truth.


The people behave as if Lot's warning is the shameful act and their practice is the norm that must be protected. Their response reverses the moral positions. Instead of examining themselves, they label the corrector intolerable. This is a common feature of entrenched wrongdoing: correction is experienced as aggression because it threatens comfort.

The Qur'an does not ask the reader to accept every accusation made by a dissenter. Truthful correction requires knowledge, wisdom, and justice. In Lot's case, the surrounding verses establish his trustworthiness and the revealed nature of his warning. The threat therefore confirms resistance; it does not establish the people's innocence.


Quran 7:82 records Lot's people responding to his warning by saying that they should be expelled from the town. That parallel confirms that expulsion was not an isolated metaphor but a stated social response to Lot's moral opposition.

The repetition across the accounts shows the cost of challenging a community's identity. When wrongdoing becomes a badge of belonging, the people may prefer to remove the truthful person rather than reconsider the practice. Lot's faithfulness is tested not only by the content of his warning but by the pressure to leave.

**A Threat Cannot Make Wrongdoing Right**

A community may have the power to remove a person, but power does not create moral legitimacy. If a crowd threatens the messenger, the truth of the message must still be judged by God. The threatened person should not answer oppression by becoming oppressive, but he should not call the threat justice simply because it is popular.

This principle applies beyond religious dispute. Institutions sometimes protect their reputation by expelling whistleblowers, critics, or victims who name abuse. The act of exclusion can hide a problem for a time, but it does not repair it. Lot's story warns against confusing silence with peace.


A healthy community can survive correction because its identity is not built on denial. It may disagree with a messenger while preserving room for honest examination. Lot's people have made belonging conditional on moral surrender, so their community becomes a cage rather than a source of mutual protection.

The threat asks the reader what kind of belonging he wants. Shared place and custom are valuable, but they must remain under God's authority. A community that demands disobedience as the price of membership is asking for loyalty that no servant can rightly give.

**Lot's Warning Has Already Changed the Balance**

The people threaten expulsion because Lot's words have exposed a vulnerability. They cannot silence the question by answering it, so they try to remove its speaker. The threat is evidence that the warning has reached the social structure, not proof that the warning failed.

A truthful word may appear weak when the powerful can punish its speaker. Yet it can continue to work in the conscience of those who hear it. Lot remains responsible for speaking faithfully; God remains responsible for judging the people who threaten him. No expulsion can erase that accountability.


The verse does not command every person to seek conflict or abandon lawful social ties. It teaches that belonging cannot be purchased through surrender of God's command. A wise servant speaks with patience, uses lawful means, and protects others, but he does not accept exile as proof that falsehood has become true.

Lot's people threaten him; the reader is asked not to become one of those who make truth homeless. Make room for correction, distinguish the person from the wrongdoing without approving the wrongdoing, and remember that the Lord's judgment is higher than the crowd's decree.

A community that expels every honest critic eventually loses the ability to correct itself. It may keep its outward unity, but its unity becomes the silence of fear. Lot's threatened removal shows that moral health requires room for a truthful voice, even when that voice unsettles the majority.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:168

> Lot responded, “I am truly one of those who despise your ˹shameful˺ practice.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lot Clarifies What He Rejects**

Lot responds to the threat by identifying himself among those who despise the practice. His words do not conceal his moral position to preserve his place in the community. He refuses to pretend that the conduct is acceptable when revelation has condemned it and when its public form is tied to wider corruption.

The object of his rejection is the practice, not a claim that every person involved has lost all human worth. That distinction matters. A messenger can condemn an act clearly while still wanting the people to repent. Lot's position is not indifference to the people; it is refusal to approve what is destroying them.


The word conveys strong moral revulsion. It should not be weakened into polite approval, because Lot is warning about a serious transgression. Yet moral revulsion must remain under God's law. It cannot become permission to insult, assault, expose, or deny basic justice to a person.

A believer may despise a sin and still hope for the sinner's return. This is the balance Lot embodies. He does not join the community's practice, but he also does not respond to its threat by inventing a private license for revenge. His anger is governed by revelation rather than by wounded pride.

**The Messenger Will Not Bargain Away Truth**

The people have offered Lot a choice between silence and expulsion. His reply shows that the threat has not made him uncertain about the command. He will not call shameful what God has forbidden merely to preserve social comfort.

This is an important test of prophetic integrity. A messenger who changes his moral judgment whenever the crowd threatens him is not trustworthy. Lot's firmness does not arise from confidence in his own strength. It arises from knowing that the Lord's approval matters more than the community's permission to remain.


Quran 29:28–30 describes Lot's rebuke of the men and also mentions their abuse of travelers and misconduct in their gatherings. That parallel helps explain why Lot's detestation reaches beyond a private preference. He is confronting a public culture in which sexual wrongdoing, aggression, and communal celebration of immorality reinforce one another.

The wider setting does not justify treating every individual as identical. It does show why a prophet must address the community's norms rather than only isolated acts. When a practice is protected by threats and imposed as a social ideal, silence would leave the vulnerable without a truthful defense.


Some people assume that compassion requires avoiding clear words. Lot shows otherwise. He speaks plainly because ambiguity would strengthen the community's self-deception. Compassion tells the truth about danger so that people can leave it; it does not rename the danger as harmless.

At the same time, clarity should not be used to enjoy another person's shame. Lot's words are directed toward correction and separation from wrongdoing. The believer must guard his own heart while speaking, because pride can imitate moral courage and turn hatred of sin into hatred of people.


The people threaten to expel him as if his objection were the offense. Lot refuses that inversion. He will not accept the idea that the person who warns is more blameworthy than the practice being warned against. His reply restores the proper order: wrongdoing is wrong even when a powerful group protects it.

This restoration is especially important where public language has been captured by the dominant culture. Words such as tolerance, freedom, or normality can be used to silence any appeal to revelation. Lot's response shows that a servant may respect people while rejecting the moral vocabulary used to defend disobedience.

**Detestation Must Be Joined to Personal Obedience**

Lot does not merely denounce the community while exempting himself from moral discipline. He stands among those who reject the practice, which means his position begins with his own obedience. A person cannot condemn an act in others while secretly cultivating the same disregard for God in his own life.

This is why prophetic warning has credibility. The messenger's disgust is not a performance to gain power. It is the public expression of a submission he practices himself. He does not ask the people to accept a burden that he refuses to carry.

**A Strong Reply to a Threat**

Lot's sentence is firm but not boastful. He does not claim that he can defeat the entire community by his own ability. He identifies where he stands and leaves the final judgment to God. Moral courage does not require theatrical anger; it requires steady refusal to call wrong right.

The believer can learn from that steadiness. When pressured to praise what God forbids, answer with truth without adding injustice. Do not bargain away conviction, and do not let the enemy's threat make you adopt the enemy's cruelty.


Lot despises the shameful practice, but the existence of a condemned act does not mean repentance is impossible. The prophetic call remains meaningful because people can stop, confess, and return. A society should not protect wrongdoing, yet it should not close the door of repentance for those who seek it.

That is the difference between moral opposition and dehumanization. Opposition says the act must end and the person must answer before God. Dehumanization says the person has no capacity for good and may be treated without justice. Lot's response supports the first and rejects the second.

His words also show that moral opposition can be sorrowful rather than triumphant. He does not relish being separated from his people or seek the humiliation of those he corrects. He detests the practice because it harms their relationship with God, and he continues to speak in the hope that the people will abandon it.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:169

> My Lord! Save me and my family from ˹the consequences of˺ what they do.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lot Turns to God After the Threat**

The people have rejected his warning and threatened to expel him. Lot responds not by boasting of his own power but by calling on his Lord to save him and his family. The prayer shows where a messenger places ultimate dependence when a community becomes hostile: with God, who can protect beyond the reach of social pressure.

This is not an escape from responsibility. Lot has spoken clearly and resisted the practice. Prayer follows faithful action; it does not replace it. He seeks God's help after doing what a messenger must do, acknowledging that the outcome is beyond his control.


Lot asks for himself and his family. The request recognizes that communal corruption can place households under pressure. A person may reject wrongdoing while relatives, neighbors, or dependents remain exposed to its consequences. Salvation is sought as a shared protection, not as a private badge of superiority.

The wording also leaves room for divine judgment within the family. The request does not mean that biological relation automatically saves everyone. A family member's loyalty to truth and response to God's command still matter. The verse holds together the tenderness of family concern and the seriousness of individual accountability.

**Saving Means Rescue From the Consequences**

The translation makes clear that Lot seeks rescue from what the people do. Their practice is not simply a private disagreement that leaves everyone untouched. It has consequences for the community, for outsiders, and for anyone who refuses to participate. Lot asks God to separate him and his household from the harm generated by that order.

This separation is not contempt for the human beings around him. It is protection from complicity and punishment. A believer may love people while refusing to remain inside a system that demands participation in wrongdoing. Lot's prayer gives language to that difficult need for moral distance.


Quran 29:30 records Lot asking God for help against the people of corruption. The parallel confirms that his response to the community is supplication, not personal revenge. He names the corruption and seeks divine aid because only God can deliver him from a people determined to persist.

The prayer also keeps the messenger from imagining that moral clarity makes him self-sufficient. Lot knows the truth, but he still needs God's protection. Correct belief does not remove vulnerability; it teaches the servant where to take vulnerability.


Lot's concern for his family is natural and honorable, but it is not a request that God overlook wrongdoing for the sake of blood ties. The Qur'anic stories repeatedly separate biological connection from faithfulness. A family is protected by obedience, not by lineage alone.

This principle prevents the prayer from becoming a defense of nepotism. Lot asks for those who belong with him in the path of truth, while divine judgment remains free to distinguish among them. Love does not ask God to call corruption good simply because it occurs within one's household.

**The Prayer Recognizes the Limits of Human Control**

Lot cannot persuade everyone, reform every institution, or force the people to accept the warning. His prayer accepts that limitation without surrendering the truth. The servant speaks, resists, and then asks God to act where human ability ends.

That pattern protects against two errors. One person may rely only on activism and forget prayer; another may pray while refusing to take any truthful stand. Lot's example joins both duties. He confronts the wrongdoing and turns to God for rescue from its consequences.


When a society threatens to expel the messenger, the danger extends beyond his own body. Family members may lose shelter, status, or safety because of his faithfulness. Lot's prayer acknowledges the cost without asking him to compromise. He seeks a path in which the household is preserved without joining the community's wrongdoing.

The believer should also protect family members from harm without teaching them that safety requires moral surrender. A household can be patient, discreet, and wise while remaining clear about what God forbids. Protection is strongest when it includes spiritual integrity rather than only physical escape.

**The Prayer Is Hope, Not Despair**

Lot does not say that the people are beyond God's power. He asks God to save him, which implies trust that deliverance is possible even when the community appears dominant. The prayer turns fear into dependence and danger into an occasion for worship.

Hope does not require knowing exactly how rescue will occur. It requires confidence that God sees the situation and can judge it rightly. Lot's prayer is a model for the servant who has done what he can and now places the hidden outcome with the Lord.


Lot's supplication comes after the threat, but its lesson should be learned earlier. A household should cultivate prayer, truthfulness, and mutual protection before pressure becomes unbearable. Then, when danger comes, turning to God is not a new performance but the continuation of a practiced relationship.

The verse asks the reader to distinguish between saving a family from consequences and hiding a family's wrongdoing. The first is mercy; the second is complicity. Lot seeks the Lord's protection while remaining opposed to the practice that brought the danger. That is the shape of faithful concern.

A household may therefore need to make difficult decisions about proximity, support, and safety. Those decisions should be guided by justice rather than panic. Protect the innocent, avoid participating in wrongdoing, and keep the possibility of repentance open. Lot's prayer is not an escape from moral duty; it is a request that God preserve a faithful path through a corrupt environment.

It also teaches that rescue is ultimately God's gift. Careful planning and family solidarity matter, but neither can control the final outcome. The servant does what truth requires and asks the Lord to separate him from the consequences of a people that refuses correction. Dependence on God gives courage without turning fear into despair.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:170

> So We saved him and all of his family,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Deliverance Answers Lot's Prayer**

Lot asked God to save him and his family from the consequences of the community's conduct. This verse records the answer: God delivered him and his family together. The rescue is not presented as the result of Lot's political power or the community's sudden reform. It is a divine act that separates the faithful household from a society committed to its corruption.

The answer also confirms that prayer and action belong together. Lot warned the people, refused their practice, and turned to God for protection. Divine deliverance does not make his earlier courage unnecessary. It shows that the servant's efforts are held within a power greater than the hostility around him.


The phrase all of his family expresses the tenderness of the rescue. Lot's concern for his household was not ignored. Yet the wording must not be turned into a rule that ancestry guarantees safety. The following verse makes clear that one family member is excluded from the saving group. Belonging is ultimately moral and spiritual, not merely biological.

This distinction protects the meaning of family prayer. A believer should care for relatives, warn them, and seek their safety, but cannot compel their hearts or claim God's forgiveness on their behalf. Love asks for rescue; God judges each person's response to His command.

**Deliverance Creates Separation From Corruption**

Lot's family is saved by being removed from the environment that has become hostile to God's guidance. Separation here is not an expression of superiority. It is protection from participation in a public evil and from the judgment that will overtake the people who persist in it.

A believer may need distance from a corrupt institution, gathering, or social pressure in order to preserve obedience. Such distance should be taken with wisdom and without contempt. Lot does not leave because his family is inherently better; he leaves because the community has chosen a path that cannot be shared by those who fear God.


God saves a family together, showing that faith can shape a household's common direction. Shared worship and mutual protection make endurance easier. A family can encourage truth when the surrounding society mocks it and can preserve the vulnerable when public norms become dangerous.

At the same time, the household is not a substitute for individual faith. Each member must respond to God. The rescue of the family is a mercy to people who stand with Lot, not a declaration that every relative is safe regardless of conduct.

**A Parallel Confirms the Pattern**

Quran 7:83 likewise states that God saved Lot and his family except his wife, who was among the doomed. The parallel confirms that the present verse emphasizes a real act of deliverance while the next verse will qualify the household's membership in that deliverance.

The repetition across the accounts also shows that rescue is part of the prophetic pattern. God does not only punish the rejecting community. He preserves those who respond to the warning, even when their numbers are small and their social position is weak.


Lot's family may be surrounded by a powerful majority, but the majority cannot determine whether God will save them. A household can appear isolated and still be held within divine care. The measure is not social strength; it is fidelity to the Lord.

This gives courage to believers who feel outnumbered. They should not mistake loneliness for abandonment or popularity for safety. God's deliverance may be hidden until the moment He chooses, but His knowledge of the faithful is not weakened by the crowd's hostility.

**The Saved Household Has a Duty After Rescue**

Deliverance is not merely escape from danger. It creates a responsibility to remember what was saved from and to live differently afterward. A family rescued from corruption should not carry the old order into its new place. It must preserve prayer, honesty, and concern for those who remain vulnerable.

The household also learns that safety belongs to God. It should not boast over those who were destroyed, because the same Lord who saved it judges every person with complete knowledge. Gratitude is the proper response to deliverance, not pride in being selected.


The people threatened to expel Lot, as if they owned the land and could define his future. God answers that threat by taking responsibility for the messenger and his household. The community can remove them from its social order, but it cannot prevent the Lord from giving them a place of safety.

This does not promise that every faithful person will avoid worldly loss. Lot's rescue is a specific act in a revealed story. It does teach that worldly exclusion is not the final judgment. The servant may lose a place among people and still be preserved by God in a way the powerful cannot control.


The verse stands immediately before the account of exclusion within Lot's household and the destruction of the rest. It keeps the reader from seeing judgment as the only divine action. The same Lord who punishes persistent corruption also makes a way out for those who turn to Him.

Lot's prayer has been answered, but the answer is more precise than he might have imagined. God saves the family as a faithful group while leaving hidden allegiance to Him as the decisive measure. The verse therefore invites gratitude and careful humility: seek the Lord's deliverance, and remain faithful to the conditions of it.

The rescued family also becomes a witness that obedience is not wasted when a society rejects it. Their safety may not look like worldly triumph, but it is a deeper preservation. God removes them from the reach of a culture that threatened to make corruption unavoidable and gives them the chance to continue under His care.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:171

> except an old woman, who was one of the doomed.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Family Relation Does Not Guarantee Salvation**

The previous verse said that Lot and his family were saved; this verse identifies an exception. An old woman from his household is counted among those doomed. The distinction is essential. Divine rescue is not distributed by bloodline alone. A person may live in the home of a prophet and still choose the side of the community that rejects God.

The verse keeps family affection from becoming a false assurance. Lot loved his household and prayed for its protection, but God's judgment remained based on faithfulness and response. The saved group is defined by allegiance to truth, not by a name shared with the messenger.


The woman's old age is mentioned without turning age into an excuse. Human beings deserve care when they are weak or elderly, but age does not make deliberate opposition to God righteous. Vulnerability calls for compassion in human dealings; it does not erase the moral account before God.

This balance prevents two errors. A society must not neglect the elderly because they are weak, and a family must not assume that an elder's position makes every choice beyond question. God knows the circumstances, intentions, and degree of responsibility of each person more fully than any human observer.

**A Household Can Contain Different Allegiances**

Lot's family is not morally uniform simply because it shares a home. One household can contain people who encourage faith and another who identifies with the surrounding culture. The verse teaches the reader to distinguish domestic proximity from spiritual solidarity.

That distinction can be painful. A believer may pray for relatives who do not share his commitment, warn them with wisdom, and still be unable to bring them to faith. Love remains real, but it must not become an argument against God's justice. The Lord does not wrong a person by judging the choice that person knowingly makes.


Quran 7:83 repeats that God saved Lot and his family except his wife, who was among the doomed. Quran 11:81 likewise says that the wife would suffer the fate of the others. These parallels confirm the moral point without requiring later stories to supply details absent from this verse.

The repetition also shows that the exception is not an incidental family dispute. It belongs to the revealed account of how divine rescue distinguishes faith from outward association. The household is mentioned together, but judgment remains attentive to each member's allegiance.

**The Exception Protects the Meaning of Prophetic Kinship**

A messenger's relative is not saved by proximity to the messenger. If kinship guaranteed salvation, people could treat faith as inherited privilege and ignore their own conduct. The exception prevents that distortion. Lot's mission points the family to God, but it cannot substitute for their response.

This also protects prophets from being treated as owners of divine mercy. Lot cannot command God to save someone who has chosen the opposing side. He is a servant who prays and warns, while the Lord decides with perfect knowledge.


The woman's age may make the exception especially sobering. A long life can create a deep attachment to a community's customs, and years of proximity to a prophet do not automatically produce obedience. Time spent near truth is an opportunity, not a guarantee that truth has been accepted.

The verse therefore asks the reader to examine not only how long he has lived or how close he has been to religious people, but what he has chosen. Familiarity with sacred language can coexist with resistance in the heart. Salvation requires more than environment; it requires sincere submission.

**Divine Judgment Is More Precise Than Human Labels**

Human beings often judge by family name, age, reputation, or public role. God's judgment can distinguish what those labels conceal. The exception warns against assuming that every member of a group shares one moral status, while also warning against denying the reality of collective choices.

This precision should make the believer humble. He may recognize the outward direction of a community, but he should not claim to know every person's hidden account. He can oppose public wrongdoing and protect people from harm while leaving final judgment to God.


The verse is severe, but it does not say that a relative of a prophet was doomed merely because she belonged to a certain family. The decisive issue is allegiance. That means repentance remains meaningful for anyone who turns to God before death and judgment.

A person who has inherited a corrupt identity can leave it. A household member who has resisted guidance can return. The warning is against relying on association, not against seeking mercy. God's justice is exact, and His mercy remains open to the one who sincerely changes.


Lot's household could not be protected by sentiment alone. Faithful love tells the truth, seeks rescue, and accepts that God judges each person. It does not conceal an ally's wrongdoing to preserve the appearance of family unity.

For the reader, the verse makes a difficult demand: love relatives deeply, but do not make relatives an authority above God. Encourage them, protect them from injustice, and invite them to repent. Yet trust the Lord's judgment when outward kinship and inward allegiance diverge.

The exception also warns against measuring faith by access to sacred company. Someone may hear a prophet daily, live near a righteous family, and still nurture loyalty to the people who oppose God. Proximity gives opportunity for belief, but it cannot perform belief on another person's behalf.

This is why the verse should produce self-examination rather than speculation about others. Ask whether personal attachments are making God's command easier to obey or easier to evade. Family affection is honorable when it leads toward truth; it becomes a barrier when it asks truth to yield to attachment.

---

## Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:172

> Then We utterly destroyed the rest,

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Remaining Community Faces Judgment**

After Lot and the faithful household are delivered, the verse turns to the rest of the people. They are utterly destroyed. The contrast is deliberate: the community that threatened the messenger is not allowed to define the outcome, while those who followed God are preserved by His command.

The destruction is not presented as a private victory for Lot or as the result of his personal strength. It belongs to God. Lot warned, prayed, and remained separate from the wrongdoing, but the Lord alone carried out the judgment. The verse keeps divine authority at the center.


The phrase does not simply mean everyone who was still physically present. It refers to those left outside the saving group because of their rejection and corruption. Divine judgment separates people according to allegiance, not according to wealth, age, social rank, or the confidence with which they defended themselves.

That separation may be invisible before the judgment arrives. A crowd can look united while some people have already chosen truth and others have chosen resistance. The rescue and destruction reveal a distinction that God knew all along. Human beings should therefore be humble about appearances and serious about their own response.

**Utter Destruction Is Divine Judgment, Not Human License**

The severity of the verse can tempt a reader to imagine that later people may pronounce the same verdict on their enemies. That would exceed human authority. The Qur'an discloses this judgment as God's act after the community's persistent rejection and corruption. Human beings may resist evil and establish justice, but they do not possess the complete knowledge required for God's final sentence.

This distinction is a safeguard against cruelty. The believer learns fear of God from the destruction, not pleasure in another people's ruin. The event should make him cautious with power and eager to prevent wrongdoing before judgment reaches its end.


Quran 29:32 records that the angels knew who was in Lot's city and would save him and his family while the wife was among the doomed. That parallel shows that the division is deliberate and known to God. It is not a confused disaster that happens to catch some people and miss others.
